The other day we remarked to one of these ani- mated apothecary shops:" An idea struck us yesterday" ' CLOOD COMPLEXION —and before we could finish he advised us, "Rub the affected parts with arnica." "All the new-born child wants is warmth and nourish- aOOD COMPLEXION reent," says an authority, but if you should judge by k-A the noiee it makes during the first three weeks of its GOOD existence VOU would say that it wanted the whole earth, COMPLEXION with a set, of the " Encyclopeedia Britannica " thrown in I for a premium. i To some military gentleman who was appoint GOOD COMPLEXION ; governor of one of our islands in the West Indies, and ; who expressed his apprehensions of not being able to discharge his duty as chancellor of his province, Lord Mansfield gmve him this advice :—" Always decide, and never give reasons for your decision. You will in general decide well, yet give very bad reasons for your judg- ment." Texas man: "You must not expect the same amount of energy in Texas as you have in Nebraska. Remember that Texas is in a very warm climate, and people are obliged to move slowly." Omaha man: "I have been There, and I have seen Texas men move across a room faster than ever they do in Nebraska." "Eh! Was there an earthquake going on ?" "No; the crowd had been invited up to drink." Young wife: Oh, Mr. Jones, I'm so sorry Tom brought you home to dinner to-day. If he had told me you were coming, I'd have had something nice, and I haven't a thing in the house fit to eat." Mr. Jones; " Now, please, don't say a word about it, my dear madam. You needn't worry yourself a particle. I take most of my meals at home myself." An aged musician with a violin under his arm walked into a cafe. A stout gentleman told him to begin. The poor fellow did not move. At last he produced his violin, and showed that it had no strings. The astonished gentle- man asked why on earth he carried such a thing about with him. "Alas, sir," replied the philosophical beggar, " it is not an instrument, it is only a threat." "What sort of a watch is this?" asked a gentleman, picking up a curious old timepiece in the shop of a dealer in curiosities. "That," replied the dealer, "is a real curiosity. It is a watch that belonged to Alexander the Great when he died on the barren island of St. Helena." "The deuce it is! Why, man alive, in the days of Alex- ander the Great there were no such things as watches." "That's just what makes it such a rarity." "And Alexander the Great didn't die at St. Helena." "He didn't, eh ? Well, that makes it a still greater curiosity." And taking up the rare relic, the dealer locked it up in his burglar-proof safe." The following experience of a Mississippi lawyer was related by himself to the writer many years ago. Ile said :—" I was defending a prisoner for horsestealing, and seeing no other means of defending him, under the circumstances, I set up a plea of insanity. I argued it at length, read many extracts from works on medical jurisprudence, and had the patient attention of the court. The prosecuting attorney did not attempt to reply to my argument or -controvert my authorities' I seemed to have things my own way, and whispered to the prisoner that he needn't be uneasy. Then came the Judge's charge, in which he reminded the jury' that there was no dispute between counsel as to the facts of the case. Indeed, there could not have been, for several witnesses swore positively that they saw my client steal the horse. • But,' continued the Court, 'the plea of insanity has been set up, and I charge you, gentlemen of the jury, that it should receive your very grave and serious deliberation; but I must be allowed to say, gentlemen, that for myself, upon a review of the whole case, I can discover no evidence ofeinsanity on the part of the prisoner, except, . perhaps, in the selection of his counsel.'" TEE SCIENTIFIC ASPECTi OF WATER—In a lecture on 46 Water," Professor Smithells, of the Yorkshire College, dwelt upon the difference between pure and impure water. A sample of what people called pure water was far from being pure. The difference between pure and impure water was evident to the eye alone when seen in large quantities. If they converted a quantity of water into steam they would find that a certain amount ot solid substance adhered to the sides of the vessel in which it was boiled. On boiling ordinary water by far the most of its substance disappeared in steam; but there was left a residue of soul matter, which existed in different waters in a greater or lesser degree, but in rain water least of all. Pure water could be entirely ' converted into steam, and left no isolid matter. The boiling of water left the solids behind, and thus afforded means of preparing perfectly pure • water from that which was far from being pure. Distilled water was most unpalatable, owing to the absence of sends and gases. In passing through the air, in its descent, rain gathered and dissolved some of the air, which was found to exist in the proportion of 18 gallons of air to a thousand of water. If water did not contain those 18 gallons °flair, marine life would not be possible. On reaching the earth and coursing over it in streams, the water came into contact with the solid constituents of the earth's crust. For the most part the substances of which the latter was composed were not soluble in water, but there were certain substances • which were dissolved. The most important solid sub- stances in natural water a ere known as common salt, chalk, gypsum, magnesium, and ammonia and its com- pounds. It was self-evident how salt and gypsum, and such substances, got into Mater; but chalk was not soluble in water unless the latter contained a certain amount of carbonic acid gas. This gas was to be found L ail natural water, but in some a great deal more than others. Lime was a desirable constituent of water. Water containing lime was not only a drink but a food, on account of its bone-forming capacity. Ammonia was another important constituent of wafer. The lecturer then proceeded to show that water was in reality a chemical compound of the two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, and illustrated his assertion by means of a num- ber of experiments. A barrister in a court of justice, examining a woman as a witness, said, "Facts are stubborn things." Witness: "Yes, sir, and so are women; and if you get anything out of me just let me know it." garrister : "You'll be committed for contempt." Witness: "Very well, I'll suffer justly, for I feel the utmost contempt for every lawyer present." • A travelling sleight-of-hand man visited an Indian encampment, near Lewiston, Idaho, the other day. 'See- ing a small dog, he asked how much they would take for him. The Indians said that they didn't want to sell. "him very good dog," said the magician, rubbing him down the back, at each stroke taking a handful of money from the end of his tail, also from his mouth' ears, and nose. The Indians looked on in stolid silence, but after the magician went away. they took the dog down to the river bank and killed and dissected him. To their great chagrin they found that the sleight-of- hand man had drained him of all the money. A MODERN SOLOMON.—At a trial which took place in German court of law the other day, M. Chevreul's re- searches into the law of colours enabled the jury to arrive at a decision in the face of some very conflicting evidence. A man employed in a manufactory at Dresden had let a hammer slip out of his hinds and had seriously injured one of his fellbw-workmen in the region of the left eye. The wound was at once_dressed by a surgeon, and after a time all traces of it had disappeared. The man maintained, however, that he had lost the use of the eyetand demanded compensation. But his employer, assured by the surgeon that his eye was uninjured, re- fused to meet his claim, and an action was accordingly brought. Although several medical men asserted that they could discover nothing wrong with the man's eye, he stuck to his statement, and the jury would have been I very much puzzled to decide had not one of the experts hit upon the following test :—FIe handed the plaintiff a pair of spectacles, the glass for the right eve being red and that for the left eye ordinary white. He then asked him to read through them some words which he had written with a green lead pencil upon a black screen. The plaintiff unsuspicionsly read them out, whereupon the expert pointed out that he must be able to see per- fectly with his left eye, as the red glass in the right eye of the spectacles would turn the green letters into black and make them invisible upon a black ground. The test was conclusive, and the plaintiff, who thought this a very unsportsmanlike proceeding, nonsuited with costs CANDOUR went WORKING-MEN.—Whatever we may ' have to say to the working-classes' the spirit is likely to be as important as the matter. It is a thing of course that politicians, having respect to the recompense of re- ward, will flatter and fawn upon those who hold so large a mass of pelitiCl4 ;l9Wer ; but more sense and more self- respect mtght fairly have 'Wit fnectedo Man.; of the persons, themselves altogether disinterested and griend, who have of late contributed to the literature of the labour question. Some ot these writers cannot refer to the general issue between labourers and employers, or even to a specific demand for higher wages or fewer bout% without gushing over the virtues of the working- classes: without talking as if there were something pecul;arly noble and self-sacrificing in occupying that position; without assuming, in advance of investigation, that any body of labourers must be right in any claim they may choose to make, and casting reproachful glances at every employer who entertains notions of is own regarding his interests or righfs, as if he were a persecutor of the saints. Some of these social philoso- phers always speak of the position of a day-labourer or a factory-operative in a tone which intimates regret that the deficiencies of their own early education prevent their sharing in the moral and spiritual advantages of such a lot. Others write as though they felt it a duty to make up to the labouring class in "taffy" all that, owing to the hardness of the employers' hearts, they may not be able to secure in bread and meat. Now, this sort of thing is foolish, and, so far as it has any effect at all, is mischievous. If the working-classes are not spoiled by the unceasing adulation of which they are the sub- jects, it is because they have too much rugged sense of their own and too much native insight into character. But there is little reason to doubt that this kind,of talk has its effect, in a degree—that many a labourer has been made restive by it, and that it has prepared the way for the seductions of the demagogue.—Scribner s Magazine for November.

His opinion was that such a depot should be established in a country district, where the surplus milk could be dealt with in a more favourable manner than in a large town like Man- chester. The milk supply this winter was likely to be scarce, and it would be better to undertake this matter in a time of scarcity than in one of plenty.—The minutes were adopted on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, secon- ded by Mr. J. MARSH, and it was also decided to com- municate with the Central Association in Manchester, asking that a committee should be appointed to consider the question of establishing milk depots.--It had been intended to discuss the state of agriculture, especially in regard to the agricultural returns, which now show each year a heavy loss of agricultural wealth to the nation, but this question was postponed for future consideration, and the meeting was brought to a conclusion.

MR. BRUNNER, M.P., ON HIS ASSAILANTS. An enthusiastic Liberal meeting was held, on Saturday evening, at Wheelock, in connection with the Wheelock Liberal Club and the Women's Liberal Association. Mr. J. J. Watts presided, and a num- ber of visitors attended from Sandbach and Crewe' Mr. B. S. Bostock (Haslington) moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting emphatically con- demns the tyrannical action of the Government and the Irish Executive in their attempt to tamper with the right of public meeting and free speech in •Ireland, considers their policy a gross interfer- ence with public liberty, and hereby expressed sympathy with the Irish people in their Atrtlggiii for :MOM,' lr, Arthur. Taylor seconded the motion. Mr. Brunner, M.P., in supporting th 6 lesolution, had a very hearty reception. He said that Mr. Chamberlain, ha one of his recent speeches, had spoken of Mr. Cham- pion, the Socialist, as a man of comparative obscurity, but he did not think he had fairly de,scribeel him. Mr. Champion had been a very prominent man in the coun- try lately; he had had a place of honour in the Chureh Congress, •and he did not think the Church Congress would be ilia hurry to invite Mr. Chamberlain. (Laugh- ter and cheers.) Since,his (Mr. Brunner's) election for the Northwich Division the Socialists appeared to have made a dead set against him. They said that his claim to represent working men was a fraud and a sham. Well, he might rest content with his reputation among his neighbours—(cheers)—but he had come to the con- clusion that in this matter he owed a duty not only to his neighbours, but to the Liberal party, for Mr. Cham- pion's misstatements about him and his business had been circulated with great industry by the Tory party in every place in the country where he had been speak- ing lately. If the Tories could only persuade the petple who had listened to him, and who had perhaps been im- pressed by his arguments in favour of Home Rule, that he was a fraud, they would score one against him. But he was going to deal with Mr. Champion's statement. He said that he (Mr. Brunner) was a tyrant, who worked men on an average twelve hours a day throughout the year for 18s. per ,week. Now, that was not true. (Cheers.) He was now among his own people, and those before hun knew better. He did not know exactly what was the minimum wage for shift work at Sandbach, but it was more than 18s. per week. (Hear, hear.) Fuether than that, he became convinced three or four years ago that they, the direttora of Brunner, Mond,and Company, Limited, were doing an unkind and unwise thing in working men 365 days in the year, and he proposed to his colleagues—and the proposition met with their very cordial acceptance—that every man who worked steadily during the twelve months should have a week's holiday and a week's pay fel. it. (Cheers.) He would, therefore; leave them to judge whether he was such a terrible tyrant or not. (A Voice: "We want a few more like you," and cheers.) Mr. Champion went on to say that he (Mr. Brunner) was parrying on a business so unhealthy that no man who was engaged at the works with which ,he was connected could live more than three years. (laughter.) Well, he knew a great many who were lads twelve years ago, and were to-day with them, fine broad- shouldered fellows. There were men present that even- ing who had grown grey in the service and were as hearty as he was. (Cheers.) He knew there were cor- ners in the works that were not as they ought to be 'for men to work in, and he had been occupied for many an hour for year past in endeavouring to improve the con- ditions of the men who worked with him. (Cheers.) Men who worked at night one week and day another could not be as rosy as agricultural labourers, but he did believe that at Sandbach and Winnington they had brought their works into a decent state for men to live in. (Cheers.) Mr. Champion went on to say that he had been heaping up wealth by denying those who pro- duced that wealth a fair share in it, but there were a great many alkali works and blast furnaces in the coun- try that were being run continuously from one year's end to the other. Why was it there were good dividends from Brunner, Mond, and Co., and very little from other i alkali works n the country. He believed that one of the reasons was that they began early and worked late, whereas at other alkali works he knew they began at ten and left off at four. It was absolutely untrue that they I made up their money by not paying their men sufficient wages. They paid full wages—rather more than the average wages. Their profits did not come from grind- ing the men, but through his partner's brains and his in- dustry. (Cheers.) Mr. Yerburgh, the member for Ches- ter, had made a most untrue statement recently respect- ing him. .He said that when his men wished to support a trades union for their benefit he (Mr. Brunner) put his foot down, and forbade it, and threatened to dismiss any man who took any part in it. That was a Salisbury. (Laughter.) No proposal to start it trades union had ever been made among his workmen to his knowledge, and he never in his life had said a single word or done a single act to discourage the formation of a trades union. (Cheers.) Mr. Yerburgh also said that he (Mr. Brunner) had stated at the last election that if he were defeated at Northwich, he would close his works. Mr. Yerburgh must have known that, if used, such a statement was a deliberate, 'a cruel, infraction of the law. He (Mr. Brunner) never made such a statement. He had not the power, even if he had the will, and he had not the will, to close the works. The shareholders of the company would have something to say abont that. The statement was obviously and plainly untbue. Mr. Brun- ner then went on to give his experiences in Ireland. (Cheers.) . The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. A. M. Latham (Bradwall Hall) moved a resolution of confidence in Mr. Gladstone and those who act with litra, and especially Mr. M`La.ren, M.P. for the Crewe Division. Mr. C. H. Pedley seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Abraham. M.P.. and carried unani- mously. Mr. W. S. B. M‘Laren, M.P. for the Crewe Division, afterwards addressed the meeting.

for nothing--' came, hurrying across the farm- yard, lantern" in hand, as fast as his stiff joints could carry him. "Have you seen any one about—any strange man ?" was Anne's first inquiry—the conviction that Susan had been muedered, and that she hadactually touched the murderer in the darkness, rushed iaith Anne's mind, and theye wee even now just a chance of capturing this unseen, deadly foe. "There be never al soul about the place as I've seen. I did hear suirnaat like footsteps; but Lose. bless me, whatever be the matter with you, Miss— you look fit to drop ?" " Come with ine,quick—my sister—" Anne's voice failed her. She took Richards by the arm and hurried him into the parlour, to the sofa where Sum, was lying; then she went to a cupboard, poured a little -brandy into a glass, and held it to the lips of the prostrate woman, was it not possible that life still lingered in her ? The old man, transfixed with horror, at last gasped out—" The Lord have mercy upon us, look there !" and he pointed to the side of Susan's fore- head, where, baaleath her dark nasses of hair, rat a small blacknied, airßhind from which a little blood was still oozing. " She has -bean shot,'' said Anne, under her breath, and then she gave a fearful, shuddering, glean round the room, half expecting to see sopa, gun or Pistol lying near. Bat nothing of tbaa sort was visia " Put the lierse WO the trap again,'' said Anne, " and drive tack as hard as you can to Tavistock to fetch Mr. Prior, or the first doctor you can find, and call at the policeman's house and send him here, too, as quick as possible." "Yes—yea, so I will," replied Richards, in a dazed sort of way. "But I can't go and leave you all alone in the house, miss,—with her—Where in the world is Eliza, I wonder?" "Oh, heavens ! " and Anne clasped her hands tight to her heart with a sudden remembrance, for where, was the girl, was she too— , But at that moment girlish footsteps were heard pattering across the farm-yard and into the house. Anne gave a cry of thanksgiving, and then saying —"Stay here till I come back, Richards," she went out of the parlour, shutzing the door behind lier, and found her servan t girl Eliza.Richards' eldest daughter, safe and sound, bat rather out of breath, in the ' kitchen. ' "Please, miss," said Eliza, as she struck a match and lighted a candle which had been left on the kitchen table, "I've just been down to Miss Taylor's, the dressmaker, with a message fret-a Miss Susan." Anne had all her wits about her now, and she said quite calmly, " Did you meet anyone as you came 9long ? You were not frightened by anyone, were yon—any man?" "No, miss. haven't seen a living soul. There's ne'er a man to frighten one about here," 'coned the girl, in rather an injured tone, for she considered that living at lonely Row-tor farm, her chances of matri- mony were but small. Anne, having by a quick glance around, satisfied herself that no one was hiding in the kitchen, shut the door upon the girl and went back to Richards. "Eliza is all right--she has seen no one. I have not told her yet. Go now, Richards, as quick as you can, take the girl home ,with you for the night, she will be too frightened to stay here, and ask your wife to come to me instead—but don't lose a moment." ' "Be I to leave you here all alone, Miss Derrick ? It doan't seem right, surely. Wherever can the masiass be that he baba home yet ?'• "Oh', go—go Richards, you are losing time," cried Anne. And then at last the house door closed upon the old man and his daughter, and Anne, for the second time in her life, was left alone with a corpse. This time it was her only sister who lay dead beside her--the handsome, lively, coquettish, young woman, who was to have been married in a fort- night. Some of her wedding finery—a gaily trimmed hat, a handkerchief that she was embroidering— lay upon the table. There was a look of fear and anguish In Susan's eyes, but when her sister had gently closed them the face presently relaxed into the placidity usually seen in the countenances of those who have died an instantaneous death from gun-shot wounds. *Anne locked herself into the parlour, and then sat down beside the fire in the desolate room, where there was not a sound but the ticking of the great clock in its tall, mahogany case. She felt no fear— alone though she was in a solitary house, while all around it lay the moors like a dark and silent ocean, and withr perhaps, her sister's murderer lurking somewhere near—she felt n,o fear, for one thought alone possessed her. "Martin, where ate you—why don't you come home? If you had only been here, you would have saved her—" And then she began to realise what it would be,to have to tell Martin when he did come homaand what he would feel when he looked upon the face of his dead sister. "All thy waves and thy blews have gone over me I" Anne eriecl in anguish.. .What had they dono, she and Martin, that such a fate should pursue them? a fate, blind, unjust, relentless, irresistible, such as the ancient Greeks believed in. "God knows Martin and I were guiltless of the death of that young man, and yet, is it for that, is it as a judgmentupon us, that our sister is murdered by our own fireaide?" It was nearly half-an-hour before Mrs. Richards came into the house and knocked at the parlour door, and Anne, thankful for the companionship of some living being, rose hasstily,and let her in. Mrs. Richards was a woman of tough nerves, and a few words from her husband had prepared her for what she was to see lathe farmhouse parlour. Her stolid calmness was some little support to Anne, but when she said- - "I can't think how 'tis the master is not come home; 'taint like him to get lost on the moor, though, to be sure, the iog is as thick to-night as ever I've knowed it—" ' Then Anne wrung her hands together, and broke into a sort of wild cry: " Oh, why doesn't he—why doesn't he conic home? I wish—oh, how I wish ,Richards had gone out on the moor to look for him, instead of going to Tavistock I " "Now, don't ye take on so, Miss Derrick, there's a dear soul. He'll come back all right enough Pre- sently; he knows his way about the moor.better than any man; and as for Richards not going to Tavis- tock, you know you must get the doctor here as 4uick as possible, and the policeman, too. You didn't ought to move her, Cr touch a thing until the, have been, and there'll have to be a coroner's in: guest." "I know, I know," moaned Anne. _ time—the second time—my poor Martin I" The two women sat by the fire hour after hour, lb the profound stillness—the atmosphere of death. Anne was willing to accept Mrs. Richards' kindly offer of making some tea, but she found it impossible to touch, food. They exchanged a few words from time to time. Once Anne started up with an almost un- controllable impulse of going out to look for her -brother, but at Mrs. Richards' reasonable rerhark— " And what good will that do? The master 'll come home and find you last, that's what ' 'twill be; lost both his sisters, poor man. Now, you bide still, there's a dear soul; there'll be a bit of a moon up by nine o'clock, and maybe the foe.. will lift—" Anne's good eense and habit of self-control resumed their usual power over her. But her companion grew a little uneasy as the time went on. "I wish one could have some notion of who's done it. Maybe a tramp, or more likely a eonvict broke out of Dartmoor Prison. But then,'how should one of them soft have a gun to do it with? You haven't looked round, have you miss, to see if anything's missing ?" Anne shook her head. "We will wait until the policeman comes." "And she was to have been married the week after next, poor soul," Mrs. Richards went on." 'Twould break a heart of stone to think upon it. And that poor gentleman, Captain Starnbridge, as knows nothing about it yet.' Anne started. She had been so much absorbed in her own grief that she had not once remembered the man nho wit§ to have been Susan's hasband. There, indeed, had seemed so little love on Susan's side. that Anne had not, as would otherwise, have been the ease, naturally and involuntarily thought of Starnbridge's loss at the ,first moment. 4 (To be corainzteci.")

THE LONDON VNEMPLOTED.—In a General Order, issued on Monday night, the Ctimmissioners of the Metropolitan Police-call attention to the manner in which the mob, called the London unemployed, is organising to avoid the vigilance of the page and terrorise the inhabitants. Should a procession perambulate the streets and terrorise the inhabitants by yelling and hooting,, the Commis- sioners direct that it should be dispersed and the prin- cipals arrested; and should the mob block the streets and refuse to act under the instructions of the police, it is to be treated as an obstruction accordingly. div.head: CHAPTER VI. IN THE DARK.
div.p: CHAPTER VI. IN THE DARK.

Anne Derrick, ever quick to discern the varying moods of those about her—at once observed that Susan had come home.,from Tavistock a different 1 woman from the lively bride-elect—satisfied with her 1 1 lover, and still more with herself—who had left Row- tor Farm that morning. • Anne said nothing to her 1 that night • thinking that Susan was probably tired 1 from her day's Shopping and knowing how fatiffite magnifies all annoyances. But next morning the ! younger sister came downstairs, even later than usual : for breakfast—looking feveiish and haggard, with ' m.-lark lines under her eyes, as if she bad not slept all ! night. ; te.tlltittiala SUtt are not well," said Auu. I II Oh, lam all right; don't bother," WU gii3s,ll'a ; hasty answer, as she took up one'of her half-finished I gowns, and began sewing in a great hurry. "You look so poorly, my dear, and you haven't eaten a mouthful of breakfast," Anne went on. "I don't like being out all day, and leaving you alone in the house with only the girl. I have to go to Tavistock ; it is market-day you know, and Martin I is going a long way over the moor to see after some ! sheep." . I"Oh, fer geodnesa,sake don't stop at home er. my account 1" Susan threw down her work, \ and ! looked at Anne with sudden terror. "I am as i well as ever I can be," she continued, speakint, i with a sort of hurry and excitement, "only trml out I with poking about stuffy shops all day long with I ,James Stambridge. He hasn't a morsel of taste. I 1 was quite sick of him yesterday, he seemed so common-minded and se . common-looking "—Susan's I' head bent over her work again, and her last words were uttered almost inaudibly, in a tone of brooding discontent. _ _ _

Anne was startled.' "My dear girl, what a way to talk about the man you are just going to marry I If you don't think better of him than that, you ought to give him up for his own sake." I don't know that I shall marry him," 'Susan muttered. "It remains to be seen. We had an awful flare up yesterday; and if the wedding is put off for good and all, you mustn't be surprised." Anne stood looking at her in distress and per- plexity. "I wish I knew how much you really mean of what you are saying." "How many times must I ask you not to bother me I" cried Susan, giving her work an angry jerk. "You and Stambridge are jugt, as bad as one another. I wish you would go off to Tavistock and mind your own business." _

"Vary well, Susan, I will," replied Anne, with great dignity. And she left the room, ' feeling that her younger sister was like a spoiled child, • who would be all the better for a little "wholesome neglect." Anne was driving homewards that evening, after a busy day. She bad sold her butter, fowls, and eggs, to the tradesmen whom she had regularly supplied with the produce of her dairy and poultry- yard • she had laid in a stock of groceries for her houselold • she' had bought a new bonnet to wear at her sister's wedding; and she had lingered a little while over the railway book-stall, and purchased some newspapers and magazines, by which she kept the lonely farm-house upon the moor linked with the great, busy world beyond. It was not much past six o'clock, but it was a pitch-dark night. All that afternoon the low clouds had drooped right down to the ground, sweeping along with ringed edges blotting out the hills with thick white mist. About half-a-mile from Row-tor Farm, at the junction of two lanes, a familiar voice sounded out of the darkness, and the old labourer, Richards, ‘.wertook Anne, and walked beside the trap along the road. _ _ .

._... ......___ " I thought I should come up to ye, Miss Derrick, very like. I've just been taking along one of the best cows as we 've got to Mrs. Lawson's, and put her into the field, as the master told me to. But -I sup- pose you know all about it." Anne briefly assented. Even to this day, she could hardly bear the mention of Mis. Lawson's name. Th,i widow had lost her se and in a way for which Aims p felt herself partly rem nsible—" Yet," thought she, * "have I not suffered, too, in watching the spoilt life of one of the kindest and most just of men ? " " There'sj some, do what they will, never gets no Credit for it," pursued the old man, meditatively. "It's like this yere—if an angel from heaven was to settle down on Dartmoor and take to farming, peopic. wouldn't be friends with lie, because he'd got wingP to. 'un, , awl warn't made like other folk. Now you see, miss I've knowed Mr. Derrick ever since he were in his cradle, and I've got used to his ways, like, and I know as there b'aint a better man anywhere, nor a man more ready to do anyone a good turn at his own expense—but he'll never get no thanks for nothing he does, and for why? 'Cause he don't go to the races, nor church, nor chapel neither; 'cause he don't care for sport, and would rather have a book in his hand nor a gun. . He b'aint never seen at the public, and he b'aint never seen at the prayer-meet- ings; so nothing he does looks right in other folks' eyes." . . Never mind, Richards," ,replied Anne, serenely, "He doesn't mind." "I be none so sure that he don't mind, though. He looks wisht enough at times, poor sonl." By this time they had arrived at the farm. Richards held the hors's head, and Anne sprang lightly down from the trap. The house looked all dark; there was not a light in any window, only a dull red glimmer just-visible from the parlour fire. "Mr. Derrick is not come home then r" said Anne. "Can't say as to that, miss, but he warn't come home two hours a.gene when I . went away with the oow," and Richards led- the horse and trap across the farmyaril to the stable. Anne opened the house-door and entered. It was as pitch-dark within as it was outside. ' The lamp which always stood on a table in the entrance hall was unlighted. "Eliza must have forgotten it," thought Anne; "but where' is she, and where is Susan ?

Anne groped her way through the profound dark- ness of the little hall, . putting her hands :before her to feel whither she was going. Suddenly she felt her hand was touching some- thing solid, warm, living—something that had the softly rough texture of a man's cloth coat—some-. thing that stirred and shrank away as she touched it. Her very heart stopped beating with the sudden shock. Then something—somebody rushed past her with a bound, and was out at ihe house-door, which she had lf ft ajar, and was gone, before she had recovered her senses. Anne gave a. shriek of terror. Brave as she w'a.s, this unlooked, for encounter with an unknown man, evidently in hiding the unwonted darkness and silence of the house, quite unnerved her. She made a desperate plunge forward—found the parlour door, pushed it open, and then all but fell into the room. ' A sullen red glow from the fire just enabled her to see her way. Her need of light was supreme, sin' went straight to the fire place, felt out a box ot matches, and lighted the two candles in the tall, antique silver-plated candlesticks which stood upon the mantel-piece. This done, she somewhat fearfully glanced round the room. And then—though she haei heard not a sound, not a 'breath as she had entered_ she saw that she was not alone.
CHAPTER VII. A TERRIBLE VIGIL.

- , The candles burned dimly as they were first lighted, and all Anne could discern was her sister Susan stretched full length upon the chintz-covered sofa, which was placed beneath one of the several windows. " Susan I" cried her sister—" You there! Are you asleep ? " There was no reply. Anne went towards her in growing alarm. "My dear Susan, I am afraid you are ill 1" The candles were burning brightly now, and shed a full light on Susan's face. Anne bent over her sister—what did it mean, why was she lying there, silent, motionless? She was dead. For a minute or two, Anne stood as if she were frozen. Then the blood rushed swiftly through her veins again, and her numbed senses returned to keenest life. She ran from the room, holding one of the candles in her hand, across the passage to the house door, which stood wide open. "Richards 1" she shouted, "come to me in- - stantly I " The old man' taking the alarm at once, for as he said afterwards, "the missus 'btkiut one to cry out

div.head: REPLY TO THE SOCIALISTS.
div.p: REPLY TO THE SOCIALISTS.

A gentleman at Pendleton, having directed the attention- of Mr. Brunner, M.P., to two paragraphs which recently appeared in a Liverpool evening I paper, has received the following reply:— Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, '24th Oct. 1887. Dear Sir,—l have received many letters on the same subject as yours, but for the most part they remain unanswered. In the first place many are simply abusive, and in the second it is impossible for me to find time to answer all the letters I re- ceive. Yours is so friendly that it deserves a reply. In the first place Mr. Champion is not usually "described as a thorough-going Radical," but as a 'Socialist. Secondly, it is untrue that I have made enormous wealth by "grinding the faces of the poor," but through my partner's exceptional abil- ity and my own exceptional industry. Only a few weeks ago the same Tory papers, who now quote Mt. Champion with so much gusto, attributed our great Liberal victory not to my votes as a meniber and my speeches as a candidate, but to my great popularity as an employer of labour. My father was not a "German teacher of language" but a Swiss, and the proprietor of a large private school. Though never a rich man he was enabled to lend me a considerable sum with which to start busi- ness. Only a small proportion of our men work in shifts, and amongst those the smallest wage is 245. per week. All steady men in our employ get a week's holiday every year and a week's pay with it. It ih absolutely false that on any occasion I ever said one word to discourage the formation of a trades union, either among our men or any others. Lastly, it is not true that our business is an un- healthy one. Most of themen who joined us in 1873 are with us still, and I will back them for mus- cle and sinew against a similar number of Mr. Champion's folio sTers any day.—Youratruly, JOIEN T. BRUNNER.

OPENING OF TRURO CATHEDRAL.--The Prince of Wales, accompanied by Lord Suffield and Colonel Clark, arrived at •Truro from Falmouth a few minutes after ten on Thursday morning, and had a most enthusiastic recep- tion. On alighting from his saloon the Prince was pre- sented with an address, of welcome by the Mayor of Truro (Mr. Paul.) His Royal Highness in reply, said it afforded him unfeigned satisfaction to be able to attend the great religious service to be held at Truro, and to be present at the consummation of the important ceremony in which he took a leading part more than 7 years ago. At the door of the Cathedral the Prince was received by the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of Truro, and other prelates, together with the choir and clergy. Prior to the arrival of his Royal Highness the ecclesiastical dignitaries had proceeded round to the outside of the church, singing the hymn, "Blessed city, heavenly Salem." On the arrival of the Prince the ceremonies 'were at once commenced by the Bishops outside the Cathedral. After the opening prayer, tho Bishop knocked with his pastoral staff at the west, door, saying, Open ye the gates." The door having been opened, the Bishop, entering, invoked the blessing of peace on the sacred edifice. After the service, the Prince was entertained to luncheon by the Mayor. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. TIII7ItSDAY NIGHT.

By a cruel irony of fate, Mr. Chamberlain, who is accustomed,to taunt as-" Separatists the men who are working to strengthen the union with Ireland, is himself the personal and active agent in shaping a courae of events that may lead to the separation from the Empire of one of its most cherished 'colo- nies. On the very verge of setting forth on a mis- sion of conciliation, Mr. Cham'A'erlain has had the ill luck hopelessly to offend the two nations to whom he is cotniansioned. For an ordinary man it would be a fair day's work to set the United States against him. Mr. Chamberlain, within the coursplof a week, succeeded in rousing, the anti- pathy of two nations. This would be bearable if only Mr. Chamberlain were concerned. In truth, Liberals would be more than human if they did not experience some secret twinges of satisfaction at seeing this great apostle of union embroiled with our Colonial cousins and our American aunts. Unhappily there is more at stake than Mr. Cnain- berlain's reputation. In the curious involution of party tactics, he came to be selected as the repre- sentative of Great Britain in a critical and delicate negotiation. If he fails, and he has so managed matters at the outset that success is impossible, the interests of three great countries will suffer. The mere fact that a Conference on the Fisheries Ques- tion had been proposed and accepted by England, Canada, and the United States, showed the general desire for a settlement. It was a great opportunity for Mr. Chamberlain. Everything was ready te his band. He might have been instrumental in conclud- qng a treaty that would have finally settled a long- -Vexed question, and might have come back to Eng- land rehabilitated in public opinion by his success. But the curse of Ireland is upon him. He, of all men; moved by personal spleen, has associated him- self with the Conservatives to coerce Ireland, and to help the rack-renting landlord to evict the struggling tenant. With this new and strange de- parture, his habitual luck has deserted him. Every- thing he touches goes wrong, and, discredited at home, he is received with howls of execration and contempt when he crosses the Atlantic. Lord Salisbury may be able to bear with some equanimity the misfortune attached to his Govern- ment in connection with Mr. Chamberlain. His selection was an admirable one. No one could fore- see that Mr. Chamberlain himself would in such surprising manner destroy his own chances of suc- cess. But in another personal aspect of our relations with foreign countries Lord Salisbury has only him- self to blame. His appointment of Lord Lytton to the Paris Embassy is such a wantonly monstrous act that the earliest report of it was received with incredulity. A week lgefore the appointment was officially avowed, the f' Daily News stated it as an acconiplished fact, and the general impression was that the Liberal journal had been misled. But it turns out to be true, and Lord Lytton is actually , going to Paris. Now people are worrying each other other in search of reasons for this extra- i ordinary step. There is nothing in Lord Lytton's ; official career which recommends him for the post, but rather everythipg that is known about him condemns the appointment. The active penance of ,the longest life could not atone for the mischief ,wrought by him during his disastrous vice- royalty in India. lAs blunders then reached the magnitude a crime, and are of themselves sufficient to ostraetse him. But what makes the appointment at the present crisis the more amazing is the fact that Lord Lytton's sternest 'critics are to be found among the very men, once members of the Liberal party, who now keep the Government in office. Lord Hartington wps moved out of his habi- tual attitude of stolidity when he discoursed on Lord Lytton's viceroyalty. Mr. Chamberlain poured upon his head the vials of his just wrath, and the Duke of Argyll was foremost in the attack both in the House of Lords and in the press. With the memory of this outburst fresh upon him. Lord Salis- bury appoints Lord Lytton to the most important post in the diplomatic service, and , has hitherto been justified in his confidence that neither Lord Hartingtian, nor Mr. Chamberlain, nor other of the quondam Liberals who stormed at Lord Lytton nine years ago, would now utter a word of protest against this trifling with imperial interests. The first Cabinet Council of the recess is being held to-day. Simultaneously an informal Cabinet Council of the Government's allies is being held at Devonshire House under the presidency of Lord Hartington. It cannot be supposed that either -proves an exhilarating affair. The fortunes of the Dissentient Liberals and the Government are noav indissolubly bound up with each other, and one cannot suffer without the other feeling it. The confident talk about a reconstruction of the Minis- try, involving the retirement of Lord Salisbury from the Premiership, and the promotion of Lord Hartington has dwindled down to the smallest pro- portions. The utmost now said is that room is I somehow to be made for Sir Michael Hicks-Beach,

whom everyone is glad to welcome back to active public service. What seems most probable is that Mr. Henry Matthews will go. He has been an un- mitigated failure, the cup of his humiliation being filled by the rebuke conveyed to him from the Bench by Mr. Justice Stephen, presiding in the Cass cad. Whilst Ministers are naturally uneasy under the unbroken storm of obloquy which their actions bring upon them, they are serenely satisfied in the great fact that at least they are safe in their office for an indefinite period. Lord llartington, having swallowed not only Coercion in Ireland, but Lord Lytton, as Ambassador to Paris, is now too deeply committed to break with the Tories. Therefore, they will retain their majority in the House of Corn- mons, It may be worn away by the results of bye- elections, but it takes a good many bye-elections to wipe off a working majority of from seventy to eighty. i am told the "Times" is straining every effort to delay the hearing of the libel case which Mr. Frank O'Donnell has brought against it., This cause when 1 it is heard will take its place amongst the most cele- , bratecl' of the century. It involves, incidentally, the whole case of the forged Parnell letter, and the al- leged relations of the Irish members with the Fenian conspirators. Mr. Parnell will be one of the witnesses, and Mr. Gladstone will also, I belier, be subpcened. If matters were permitted to take their ordinary course, the case would be disposed of in the present term. But the " Times " does not mean to let things take their course, if it can help it. As long as the charge ie uncontroverted it may be use- ful in political controversy, arid even six months delay is worth something. The 20th of October was the day originally fixed for the " Times " to lodge with the court fts defence to Mr. O'Donnell's claim fbr damages. A private application was made on behalf of the "Times" to Mr. O'Donnell's solicitor for a delay of ten days. This wasconceded ; lant be- fore the time of grace had elapsed notice was given of a Motion to be made in chambers for 'a further delay of ten days upon the ground that it was neces- sary for the preparation of ,the defence. The result of this application, if successful, would be to throw the case out of this term, and the session would be over before the matter at issue was settled. A brief was offered to Sir Charles Russell on behalf of Mr. O'Donnell, but it apppars that the "Times" has most astutely secured the services of that eminent counsel by a general retainer. Mr. Harry Furniss has not sold his sketch of Lord Beaconsfield's last visit to the House of Com- mons, originally drawn for the "English Illustrated Magazine," to accompany an article by Mr. Lucy, on the House of Lords. aloo is a good deal to pay for a pen and ink sketch, however historically in- terestin.g, and however beautifully drawn. As Mr as sale is concerned, the prices fixed have proved rather a drawback to the enterprise. Nothing is to be had under five guineas, and twenty guineas for a sketch with two or three figures in it is quite com- mon. Amongst the single figure sketches of M.P's. .which have already appeared in the pages of

"Punch," the one which excites the greatest curiosity amongst the visitors is an excellent por- trait of Colonel Hughes-lfallett. Whilst there has been no rush on the part of the public to pay the high prices demanded, the little star onthe pictures shows that a good many of them have been sold. This new fashion of exhibiting for sale the original sketches of contributors to the periodicals opens 121! a mine of wealth for popular artists. The paYteeh: for work done by the exceedingly small staff of "Punch" is understood to be exceptionally high. lii addition, as! in the case of Mr. Du Manner and Mid Furniss, they pocket large sums as gate money f,(..!- an exhibition of their works, and then sell the originals, being thus thrice blessed in their work. Many people ask why Mr. Tenniel does riot have his show, and make a supplementary fortune like,„ his colleagues. The answer is, I believe, that t"1; exigencies of the paper require Mr. Tenniel to directly on the bloek, and that there are not in ell' tence any originals of his famous cartoons.

Indeed, its great and admitted worth led to its being used in all public ceremonies as an acceptable offering to their deity—the Sun God. The leaves of this marvellous shrub, when ready for market, are transported on mules up the steep mountain sides, across the icy and desolate platemix, and through the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many -of than 13,000 and 14,000 feet above the level of the sea, and thee downwards on the other side of the mountains into Peru for shipment from the port of Callao (Lima.) And so terrible Is the icy rigour of the climate amidst the lofty heights of the mountains, especially of the icy plateaux of Lipes, that the muleteers find the chewing of these leaves alone enables them to withstand the icy rarefied air, and tosupport the long night- watches to prevent the mules they are transporting to Peru from ',fraying. Several natives, who, never allowing a day to Peas without chewing the leaves of the "Pearl of South America at least three times daily, attained the truly patri- archal age of 130 years.

As the ordinary food of the nafive Peruvian consists almost exclusively of roasted maize, barley, or seeds of the qttinoa. which are eaten without any addition, they suffer with fre- quent and obstinate obstructions and derangements of the di- gestive system, which are entirely cured by the use of

THE SHOCKING DEATH OF A ' CARTER- At the Ram's Head Inn, Horsemarket-street, on Monday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy Coroner, and a jury, investigated the circumstances of the death of a carter named Duckers, which oc- curred yesterday -week: Evidence was taken as follows :—Catherine Haddock, wife of Tbomas Had- -1 l' lock, 63, Knutsford-road, Latchford, A labourer. • Identified the body of the deceased as that of , Joseph Philip Eyes Ducker", who had lodged at the house of witness. iDeceased, who was a carter, was 20 years of age.—James Newton, carter, 38,Victoria- street, said that on Friday evening, at about 5-30, ~, lie was near Foundry-street; When he saw a man 1, lY charge of a horse and furry. The man was start- -4' ...tngthe horse to go through a gateway leading into It i,Sir. Halford's yard. When he started he got too,.titr past the gate, and was trying to get the horse , through, when the shaft of the cart caught him in he side,, and jammed liim against the gate post. The man had hold of the horse's head at the time, and witness did not think he was much hurt. He, 14 owever, afterwards learned that he was dead. „homas handers, 44, Pierpoint-street, said that on zrid- evening he was in Mr. Halfbrd's office, at ,the corner of .Bewsey and Foundry-streets. A .river came with a load of machinery, and witness' Eold him to draw down the yard. Witness went itway for about four minutes, and on returning ,°_lPod that the gates had been opened. He saw the rpver lying on the ground, and the horse was par- nally inside the yard. Witness and another per- fl removed deceased, who was bleeding, and sent Or a doctor, who, on arriving, immediately pro- °llnced that he. was dead.—The jury returned a eveoeclict of accidental death.—, A relative of the de- l. red mentioned that it waa rather painful to the aet at,ives to find that the body had been put, in a ti able, and the Deputy-Coroner said that was some- znes unavoidable.

Gt.:ivy. the Jeered La Pair to-day I announces that the President's health is excellent ' I PARIS, MONDAY.—The Extreme Left. has addressed the I following telegram to the Government of Illinois:—" In the name of humanity and of the solidarity between the two great Republics, the Deputies assembled in Paris who are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment ' for political offences ask of the Government of Illinois the lives . 'he seven Chicago anarchists now lying under sent. ti of death." PARIS, MONDAT.—The, French papers that Lord Lyons will present his letters of recall to the President of the Republic in the beginning of December. and that Lord. Lytton, his successor, will he installed at the British Embassy before Christmas.

, TURKEY.—THE PORTE AND THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, SIINDAV.—Stvi-official negotiations have again been initiated by the Porte for tranquili4ing the Soudan. The Porte suggests the occupation of Gongola by Turkish troops, and offers to reconquer and occupy the Soudan. which would then be considered independent of Egypt until the latter is in a position to hold it herself. Mulch- tar Pasha, who is of course the agent for Turkey in the matter, says that the only object of these proposals is to assure the safety of the Egyptian frontier and relieve Egypt of a portion of its heavy military expenditure. The proposition has been very adroitly submitted to the consideration of the Khedive and the Egyptian Govern- ment, but its rejection is nevertheless certain, as it would naturally have the effect of introducing the principle of Turkishinterference with Egypt and would lead to end- -1 less complications. Solna. MONDAY.—A . large group of deputies have decided to arraign AL flaraveloff and two other members before the Sobranle for having taken part in the attempt against Prince Alexander on the 21st. August last year. The proceedings are likely to make a great sensation.

div.p: ILLNE- SS OF THE GERMAN EMPEROR.
Hamm Fan:mi.—The Emperor William has had to abandon the attention of.attending the annual hunt at Suheituestock on account of a alight cold.

nuatix, MONDAY Niour.—His Majesty did not leave his bed to-day, and was not allowed to receive any visi- tors. A:weekly paper publishes the statement that the Emperor has expressed the wish to seethe Crown Prince, about whose condition he daily receives satisfactory re- ports, back again in Germany. The paper adds that the Crown Prince will therefore spend only`a short time in San Remo where a German specialist. is to be sent to consult with Sir Morrell Mackenzie about the return to Goamenv.

HE FRENCH. M,LLITARY SCANDAL. Pante, THIIRSDAY)--A Cabinet Council was held yes- terday evening to 'decide upon what attitude the Gov- ernment should adopt in regard to the Conversion Bill and the proposed Parliamentary inquiry into the recent scandal. The Ministers will submit the decisions arrived at to President Grevy this morning. The "Journal des Debate" to-day states that a strong coalition has been formed against the Government on the conversion ques- tion which comes on for discussion in the Chamber of Deputies this afternoon.

div.head: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN A LEAD MINE.
div.p: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN A LEAD MINE.

Shortly before seven o'clock on Thursday morning information was received at Matlock Bath of a ter- rible explosion in the Mill Close Mine, some three miles distant, near the villages of Winster and Barley Dale. The mine is extensively worked, and up- wards of, 100 men are employed in shifts of about eight hours each. They usually work in companies of six, scattered throughout the workings according to the direction of the veins of lead ore: About three o'clock on Thursday morning twenty-five men were working in the mine when an explosion of fire damp occurred. A rush was made to the shaft, and several of the men were brought safely to the surface. On these being counted the officials found that a number were missing. Search parties were organised, and descending, discovered three men, named respectively. Ellis, Smith, and Marden, in- jured by scalp wounds, though not seriously. The search party proceeded along the workings, and it was found that hundreds of tons of soil and stone had fallen. It was feared many men must be buried beneath the debris. Search was actively made, and from the time of the explosion to seven o'clock, three dead bodies had been received. Two more were subsequently brought to the surface, The five killed are Benjamin Roam, single; George Allen, married, with two children; Job Stone, married, with family; George Stone, and George Needham, married, with family. Large. crowds were collected at the mouth of the mine anxiously awaiting news from the searchers.

div.head: GALE.
div.p: THE GALE.

Telegrams from corresppndents in various parts of the United Kingdom report a serious gale during Monday night and Tuesday morning, and a number of shipping casualties are reported. At Falmouth a Danish vessel was driven ashore in the harbour, and is now covered with water. One man is missing. The Dutch brig Nautilus was wrecked at the same place and one of its crew drowned. In the course of the gale at Burton-on-Trent, a man' named Matthew Jackson, employed by Messrs. Bass and Co., is believed to have been blown under one of the brewery trains, as he was found decapitated. A young man named Dean, of Chardstock, Dorset, was killed in the storm, while delivering milk, by a tree falling upon him. The gale had raged there throughout the night, accompanied by heavy rain, doing much damage to house property. At Bournemouth slates and chimney pots were blown down, and the scaffolding around a new spire of the Presbyterian Church was dislodged, and fell. The sea was exceedingly rough, and the railway across Parkstone Bay—between Parkstone and Poole—has been washed away. LIVERPOOL

The scene on the Mersey at the turn of the tide, on Tuesday, was very striking, the wind being SO fierce and the waves so high that the ferry traffic on the river had to be entirely suspended. Several vessels broke their cables and drifted up the river, broadside. The barque Egeria came into collision with- the Birkenhead landing stage, and the tug Vigilance, which went to her assistance, was very severely damaged. The training ship Akbar, on which there was recently a mutiny, broke her moorings in the gale, and went adrift. She was moored near the other training ships, and almost came into collision with them. As many hundreds of boys are on board these old vessels, a dread- ful calamity WWI only narrowly averted. The Akbar was taken in tow of several tugs. The large floating bridge tt the Liverpool stage was broken in the middle, and traffic was stopped, and the Woodside and Tranmere stages are almost complete wrecks. The Tranmere stage broke adrift and floated down the river, coming in contact with the Birkenhead stage. The disaster wae caused by a schooner breaking from her moorings and drifting against the bridge which con- nects the stage with the p•er, carrying it away. The stability of the Woodside stage is in danger. The sub- stantial wooden houses and waiting rooms on Woodside stage were swept clean away, and it was expected that the New Brighton landing stage had given way. A small vessel, bottom upwards, probably a fishing smack, was swept past the pierhead. The Isle of Man boat did not leave Liverpool as usual. as it would have been irn- possible to enter Douglas Harbour. An the stagernen agree that the hurricane blowing off the land was the most extraordinary they remember. All previous gales have been northerly or westerly. the Central News says : Another terrible and fatal catastrophe has occurred on the river Mersey. Soon'efter the 'rranmere pier was smashed, and the stage wrecked, a schooner fouled two of the pier. supports, which w&e carried away. The vessel drifted, struck the wrecked stage, and immediately turned over and sank. Three of the crew get into the boat, which drifted and capsized; and they were drowned. Two others got into the rigging, but were washed off by the action of the waves, and also lost. This occurred within a rope's length of the Tranmere pier, and a man who was there threw a rope, but it was blown away. The name of the vessel is not yet known. Captain Davidson, of the ship Caloric. which arrived at three o'clook, re- ported terrible weather in the Channel, and that he passed a large number of boats and floating wreckage. The Tmnmern wreck was one of the most dreadful and sensational scenes ever witnessed, and quite unprecedented in its character. Large numbers of people saw the whole of the dramatic incident from within a distance of 100 yards, and the Isle of Man steamer King Orry, which was passing on her way to the stage, Saw the schooner go down, and the captain was unable to render any help to the poor fellows, who were clinging to the rigging. The boat that left the schooner with the other three men was whirled away in the ter- rible flood, and suddenly disappeared. It is thought by the stagetnen that the schooner was one that was at anchor in the Siovne, and that another drift- ing vessel got foul of Iter and broke her cable. She, like many other vessels yesterday. would have been quickly taken in tow by one of the many powerful tugs that were in the river only for her getting adrift of the Trannaere piers. After the blow she was carried completely round in the swirling waters, and turned over, as stated; within a few minutes. • A later telegram says that only two lives were lost by the disaster OR the Mersey.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1887.
CURRENT POLITICS.

, 2 4 • Mr. Wilfrid Blunt has issued an address, aeltnoWleAg. tog on behalf of himself and Lady Anne Blunt, a vast number of resolutions and private letters of congratula- tion and sympathy. He will endeavour to send to Ire- land a large body of courageous workers to carry on the campaign against coercion. Arrangements are now practically"- complete fur the two counties' demonstration at Penrith on the 23rd November. There will be a conference of .Liberal dele- gates from alk parts of Cumberland and Westmoreland. which will be presided ov,tir by Sir James Itriteon, President or the National Liberal Federation. In the evening a Miss meeting will be held in the Market Hall, Sir Wilfrid Lawson in the chair, when Sir William liar- court and other leading Liberals will speak. Six Parlia- mentary divisions and two borough constituencies will be represented, and great enthusiasm is already been shown with regard to the proposed meetings. Alderman Itenrick„ M.P., addressed a meeting of his constituents at Hospital-street Board School, Birming- ham, on Monday. Admission to the greater part of the room was by ticket, but to the free part a large body of Gladstonians obtained admission, and the proceedings were attended with some excitement. Alderman Ken- rick defended his adherence to the Unionist muse, and a resolution of confidence was carried by a narrow ma- jority. At the conclusion of the meeting the carriage containing Alderman Kenrick and Mr. Collings, M.P.. was surrounded by an angry crowd, and one of the windows was smashed to atoms, hut the occupants were unhurt.

The Executive Committee of the Deptford Conserva- tive Association, at a meeting on Friday night, passed the following resolutions i--1. "That this meeting, hav- ing considered Mr. Evelyn's letter announcing his inten- tion of resigning his Seat at the reassembling of Parlia- ment., approve.; of the course he proposes to take, and trusts that he will carry his intention into effect as soon as circumstances will permit." 2. "That apart trom the Irish question, on which this association totally differs from Mr. Evelyn's views, the association desires to express its thanks to Mr. Evelyn for his past services to the borough as its representative." The association re- solved to invite Lord Frederick Hamilton to meet it with a view to his candidature.

LORD GRANVILLE AT MANCRESTER.--LOrd Granville, addressing the members of the Manchester Reform Club, on Tuesday, said that the Liberal party was not at all in a drooping position, but was increasing in strength every day.. The present Government were sticking in the mud, and that mud was of their own absolute crea- tion. The Liberals could afford to look on. It would be great folly for them to be in a hurry, though it was a sad thing to see so much bad feeling being created be- tween Ireland and Great Britain. That bad feeling, would not, however, be increased by the knowledge of the hearty sympathy which such enormous numbers of people in this country felt for Irishmen in their trouble. It was not wise to prophecy that the Liberals would be called into action; but it was necessap, that they should at once prepare for the contest—come when it may. SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN AT CARNARVON.—The Liberals of Wales gave a magnificent reception to Sir G. Trevelyan on Saturday at Carnarvon. In the morning, at the first annual meeting of the North -Wales Liberal Federation, Sir George, speaking to a resolution in favour of dises- tablishment and disendowment of the Church in Wales, said lie did not agree with Lord Hartington that nothing could be carried into practical effect until the Irish ques- tion had been settled. -When the time came that the BA- fish electors ordered the Tories and their allies to stand aside, the work of reform in Great Britain as well as in Ireland would go on concurrently side by side. In the evening Sir George addressed a crowded meeting of 10,000 persons held in the Pavilion and presided over by Mr. RathbOne, M.P. The general policy of the Gov- ernment was dealt with. On the old controversy raised by the Liberal Unionists, Sir George said it was a shame and a scandal for people who were Liberals to join with the Primrose League in crushing out the Liberalism of rural districts, and the assertion that the split in the Liberal party was kept up on account of the differences of opinion about the Irish Bill was a sham and a pretext. At the conclusion of the meeting Sir George was escorted to his hotel by a torchlight procession. LORD HARTINGTON AT TRI7RO.—A conference of Liberal Unionists of Cornwall was held at Truro on Mon- day. Mr. Courtney, who presided, declared that the future of the Liberal Unionist party was full of promise, and they intended to pursue their way in a spirit of faith.—The Marquis of Hartington addressed a very numerous gathering at night. He devoted his address to the Irish question, and a great part of it consisted in replies to criticisms on his speech at Nottingham. He (Lord Hartington) was a protestant in politics as wOl as in religion, and he protested when he saw vast masses of people swayed from one point to another, not as the result of the conviction of their judgment, but the blind following of one hero. Cavour and Bismarck had been raised to a pinnacle in the esteem of the Italian and Ger- man peoples, not because they were followed as heroes by these countries, but because they were the means of consolidating those countries, and did not hesitate to spill blood in their determination to accomplish national unity. The only way in which the nation could safely proceed was irt the direction of the absolute and uncon- ditional withdrawal of the principle of the bill of last year. The only principle on which a stand could safely be taken was that no legislature oradministration should be granted to Ireland that was not demanded by and might be given to the countries of Scotland, Wales, and England. Resolutions similar to those adopted at the afternoon conference were carried by large majorities.

div.head: MR. MUNDELLA, MP., AND CHILD LABOUR.
div.p: MR. MUNDELLA, MP., AND CHILD LABOUR.

Speaking art he opening of a new Board School at Loughborough, 011 Monday, Mr. Mundella, M. P., said there was too much competition for child labour. The trades unions had been asking that the State should step in and say men should only work on, certain conditions, and so many hours a day.. If he was a working man he would resent, that to the last degree. A man was the master of his fate, and no State should step in and dictate the hours of his labour. Because, if the State could limit them the State could extend them. But he would go farther than that. Instead of seeing too much of men with strong sinews and muscle idle, while the weakly children were at work, he, would say—raise the age ut which a child shall work. (Bear, hear.) Protect the child. Let its intellect and also its physique be sufficiently developed, that they might be able to fight the battle et life, and grow up men and women possessing the two things they desired —a healthy mind in ó healthy body.

13111. W. LAWSON, M.P. Sir W. Lawson, speaking at the annual meeting of the Mid Cumberland Liberal Association at Penrith on Mon- day, said the political situation In this country Was one of the most extraordinary ever seen. in Parlia- ment they had the most reactionary, the most oppres- sive, the most pig-headed, and the most Tory Covesn- ment which had ever existed; and at the head of the Ministry they had a Prime Minister who was the greatest opponent of freedom that could be found in the kingdom. The wonder did not end there. The most extraordinary thing was that such a Government with such a head was maintained in power by some of the greatest Liberals, such as Mr. John Bright, Lord Harting- ton, and M. Chamberlain. That was the amusing part. The tragic part was had enough. At the present moment they were carrying on war with the Irish nation. The Times said no new crime had been created, but Sir G. Trevelyan had knocked down that argument.; they had created the new crime of belonging to the National League. Mr. Chamberlain, when setting out upon his American fishing expedition, said to his friends at Birmingham, * Stick to the Union." Mr. Chamberlain's union, however, was that abominable union of handcuffs enforced by bayonet and batons; and in Mid Cumber- laral,;where Liberals existed, their determination should be to stick to the union of the Liberal party with the National party of Ireland. In that union were hound up the best hopes of the future of this country.

div.head: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.
div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.

The luckiest "find" ever made in California was made by a man named Finney, who "turned up'! a solid lump of gold near Downieville, in 1866, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 1,8.00 dols. per ounce, which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget of pure gold ever discovered. heretofore the Australian nugget found in the Ballarat gold fields has been considered the largest. It was valued at £15,000. This man Finney, or "Old Virginia," as he was called, went to Wathoe, California, and there he made the great silver discoveries, where the "Comstock" lode was located, and where Virginia City, which was named after him, stands. He died in great poverty. He was cele- brated for his wonderful head of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of golden tints, and which fell in heavy curls over his stalwart shoulders. He was very proud of his head covering, and always carried in his " outfit " a brush, comb, and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his "camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great case, When misfortune overtook him, and he continued "playing in bad luck "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hair, and it became frowsy, began to turn gray, and fall out, so that a few years before he died he was nearly bald, and his few remaining hairs were quite white. Had he added to his "out" Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he lived, for it never fails ter strengthen and invigorate the hair, restore its colour, aid render it soft, glossy and strong. It can be found at any chemist's or perfumer's ii. the world. It is the best and most agreeable hair dress- ing known. Try it.
