div.head: TEN MEN DROWN ED.
div.p: TEN MEN DROWN ED.

A very sad accident happened about three o'clock on Sunday morning off Portland, by which 10 men out of 12, who had gone out for a night's trawling, were drowned. The party consisted of Sergeant Apsey, of the Weymouth police force; Mr. Arthur Russell ;tad Mr.. John Tharger, detectives, of the Metropolitan police force; Mr. fl. Palmer, of the Cutter Hotel; Mr. Keridge. brewery clerk; Mr. S. Whettam, brewers' traveller; Mr. L. Carter, boat-builder; 2,1 r. Burehell, commercial traveller; a Frenchman named Maurice Booth, staying at the Cutter Hotel; Coiporal Apsey,lsth Hussars; and two boatmen named Strickland and Dennis. The party left Weymouth about six o'clock on Saturday night in a boat. About two o'clock on "Tuesday morning, being caught in a gale, they anchored at a buoy near the breakwater. As the gale Increased, they had to let go, when a sudden squall capsized the boat, and 10 out of the 12 occupants were drowned, the two survivors managing to save themselves by holding on to the boat and then Scrambling on to the breakwater. The ORMOS of the survivors are Apsey and Dennis. Further details show that the boat was named. the Laurette, a decked cutter of 10 tons, and belonged to Mr. Carter, yacht and boat builder, of Weymouth. The party, on reaching• Portland, made fast. to a Government buoy, about midway between the floscawen training ship and the breakwater. The weather at the time was very wet, and the wind ou the increase, but Strickland. who was in charge, thought they had better stay where they were. About three o'clock, a hurricane set in, and the rope snapped, causing the vessel to drift towards the breakwater. A boat was pulled alongside, and several jumped into it, but whilst waiting for the others the craft was smashed against the side of the yacht, the occupants being thrown into the water. They were then cast on the rocks, and only two succeeded in scrambling on to the breakwater. Three bodies were recovered on Sunday, and one on Monday. In consequence of the disaster the Masquerade and Carnival procession, which were to have taken place this week, have been postponed.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S DEPARTURE FOR AMERICA.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S DEPARTURE FOR AMERICA.

Mr. Joseph Chamberlain left. Birmingham by the 11 20 a.m. train on Saturday for Liveslionl, Pll route for America. About 1,000 persons congregated at the railway station. and the right lion. gentleman was vehemently cheered. In response to loud calls for a speech, Mr. Chamberlain, after expressing gratitude for the kindness of his friends for going there to wish him good bye and 6od speed, and hoping thst ILO good feeling between the two great nations he was going to serve would he continually preserved, said: I hope that I may see you all once snore in the course of a few months. And be sure of this, I shall tigre with 'me to America the plea- santest recollections df your continued goodness to me. But, if these should be the last words I should ever speak to you—(" Never." and "No ").-ri say to you !!Stick firm to the Union." I say to you, "spare no effort to maintain the magnificent. inherits ref. which has descended to you from your forefathers." And, believe me, these are the greatest enemies of tho romtnenWealth, whether they are known as Separatists or by any other name, who would do anything to weaken or impair the integrity of the Empire. (Cheers.) The right hon.lpAit.leman's train then moved off amid loud cheers. _ _ _

Mr. Chamberlain reached Liverpn at 2 40. p.m., and was received by the Mayor at the station where a large crowd assembled. There was mingled cheering and boot- ing on the route to the Town Hall. whither Mr. Cham- berlain drove in the Mayor's carriage, accompanied by the Mayor and Mr. Richard Chamberlain, M.P. There were large crowds at one point, and A large lurry was drawn across the road—evidently designedly—and this stopped the progress of the carriage. A crowd gathered round it, and some of the bystanders seized the wheels, and for a few moments it looked as if some attack was intended. The police, who were here in considerable force; came to the rescue, and the -carriage proceeded. All the balconies and windows in the neighbour- hood of the route were filled with spectators, and there was considerable - sheering and hoot- ing. Mr. Chamberlain, on intern the Town flail. was introduced to a number of gentlemen, in- cluding the leading local Conservatives and Liberal Unionists, He then went to the balcony in front of the Town Hall, and was heartily cheered. The party then retired to luncheon, to . which about 25 leading citizens sat down. The proceedings were private, the only toasts proposed being the Queen, the President of the United States, and her Majesty's Commissioner. Mr. Chamberlain was accompanied to the tender by A Id. Livingston (the Deputy-Mayor), Baron Do Worms, Sir David Radcliffe, Sir Wirn., B. Norwood, and a few other leading residents of the city. The tender was immediately cast oft and in a rew moments had passed out of vision in the gathering twilight. . Mr. Chamberlain is accam- pained on his mission by Mr. Bergne and Mr. Willoughby Mayeock. of the Foreign Office. Mr. Chamberlain. accompanied by his two secretaries, left Queenstown on Sunday. at 1 7 p. 10., for New York, on board the Cunard steamer Etruria. The Transatlantic liner arrivstin Cork Harliourjrom Liverpool, at nine iii the Wining; Tor the .parpose of ernlgrynif, passengers and American mail. At half-past nine the company's tender Jackal left the wharf at Queenstown for the Etruria, convqing about a dozen of the towns- people who were anxious to see Mr. Chamberlain, in addition to the passengers who embarked et Queenstown.

TRIAL OF RC. ENDACOTT. THE CHARGE DISMISSED. At the Central Criminal Court, on 11briday, Mr. Justice Stephen commenced the trial Of Constable Bowden En- dacott on a charge of perjury at Marlborough-street Police Court, in connection with the Cass. ease. The Solicitor- General and Messrs. Grain, Abrahams, and Heard prose- cuted for the public prosecutor; and Mr. Besley and Mr. Gin defended. The specific allegation -.against the accused was that he find falsely sworn at Marlborough- street Police Court that he saw Miss Cass accost two men, and that she subsequent ly repeated the offence, and on that occasion one of the men complained to him. The Solicitor-General stated the case for thlt prose- cution. - .

Miss Cass was put into the box and examined at great length, detailing the 'particulars of her engagement with Madame fk)wman as forewoman, and of her habits at that establishment She was then examined as to what took place on tht 27th of „tune. She explained that when she went out on that night alio walked along Tot- tenham Court-road and Oxford-street before the arrest took place. Witness was subjected to a long cross-examination, in the course of which she admitted having. on one occa- sion walked for two hours and a half in Tottenham Court-road while waiting for a young man, named Settle. an assistant at Shoolbreds. to see her home. She was out on Jubilee night looking at the illuminations, but Mrs. Bowman and two other women were with her. She had not previo,uslw mentioned to anyone connected with the case her waik with Settle. Witness was further examined as to a journey which she took in April from Stockton to London. a 'young man named Bryan accompanying her during part of the journey. In re-examination, 'witness said she was introduced to Bryan by Bridget Costello, a barmaid. at Stockton. Sho did not, know on her first introduction that he was married.

Mrs. Mary Ann Bowman of Southampton-row, with whom i Miss Cass was working at the time of her arrest, deposed that to her knowledge between the 7th and 28th June Miss Cass was never in Itegeg-street. Jane Scott. Mrs. Bowman's sister, said Miss Cass seb dOM went out.

On Tuesday, after the cage for the prosecutlOn, Mr. Vesley said he should only call evidence of character. The Judge said it appeared to him there was no oar- rehorative evidence as to ant of the allegations which were material to the case. The only point, he thought, lie could put to the jury was whether the constable had committed perjury in saying he had seen Miss Cass in negent-street three times in six weeks, and that was not alleged to be material, and 'night have been a mistake.. The Solicitor-General, after consulting with the other counsel, said he felt, the force of the Judge's remarks, and would, therefore, not address himself to the Questions raised, hut would leave the matter to his Lordship. The Judge said be-considered the Solicitor-General had taken a proper course, and under his direction the jury returned a verdict of •• Not guilty," and Endacett was dischar.ed.

The Judge added some remarks, Pointing out that two witnesses were necessary' to establish a charge of per- jury and hilwever hard the arrest might be to Miss Cass, they intist, see justice done. In justice to the con- stable, ho must. say there NV :LS considerabto room far rms. takes, hit that was not suflivient to establish a charge of wilful and corrupt perjury. There were many passengers in the street, and although the defendant. might have seen all he described, he still might have arrested the wrong woman. If a man was to be convicted or perjury for having 'made a mistake, it would be very cruel; and even Miss Cass, who had made mistakes in the witness. box, might he open to the same: hut it would he hard to snap a verdict against her., ati It would be against the Policeman. BO again condemned tbe holding of the preliminary inquiry. .‘ „ Some applause followed the decision.

A farmer named rd'Ellicott was shot at on Wednesday night at BaneMoret half way between Tralee and Listowel, and was so dan- gerously wounded that it is feared he will not recover. The alleged cause of the outrage is that M'Ellicott had bought an evicted tenant's interest in a small piece of land, he haying been boycotted for this. SERIOUS COLLISION ON THE NORTH BRITISH RAILWAY. —Late on Wednesday night a collision occurred at King- horn Station, on the North British Railway. Two pas- senger trains are due at that station from opposite direc- tions at 6-15, and a train of empty ctal waggons should have shunted to allow one to pass; but befor4 it had done so the passenger train from Burntisland came up and ran into it. Six or seven persons were injured, some seriously, and the line was blocked for some time.

The Greek Government is negotiating with, foreign bankers for a loan of 10,00,000 francs in gold.

, Negotiations are pending for the transfer of the whole of the Bute Docks, Cardiff, for three and a half millions, to the Taff Vale Railway Company. ' Benson and Herr. who were arrested for alleged fraud At the Hotel National at Geneva, have been tried and discharged. They have been banished from the canton. At a meeting of manufacturers, mineral owners, and County gentlemen in Glasgow, resolutions were adopted In favour c'" revision of the fiscal policyof the country. The 'old warship Victor, after having worm-eaten wood replaced by new timber, will be covered in canvas, and painted to resemble wood, when it is expected she will last another century.' • : On Saturday, Josenli Prior, aged 25. newspaper clerk, residing at 24, Ardenwan-street, Glasgow, committed i suicide n the Scottish New. Office, Glasgow, by drinking a large quantity of laudanum. An alarm of fire was raised at the Canterbury Music Hall, London, on Saturday evening. A few of the audience left their seats, but the panic was quickly allayed, and the fire, which was not serious, was soon extinguished. Sir Arthur Blackwood, Secretary of the Post-office, at Windsor, on Saturday, gave notice of appeal against the decision of the county magistrates on Saturday week, -when he was fined for an alleged infringement of one of the Thames Conservancy bylaws. The Duke of Cambridge has written a letter to the Council of the National Rifle Association giving his full sanction to the annual rifle meeting being once more tield upon Wimbledon Common. The council have accepted the Duke's offer, and the association will accordingly meet at Wimbledon next July.

In the Divorce Court, on Katurday, Mrs. Mary Orton, nil actress, professionally known as Blanche Elliott, brought a suit for the dissolution of her marriage with John Nicholas Orton. professionally known as Charles Ever- ton, an actor at the Princess and Vandeville Theatres, on the ground of adultery and desertion.—The Court held the allegations to be proved, and granted a cleave

Mrs. Michael, of North Somercotes, Lincolnshire, who is well known in the neighbourhood, attained her 100th year on Saturday last. The death was recorded on Saturday of Mrs. Margaret. Brace, residing at Typatrish Farm, l'embroy, at the remarkable age of 104 years. The old lady had been in the enjoyment of all her facul- ties, and wastn excellent health to within a forteight of her death.

On Saturday a mad repairer named Bidson was found in some old workings at Deep Ash Pits. Fenton, near Stoke, after being lost for 60 hours. On Wednesday. whilst leaving work alone, his lamp went out, and being a new hand he groped out in the dark until he got into some disused working, from which he could not find his way. When discovered 60 hours afterwards he was almost dead from exhaustion.

i At Wigan Qtuirter Sessions, on Saturday, there were only two boys, 13 years of age; for trial, charged (with break- ing into a ,number of shops and the Market Hall, and ransacking the tills. Both pleaded guilty. Hilton, who had been ,previously convicted, Was sentenced to ten days' imprisonment and five veers in d reformatory; and Bradshaw to three weeks'. imprisonment, making his term three months since his apprehension.

I Statistics were laid before ho Manchester Chamber of Commerce, on Monday, shofing an enormous growth of cotton spinning'in India, and increase of exports of yarns toChina and Japan, at the etpense of Lancashire cotton spinners. The silver question and the cheapness and long hours of labour were mentioned as giving Bombay spinners great advantages. The directors were requested to report as to the causes of the supereeasion of Lanca- shire spinners. I At Coventry, on Monday, a solicitor, named Walter W. Wale, until lately in practice in that city, was charged with three charges of forgery. It was alleged that by means of bogus signatures of his brother, thp prisoner succeeded in obtaining morgages on land in Warwick- shire to the amount of £3,000 from the Coventry Burial Society, and £6OO from local manufacturers. The pri- soner, who was arrested at Melbourne, and who apparently felt his position acutely, was committed for trial.

DAIRY FARMERS AND THE PRICE OF MEAT.—At a meeting of the dairy farmers, at Westhoughton, on Mon- day night, it was decided to form a branch of the Bolton and District. Farmers' Association. A committee was appointed to arrange for the sale of fat cattle by farmers to consumers, without dealing with the butchers ; it being stated that the consumers could be supplied at. 50. to 70. per lb., and the farmers obtain £6 or £7 more per bead by not trading with butchers, who would only pay low prices. Ctostrip OF THE LIVERPOOL EXIIIRITION.—TIIO Liver- pod Jubilee Exhibition finally closed on Monday, after a by no means successful run. With a building already erected and with little preliminary expense, it, was hoped that the indebtedness with which last. year's exhibition closed would this year be wiped off, but the'resnit is understood to be most unsatisfactory, and there is eon- , giAerable prObability that the call upon the guarantors Will be now heavier than it would have been had there iTiren no show this year. Last year's admissions were :about throe millions, but it is dotibtful if this year more than one million have passed the turnstiles.

The Appleby Corporation deny that it r their eiuty to repair it, and meantime the feundatiiititi are .4.itel to be quits unsafe, owing to the , sapprlifg of them by tho water. The bridge has been repaired for 200 years out of funds left by. the Countess ' of Pembroke for that purpose. 1 The Clyde shipbuilding trade, as evidenced by the out- put in October and the contracts entered Upon, shows a briskness most unusual in the present depressed state of the industry. During the month which closed yesterday . twelve vessels of 16,635 tons were launched from the ' Clyde, being eleven steamers of 16,035 tons, and one sail- : lug ship of 1,600 tons. The production in the present. I month exceeds that in the corresponding month last year by .10,001 tons, but 131,724 tons less than in October 1885. The total ler the ten months of the year now gone hiss reached 163.435 tons. The contracts already booked represent over 37,000 tons.

TON %MORS OF AN ENOLISII Fisnma SEACK.—The ' ease of the Grimsby smack. Lady- Godly'''. is not yet Ilpttl,eq, 9n _the 13ti1 May last the vessel and her crew , were captured by a German gunboat on a charge of fishing in territorial waters. Funnel!, the master, V 711.4 lodged in prison, but when tried on the 21st of July lie was acquitted. The German Government have. how. . ever, obtained an order for a new trial, which will take place at Leipsic early in the new year. Mr. fleneage. • who is interesting himself in the case, has written to Lord Salisbury commenting on the apathy shown by the L Hoard of Trade and the Foreign Office. •

Tux Lormost Unitsretornn.—Monday's meeting of the unemployed was the largest that has been held for Kane days, 6,000 or 7,000 persons being in Trafillizar- square. Speaking commenced at noon; and at 230 a Start was made for a parade through the city. The pro- cession was most orderly, hut. traffic was seriously im- peded. On returning to the square, about, two hours later, the speaking was resumed. One speaker said that to-morrow he would bring 2,000 men from the docks ti. join the meeting. The man George made a violent speech, in which he said, that if the authorities did not provide work, a few foggy nights would settle the matter.

........... ' A Blown lr PROMISE CLAIM ov £5,000.—0n Saturday there came on in the Queen's Bench Division, before Mr Justice Manisty and Mr. Justice Charles, upon motion, the case of Stephens v. Hissey.—Mr. Moyses, for the plaintiff, said that the action was for damages for breach of a promise of marriage, and his client claimed £.5,000. 'rhe defendant upon the writ was described as " Jilllll'S John Hissey," arid the present application, by way of appeal from Chambers, was to add after that name otherwise known as John Johnson, or Harry Johnson." (l.a.nghter.)-- Mr. Justice Men isty : The notice of motion was to alter the writ by adding the name ei James John Johnson or Harry Johnson; so that it would appear that two men had promised to marry the (Laughter.)—Mr. J3.lstice Charles: Surely the Intendment was not wanted.—Mr. Moyses said that there was some doubt of the identity of the defendant— (laughter)—and therefore the amendment was asked for. —Mr. Reginald Brown, for the defendant, in an.Swer to the court, said that his client had appeared to the action months ago, and had also answered internlations.—Mr Justice Idanisty thought that there really was no :Irene,. sity for the amendment The defendant had called himself by the name of " Hissey," and he had appeared by that name.—The appeal was dismissed:

PROVINCIAL MAYORS AND THE LORD. MAYOR OF LON• DON.—The Lord Mayor of London (Sir R. hansomliart) was on Monday entertained to a banquet at the Mari- cheater Town Hall, by the Mayors of Lancashire and Cheshire. The Mayor of Manchester presided.—Respond- ing to the toast of his health, Sir Reginald Hanson said he had no doubt that the compliment which the provin. cial mayors had paid him attached more to his race than to the individual. He had had the great good fortune to be Lord Mayor during an important year, during which he had discharged the wish of the citizens of London in showing, if possible, more consideration and civility to his brethren in all parts of her Majesty's dominions. At an early period of his mayoralty he invited the provincial mayors to meet the Prince of Wales at the Mansion House with reference to the Imperial Institute, and he believed it was greatly owing to that association of mayors that the success of the object was conduce& Referring to local self-government, the Lord Mayor observed that, as he understood it, local self- government meant that those who were elected repre• sented the local ideas, the local wants, and even the local prejudices.. Theoretically. no one would deny that the best idea of government was a benevolent and omni- scient despot, if they could get one, hut they knew that was absolutely impossible, and, therefore, they must be representatives of the people, who occasionally erred, and who were frequently right. (Laughter and Hear, hear.)

IRELAND.
Lord Dillon has conceded 25 per cent. on the rent due.
Three fishermen whilst lifting their lines off Port- patrick, on Sunday, during the gale, were drowned through the capsizing of their boat.

The Duke of Devonshire has issued a circular to his Irish tenantry' informing them that he will allow an abatement of 25 per cent, in the rents now payable. Very few of his grace's tenants have gone into the Land Court.

Mr. Joseph Cox, M.P. for West Clare, was served in Dublin. on _Monday, with three surnmones. under the Crimes Act, for taking part In several meetings in county Clare, which had been proclaimed by order of the Lord Lieutenant.

On Sunday, Monsignor Persico !solemnly consecrated rather Camilus Beardwood abbot of the Cistercian abbey of Mount St- Joseph, near Birr. There were more than 10,000 persons present at the eeremony. The troops in tbemeighbourhood were confined to barracks.

A °elision took place on Saturday between an evicted tenant named Bernard Burns ana emergency men at Aughavilla, near Warren Point. Burns had retaken pos- session of the farm from which he had been evicted, and the emergency men endeavoured to eject him, and Burns offered a stubborn defence, in the conrse of which he was shot in the knee by a bailiff named M`Nulty, who has been taken into custody. MR. O'BRIEN'S MEETINGS. Mr. William O'Brien. M.P., spoke at a meeting on Sun- day in Kanturk, county Cork, which had been called at short notice by his friends in the neighbourhood. Captain • Seagrave, R.M., and District Inspector Yates were not aware of the meeting until about noon, and all the police from the district had then been sent to Middleton for Monday's proceedings there. No attempt was, therefore, made to interfere with the meeting, but permission VMS asked and granted for the Government reporter to be present.. Mr. O'Brien congratulated the tenants of the Loader estate at Currass on their strong combination against rack rents. The plan of campaign had effectually protected the homes of the Irish people, and had struck the fear of God into rack- renters and land-grabbers. They clung to the new Land Act while hope of adequate redress for tenants remained. hut after being mangled ir. the House of Lords it was now turned into a downright curse and mockery by the appointment of a gang of broken-down rack-renters and bumbailiffs to administer it.. He believed the plan would organise itself this winter on a scale which would completely dwarf its previous efforts. He repeated the advice of Mr. Wadstone ito shun outrages as they would shun poison, and to have patience to await their victory over the landowners.

MR. O'BRIEN'S APPEAL—EXCITING SCENES. Mr. W. O'Brien.M.P., arrived at Cork, on Monday. from Mallow, and was received with cheers by a crowd at the station, lie drove to the Victoria Hotel, where a similar roception was accorded him. At ten o'clock he left Cork again, by train, for Midleton, to ho present at 'the pro- ceedings in connection with his appeal against the sentence by the Mitchelstown magtstrates. Mr. O'Brien left the Midleton train at Queenstown Junction, and was there met by a large sqqpmblage of members • ..e." National f,eagne bnowl with their bands and banners, and by a large contium. of horse- men, all with their green cords of membership in their hats, and many carrying banners. The cavalcade was drawn along the roadside, and extended for a consider- able distance beyond the station. Mr. O'Brien and his friends drove to Carrington Hilt, where there was an imposing demonstration of horsemen, bands. and National League contingents. Addresses were presented from local bodies, the Gaelic Athletic Association, and National Leagueivbratiches. Mr. O'Brien. in reply, said he had never in his life seen such striking evidence of the unquestionable spirit which animated Irish people at the present day, and it would be compensation to him, not only for a wretched three months' imprisonment imposed upon him, but also for his lifelong labour in the Irish cause. He asked, in con- clusion, that the people would give evidence of their disciplinary spirit, and ref rain from marching into Midisten. Mr. John Dillon srtoke to a similar effect. _ . _

- . - Qs% rtliwnin Midleton there was a further demonstra- tion, but Ole people were kept in order by a force of police, Highlanders, and hussars. On reaching the court- house Mr. O'Brien's rase was immediately called by the clerk, Mr. Hamilton, Recorder of Cork, sitting as quarter kiessions judge.

- - Mr. Carson was about to open the ease for the Crown, when Mr. O'Brien rose and, addressing the Recorder, said he would make a statement which probably might shorten the proceedings. Ile was not represented by counsel, and would like to explain why be was not, Mr. Carson objected to Mr. O'Brien speaking at this point. , The Recorder said be would prefer to have evidence to assure himself that the Crown case was proved. Mr. Ccrson t! m opened his ease. Mr. O'Brien was then asked to reply, and he referred to the statement made by Mr. Betelltan, in which he quoted the decision lw B.tron Bramwell in the case .of the police assault, and said he should be a hypocrite if he pretended to have the smallest ground whatever to think that he shetallaye ap unprejudiced trial in a cast 'upon which Baron had already d.eided. • The 11.M'atel r, 4k-74Tiffinft ern-Vet:lion whlelche quoted referred to quite a different cause, said that, as_llf.fr. 'Brien had declined to proceed with the .'sl43;tunciii:Vii to give a decision. There was no doubt Mr. O'Brien's language complained of was an in- citement to mast the authorities, and he regretted to have to confirm the sentence in the first case. The second case against Mr. O'Brien was then pro. ceeded with.

Mr. O'Brien %ves about to leave .I,ti .:‘,•1: speak to some friends when a district inspector stopped him, and told him he could n,ot go. Mr. O'Brien insisted that he had a right to go, and struggled with the inspector and several police. The people in court grew terribly excite.d, and Mr. Harring- ton ran to his assistance, returning in a few moments to the solicitors' table, and in an excited tone led for justice for his friend. He maintained that Mr. O'Brien could not legally be arrested, as a warrant had not been signed for his arrest. _ . . . . .
- -Mr. Carson argued against Ails, but ultimately the Recorder took Mr. Harrington's view of the case, and said Mr. O'Brien should go. . .

This announcement was received with tremendous cheers in court, in the midst of which Mr. Stokes' divi- sional resident magistrate, got up and shouted, "Don't let him ,go; I will be responsible for the consequences." A fresh hubbub followed this. Mr. Harrington called out, "There you are: that is a fresh example of how justice is administered in this country! The authority of the Judge is defied." . . .

A terribly exciting scene followedl in which shouts were raised of "Open the doors' let him mit ! " and cries were repeated of "Justice! Justice!" while a struggle took o+o between the police, who were told ofT to guard Mr. O'Brien. and some of Mr. O'Brien's friends... . .

A consultation took place in the yard of the court- house, between Mr. Stokes and Mr. Eaton, MM.'s, and a warrant was in the meantime found, and sizned by the magistrate and the Petty Sessions clerk, of Mitchelstown, who Wall in attendance. A surging mass of policemen and civilians filled half of the ~,rthoilse, and the noise and confusion was terrible.
Mr. O'Brien, hoarse and pantinz, was atruggling violently with his captors, and Mr. Dillon and Dr. Tanner loudly proclaimed their opinions or rho treatment their friend was receiving.

A warrant NMI ultimately produced, and Mr. O'Brien was then removed to the back of the Courthouse in custody. Meanwhile Mr. Dillon returned to the conrt. and, addressing the Recorderolenntinced the illegal detention of Mr. O'Brien. and said that if that was justice they might as well take him into custody too. The Recorder said he should order him intocustody if be did not desist from addressing the Court. Mr. Dillon was about to reply, when Mr. Flarrington called him over to the opposite side of the Court__
Amidst. much noise and clamour the proenedingt9 in connection with the second charge were briefly disposed of, and the Recorder confirmed the t;entence in that 171,,A0 also. . _

The case of Mr. John Mendoville, on a similar charge, was then called, and as he declined to proceed with his appeal, the. sentence against him was confirmed, and he. too, was removed in custody. . . . .

There was great excitement outside when it became known that such a scene had occurred in the Court- house, and the people thronged round. The Highlanders and Hussars. who were guarding the Streets, were then called up, and a line was formed in front of the Court- house, and no person was allowed past it. Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Mandeville, after being kept in custody until nearly three o'clock. sere unexpectedly brought up from the cells and driven in a closed carriage —acecnnpanied by two police inspectors and escorted by a half troop of Hussars—to Cork. Cheers were raised as they left, but there was no attempt at rescue or disturb- ance. Shortly after- the roll kqe had passed a tnan was seen to fall on the read, about half-a-mile from Midleton. He was raised by some bystanders. but was found to be dead, the excitement having evidently killed him. It was stated that he had suffered from heart disease. The town speedily became quiet after the pri- soners bad been removed, and the soldiers and police were withdrawn from the streets.
—.„ Mr. Herbert Gladstone. addressing a meeting on Mon- day night at Glimffosv. saki in the name of those assembled he wished" God speed to O'Brien."

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., was transferred at an early hour on Wednesday morning from Cork Gaol to Tul- lainore Prison, where he will undergo his sentence. Mr. Mandeville was conveyed along With him. TEE Feta Tastinis.—A conference under the auspices of the National Fair Trade League met on Wednesday in London for the purpose of advocating a reversal of our fiscal policy. Mr. S. Cunliffe Lister, who presided, said they contended that everything foreign should be taxed. In the case of raw materials and everything within the Empire an exception would be made. Other speakers alleged that England could not regain the position she once held unlessthe proposed alterations took place.

THE BOLTON STRIKE.--THE BASES .1 OF SETTLEMENT. ry On Saturday afternoon, a mass meeting of the men on , strike at Bolton took place in the Co-operative Hall for , the purpose of receiving the bases of agreement for the i!commencement of operations. Mr. Charles Hough, I chairman of the Joint Committee, presided, and there was a crowded attendance. The following were the ;terms submitted, and tike men accepted them, and re- sumed work this morning t•--- 1 1. That the workmen now on strike agree to resume ''work as required at the present rate Of wages, and for a 'period of tnree weeks from this date overtime shall be . restricted to breakdowns and shop repairs; after the ex- ' piry of sue: 'Pm all restrictions as to overtime be re- moved, bin It the award be given within that time nit restrictions be removed from the date of the award. 2. That a committee be formed, consisting of five re- presentative.' of Bolton employers and five represen- tatives of the workmen as a Board of Inquiry and, Conciliation. 3. That this committee shall immediately examine into • the question as to whether the Mate of trade existing in ' Bolton when the strike commenced as compared with ' that existing when wages were last reduced vrarrauteit .' an advance in the rate of wages. 4. That if an advance was then warranted, the com- mittee shall recommend the amount to he granted as art advance on the present rate of wages, such advance not , to exceed the amount of 2s. per week. I 5. That should no advance be recommended, thw committee may decide that the question be adjourned to a date agreed upon to be settled • by the Board of Inquiry. I 6. That Should there be any dispute or impossibility of agreement an umpire shall he appointed by both sides, to whom the question shall be referred for settle- ment 7. That the award, if resulting in an advance, 'shalt come into operation on the first pay-day in January. 1888. _

8. That on the acceptance of this proposal the strike shall be declared at an end on the authority of the Joint Committee, and that all picketing shall ce.ase at all firma by whom the proposals are accepted. 9. That on the foregoing being agreed to it is under- stood that the employers and workmen will each feel bound to act in the beat Manner to restore the publx. peace of the town and allay the present feeling of ; irritation. Signed on behalf of the men: lt. liaatow. Secretary C. Bonin, Chairman ; Banc Signed on bebalf of the Bolton iron Trades' Associa- tion: B. A DOBAOtt, Chairman. . .

But he has strong convictions, and, as he shows himself active in promulgating his views, it is a matter of course that those who want to let things alone should el out against him. Mr. BRUNNER was so much la earnest on the Irish question that he went te Ireland to judge of the situation for himself. lie was at Mitchelstown when the affray took place with the police; and, as soon as it was seen that the official statement of what took place was 3 lying statement, it was natural for people in thie country to wish to hear what an independee! witness had to say. THOMAS MORRIS seems some.snvhcbacon„„„ judging from a letter winch appears rboon 10;0;a: porary, that those with whom he has TY a eu ing to make the Warrington, I.4hra

ing ,LitYary are not satisfied with the arrange-1 Ment that has been made to charge one penny per, book. But he should remember that it was no part of the programme of his Committee to con- sider such a proposal; and that, so far as the principle is concerned, the question remains exk- actly where it was. Surely Mr. MORRIS cannot have forgotten that he said the ratepayers were just as much entitled to have the books free, after paying the rate, as they were to the bread they ate, after paying for it. This being so, it does not touch the contention in the least to charge one penny per book instead of is. 6d. per quarter. If the second tax—the charge which is made in addi- tion to the rate—is an unjust tax, it does not cease to be unjust by being imposed at the rate of one penny per book. Mr. MORRIS set himself to the task of making the Library as free as it is in other towns; he has turned aside before it is accom- plished, and, what is more, he is disappointed with those who, having nailed their colburs to the mast, have resolved to stand by them. It is needless to say that, in a matter of this kind, the disappoint- ment is mutual. With regard to the law of the ease, Mr. MORRIS makes much of what was said at the four sub-committee meetings which he attended, along with Messrs. Alderman DAVIES, T. G. Rmkrrns, ROBERT PIERPOINT, and F. MONKS. Granted that the matter was gone into so as to satisfy Mr. MORRIS that "law- yers could twist the act from one mean- ing to another until they had twisted from him all the money and goods and chattels he was worth, and even then be left flOundering," it should still be remembered that these sub-com- mittee meetings were private, and that the state- ments which seem to have weighed ' with Mr. Moiturs could not weigh with his Committee, simply because they were not before them. What they had before them was the statement of the Attorney-General, that "there is no authority under the Public Libraries Act of 1855 to make any distinction between persons who subscribe and persons who do not." Are they to be blamed because, in the face of this plain statement, that subscribers are not entitled to any privileges over ' non-subscribers, they say "We cannot regard a penny a book as satisfactory when there is no ' authority to make a charge at all ?" Lawyers can twist, it is true, but it is to be said of them as tO this matter, that not one of the lawyers on the committee has taken upon himself to publicly , grapple with the opinion of the Attorney-General, and show either thst it is bad law, or that it car-
rie& a meaning other than that which is to be ';t. found on the surface. If the Attorney-General
is in the right, the Library -Committee are in the
Wrong; and if they ar in the wr' ong it is the duty of, law-abiding citizens to insist that the law shall be obeyed. It is somewhat surprising to 414 find Mr. Moszas in this connection, quoting /Mr.

‘s._, T. GREENWOOD, the author of "Free Public Libraries," because Mr. GREENWOOD has alreitdy 'il expressed his conviction, in the columns of this 1.. ; journal, that the Warrington Library Corn- ...'. mittee are breaking the law in making a
charge for the s loan of books If Mr. k MORRIS had not, in .submitting his quo- tation, broken off in the middle of a sen- z tence, it .‘would have been seen that Mr. GREEN-

Wool), in referring to the word " free " means, that Free Libraries are not strictly free, seeing that they are supported out of the rates. The full paragraph is as follows:—" Public Libraries and News Rooms can never be wholly or entirely free any more than can water or gas, and it would appear a misnomer to call them free. The Acts of Parliament always use the the phrase, 'Public Libraries 'never' free, but all the Public Libraries'

are not free in the sense that are these rate- supported institutions, and hence the description ,k‘ usually given them"—that is Free Libraries. Mr, tIC M. onnis is, of course, entitled to his opinion, and :If he thinks those who have worked with him should now "rest and be thankful," we have to " say that we differ from him. The questiOn now is what is the best course to take; and our advice is, as this is purely a ratepayers' question, to bring the matter before the Ratepayers' Association. It is scarcely advisable under the circumstances to have two Committees at work, and already a considerable number of those who were members of the Lending Library Committee have beconie znembers of the Ratepayers' Association. Let Others join, so that the Association may be ren- dered strong enough to bring this and other ques- tions to a successful issue.
THE Manchester Chamber of Commerce was oc-
cupied for a considerable time, on Monday, in con-

_ eidering a resolution moved by Mr. J. C. FIELDEN, i to the effect pat it was desirable to institute an . inquiry into "the recent very rapid increase of cotton spinning in India, and the exports of yarn therefrom, more especially to China and Japan, While at the same time there has been a very Serious check to the growth of Lancashire yarn ex- Ports to those countries." In the course of the ' discussion on the resolution, which was ultimately unanimously adopted, Mr. HENRY LEE gave the result of his experience in visiting the cotton mills of India. He seemed to think that the rapid pro.. grees with cotton which was being made there was clue- to low wages and long hours of labour. No nitive, he said, except he was in a superior posi- tion, got more than five shillings per week, whilst the mills commenced work at daybreak, and never 4 &topped until the sun went down. Bad as is the s, eotton trade sometimes in this country, the
workers have never been reduced to such miser- able wages, or been compelled to work such long hours, and we trust they never will. Fair Traders

are always trying to make it out that England is going to the dogs; but a consideration of the con- ditions of work in the cotton trade leads to the con- -lusion that we stand on a firmer footing than our colnpetitors in either India or America. Wages !rill certainly rise in India; Parliament will step la, as it has stepped in in this country, to interfere With the hours of labour for women and children; and then the conditions of competition being more nearly equal, we shall kedp in front, as of Y°re. As it is, it is curious to note that America " isn't in it." With cotton at

_ their doors, and "blessed" with Protection, the 'United States ought, if Protection is a blessing, to leave England behind in the race. But what says r. PIELDEN ? "kidia had cotton on the spot. Illitkso had the United States of America, with a great deal more of it, of a great deal bettei• quality, and with a more inventive population—a Polation of the energy and capacity to give ,"irth to great industries. Yet the United States "acl never dared to and could not meet us in neu- !rat markets." Again :—" We had to get our cot- "nl and send it back to-the far East. That was a :ell' serious charge on us, but we had to remember r4t America, with all these, conditions in her 'wour, could not hold her oFn markets against 48, and had to put a 35 per cent. duty on our coin- rao nest goods to keep us out." Mr. FIELDEN'S leruarks were made, it should be said, without any. 'eference to the question of Fair Trade; but we hut it to the Fair Traders, and ask them how it /7P.peris, if Protection is an advantage, that the lilted States, with Protection, and with cotton

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: ion the spot, cannot compete with England in the neutral markets? Our own explanation of the matter is simple, and it is that Protection en- hances the price of the article produced, and in the long run discourages rather than encourages trade. If the cotton trade were Protected in this country, as it is in America, the price of cotton goods would increase, and the result would be thal we should endanger and perhaps lose our trade in the neutral markets. And the same reasoning applies all round. Free Trade means low prices, and low prices mean that goods are accepted which would otherwise be shut out of the market. Fair Trade means high prices, and consequent incapacity to compete in neutral markets. America being such a vast co\mtry, and having, to begin with, such vast natural resources, can better afford to lose outside markets than other countries. Fngland, on the 'other hand, being small and an old country, has to depend largely on foreign trade. Protec- tion by raising prices would cripple us in compli- tition ; it is a cut-throat policy, and fit only for the adoption of the inmates of a lunatic asylum.

div.head: "TOUCH. AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH. AND GO."

Mr. , Spurgeon has left the Baptist Union; but the world still spins round. As the Rev. S. Guinness Rogers said the other day—" The whole piety of the world did Aot resolve itself into the Metropolitan Tabernacle."

"A widow named Drew has died near Thurles, at the age of 105 Years. During life she never re- quired the services of a physician." She was like ,the old stager of whom Waugh sings:—" He ne'er had a doctor—he deed of hissel."

It will be gathered from a report of the pro- ceedings of the Runcorn School Board that there is an epidemic of measles, and an epidemic of ap- plications for increase of salaries. It has not yet be determined which of the' two' attacks is the more objectionable.

The "Moscow Gazette" recommends that Gib- raltar should be neutralised as well as the Suez Canal. This is cool; the frost has set in early in Russia. By-the-by, how would it be for the Lon- don "Gazette" to suggest that Moscow should be neutralised? It would be tit for tat.

It is stated that the Cheshire Cheese is "to be immortalised by having its picture painted, and hung in the next Academy;" but it is the Che- shire Cheese of London—not Latchford. There are "larks" at times at the local Cheshire Cheese, but at the metropolitan hostelry they go beyond this—they have lark pies.

The "Times" is rather hard on Mr. Matthew's. In suggesting that Sir Michael Hicks-Beach will take his place as Home Secretary, it-says—" We shall certainly want in time to come both firmness and tact in a Home Secretary." This means that, Mr. Matthews is lacking in both. Poor Mr. Mat- thews! He will be tempted to say—" Save me from my friends."

Colliers will run risks, and break the law in do- ing so. At St. Helens, on Monday, William Ped- ley, a Haydock miner, was fined 20s. and costs for working underneath four, or five tons of ‘oal with- out using props. It is not long since he was cau- tioned. The fine was a heavy one; but it would be as wellto try imprisonment if heavy fines awe not found to be a sufficient terror to these under- ground evil-doers.

John Sharpe, of Walton-le-dale, was brought be- fore the Newton magistrates, on Saturday, on a charge of stealing two puppies. He was caught red-handed, or perhaps we should say, full-handed.. He pleaded that he was eccentric when in drink, .but it would seem that there is method in his mad- ness. Perhaps it would cure him to put him on. a crank--an eccentric crank—for a month. He was treated leniently—let off with a fine of 10s. and costs. •

Warrington .is becoming graceful. With refer- ence to the Mayoralty, it is stated that, on Tuesday, Alderman Sutton gracefully retired in favour of Councillor Francomb ; and that, on Wednesday, Councillor Francomb gracefully re- tired in favour of Alderman Sutton. It only remains for Alderman Sutton to gracefully retire in favour of somebody else—gay Councillor John Greening—for Warrinron to be regarded as the home of "the three graces."

Lord lierby shrewdly observed at Liverpool, on Tuesday, that the growth of debt in Europe had something to do with the growth of Socialism. It certainly is something to "give us pause' to learn that in Europe 160 millions per year are being paid in interest on debt. It is a large sum for the workers to raise before they can set aside any- thing for themselves ; and so Lord Derby thinks they become Socialists and talk of repudiating debt.

Lord Derby had a neat cut at Mr. Goschen for the way in which he laid his hand, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, on the sum set aside for regay- ment of debt. It was not, his lordship said, "that the amount withdrawn was in itself so great, but when a sum had been set apart for a purpose of that kind, to break in upon it without absolute need was like a first glass of wine to a pledged teetotaller; the rule was violated, and when it was once broken it waS harder to keep it in future." Moral: when the pledge is taken, either as to financing or fuddling, keep it.

The students of the Widnes Science and Art School do not seem to be depressed by their de- pressing surroundings. The thirteenth annual report, just issued, shows a large percentage of passes; it is considerably above the average of the rest of the country. Principal Rendall, who dis- tiibuted the prizes, urged the students to look be- yond passes and grants in their labours. He would have them "always aspire ; " like 'Shelley's sky- lark, they are recommended to go "higher still and higher."

Lord Lytton's appointment to the post of Eng- lish Ambassador at Paris pleases no one—except Lord Lytton. He succeeds Lord Lyons, but no- body believes he will succeed like Lord Lyons. As Viceroy of India, he showed himself utterly un- scrupulous in forcing war upon the Ameer of Afghanistan, and altogether he got England and India into a nice mess. "Our prancing pro- consul," as he has been aptly termed, is not the man for Paris—unless the object of the Govern- ment is to get us into trouble with the French.

-Where mere the Warrington police on the night 'of Monday, the 24th October? Where they look- ing on when the seven or eight rounds were fought in Horsemarket-street between the landlord and the pork butcher, or where they "round the cor- ner ? " The Mayor pertinently remarked thatit Was "disgraceful for respectable men to be engaged in such rows." He might have gone further, and said that respectable men who fought seven rounds in the public streets ceased to be respect- able.

Thomas, at Itincorn Police Court, •on Thursday, Elizabeth Ellen Road, a .bad character, was convicted of having wilfully broken a pane of glass at the Mariners' Hotel, and was ordered to pay £2 7s 6d, being fine, damages, and costs. • : DYsos's DIORAMA AD WinNEs.-,Mr. Dyson's entertain- ment has drawn crowded audiences to the Widnes Volun- teer Hall each evening during the past week. The dio- ramie part of the performance is one of the finest to be witnessed in theprovinces, and the.. Choruses and solos • are rendered by the gipsy choir hi a style that merits approval. On Sunday, sermons •in aid -of the same abject were • preached. • THE TALK OF VISE Towx.—Howell's* Golden Herb 4dut.

I Mr. A. Carnegie will have good reason to thank the Wolverharupton Grand Jurors for making a presentment against his brk—" Triumphant Democracy." It is a splendid advertisement of a splendid work: Fancy a jury, uncalled upon, taking upon itself to say that the work ought not to be in the Free Library because it reflects upon the Queen! The greatest resection on the Queen is this Wolverhampton Jury. They have reviewed the book without reading it; reading it would have preudiced them—in its favour.

The Liverpool Exhibition closed on Monday night, when there was a disposition to indulge in mischievous horseplay, as at the first Exhibition; but the presence of an extra number of constables was as a wet blanket to the exubeitnt roughs. As everybody knows, the Exhibition has not been a success. The attendance \ has been about one million—that is, about one-third of the attendance at the previous Exhibition. It was a piece of folly to hold a second Exhibition, and it is folly which will have to be paid for, as the guarantors too well realise.

Mr. 3. Buckley, of the Pineapple Inn, Shaw, seems to have had easy notions of engagement§ with the fair sex. "When I want a suit of clothes, I choose my own cloth," he remarked to the young woman who has since had to sue him for breach of promise. He changed his cloth, but the jury did not seem to agree with his theory of matrimonial tailoring. They have given damages against him for £BO. The landlord of the Pineapple takes a new view of things to-day; he finds that having made a choice, it is a costly thing to be "non- suited" in the matter of matrimonial cloth.

The verdict in the Cass case cannot be said to be satisfactory. It seems to be law, but is it jus- tice?. It comes to this—that it is all but impossi- ble to convict a policeman of perjury. Both Mr. Smith and Mr. Matthews, when the subject was raised in the House of Commons, suggested that it could not be a question of mistake on the part of the policeman; but, according to Mr. Justice Stephen, it is all a mistake. SO it is, and an officer who could be capable of such a mistake ought never again to be permitted to enter the police force.

In the preface to his "Letters on Sweden and Norway," Mr. R. A. Naylor says :—" If a 'person possessed an enemy, it would be very desirable be- fore issuing anything approaching a volume to ponder over the words wisely written by the, ;Teat master of "English literature-7' Oh that Mine enemy would write a book." Just so, and it would have been just as well if Mr. Naylor had pondered before referring to "the greitt master of English literature." The writer of the sentence which Mr:Naylor. quotes (inaccurately) was not an Englishman; he was a Jew, of the name of Job.

A disgraceful instance of the way in which jus- tice is administered in Ireland was witnessed, on Monday, on the hearing of the appeal of Mr. W.. O'Brien. After the decision in the first case was given against him, and while the second case was being heard, he was interrupted in his attempt to leave the court, although he was not under arrest. A struggle with the police ensued, and an appeal was made to the Recorder, who acted as jud,4e. He decided that Mr. O'Brien was at liberty for the present, but, notwithstanding this, Captain Stokes, a resident magistrate, set the Pourt at defiance, and ordered Mr. O'Brien's arrest. Talk of con- tempt of court—was ever a court treated more contemptuously ?

I In passing judgment on Mr. O'Brien, the Rebor- , der said: 4 Unless the decrees of the courts of 'law can be carried out, the existence of those 1 courts of law Ny oul d be absurd." It was shortly I after this that the Reborder had his decree set ' aside by Captain Stokes; and this, too, not in ianother room, or in another town, but under his very eyes. If the Recorder had any -respect for . himself, or for his court, he would have insisted on i 1 Captain Stokes being arrested. But, after laying I down the law, he allowed it to be broken. It is I stated that Mr. O'Brien will take action against i ' Captain Stokes; if there is such a thing as jus- tice in Ireland, his action will be successful.

The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, but was ad- mitted to bail in two sureties of £5O each. THE GALE AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN.—A gale of ter- rific violence swept over the district on Tuesday morning last. In every part of both towns slates and chimney, pots strewed the streets, and so strong was the wind that pedestrianism was rendered both difficult and dan- gerous. In the aggregate tha damage done was con- siderable, but there is no single instance of heavy disas- ter. A large shed at the-Weston Works was partially un- roofed, and the chimney of Mr W. R. Harp in Halton- lane was levelled to the ground. At Hough Green, near Widnes, the roof of Mr Peter Longton s brewery was blown off, and the shippon of Mr:Voss, Hammer and Pincers Inn, was almost totally demolished. A similar fate befel a barn belonging to Mr Ireland at Halton View. Whilst the storm was at its height the flat " Myra," belonging to Mr Lewis Kilcross, at Widnes, I went ashore at , Puffin Island, near Llandudno, and quickly became a total wreck. A young man named 1 William Dutton, son of the captain of the boat, was. drowned, but the remainder of the crew succeeded in I scrambling npon the rocks. The schooner "West.- 'wood," which left Weston Point on Monday, dragged I her anchors whilst in the sloyne, and, after coming in I, contact with the training ship "Indefatigable," became a total wreck on Tranmere stage. Two of the crew, I both Scotchmen, were drowned. The mate, John Leslie -I Hall, of Runcorn, in relating his experiences, said he had , journeyed to all parts of the world, and he had never ex- perienced such a gale before. SUICIDE OF A FARNWORTH LADY.-- A deep gloom has this week fallen over the quiet little village of Farnworth by the melancholy and tragic end of one of I its well-known inhabitants. A few weeks ago Mrs., (net Miss Maddock), wife of Mr. Jams 3 Lewis, of The Poplars, Peelhouse-lane, was confined, and since then she has been in a rather depressed state of mind. About ten o'clock on Monday morning she left home, and went to her mother's, Coroner's-lane, where she, remained un- I till half-past five in the evening, when shelrturned. At I a quarter-past six she was seen by a neighbour to leave the house, informing this person that she was going to I the Post Office. After that nothing was heard of her for some time, and a search was made, the dead body being discovered at a later period of the evening by P.C. Hea- ton and Mr. Thomas Maddock, deceased's brother, in a pond of water not far from her home. Mr. W. T. Hus- band, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Hotel, Farnworth, on the body. It appeared from HIS evidence that Mrs. Lewis, who Is only 23 years of age, became a mother in August last, and had since been in a weak and despondent state. On Monday evening she left the house about a quarter-past six, stating that she was going to post a letter. Eliza Patten, wife of Robert Patten, in whose care Mrs. Lewis was, sent a servant to ascertain if Mrs. Lewis had really gone to the post. The servant saw nothing of her mistress and a search was made, with the result that Mrs. Lewis's dead body was found in a pit on Marsh Hall Farm. The deceased had.' left a letter, which, however, was not made public, the coroner having previously rernindsd the jury that they must not pander to any idle curiosity, or listen to out- side tales. P.C. Heaton said that any one to get into the pit must do so intentionally. A verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst in an unsound state of mind was returned.

THB HYDROPHOBIA SCARP. -- At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the clerk to the magistrates (Mr. Buckton). said that a dog of the fox terrier breed had recently been seen at San- key Bridges, running towards Penketh. On its way it attempted to bite two persons, and also attacked two doge. It was kiiled by a Police constable, and a veterinary surgeon afterwards declared that it had' been suffering from a bad attack of rabies. It was stated that the Act directing the control of dogs was in force in most of the neighbouring police divisions, and the magistrates ordered that the, Dogs' Act should be put in force in the Warrington county police division until the end of January. GENERAL RESULTS OF MUNICIPAL CONTESTS.-- The Press Association says that in more than the usual number ,of instances there was no contest, and the boroughs in which eleotions were not fought upon party political grounds appear to be on the increase. The poll in some cases,' especially in the North of England, was interfered, with by the severe gale which raged during the morning. Many of the contests are stated to have been fought on personal and not political grounds, though the gentlemen returned may have shown political leanings. Fuller returns of Tuesday's ' municipal elections show that the' Liberals gained 73 seats, the Ccinservatives 51, and the Liberal ' Unionists three. 1 THE Sim, CANAL—During the week two gentle- men, engineers, who are engaged by the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company, have been staying at the Patten Arms, Warrington. It is stated that they have been busy carrying out arrangements with reference to the construction of the canal between Runcorn and Warrington, where, it is anticipated, active operations will before long commence.

VISITORS TO BI+CEPOOL should stay at the Station Temper- ance Rotel, right opposite Central Station. Central position. Commodious and aeoommodating. Terms easy.—Apply J. Itesp.—Adet. WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB. The committee appointed by a meeting of Liberals for the purpose of establishing a club for the party have acted with great promptitude. Part of the premises in Alforde-street, recently occupied by the Local Board 7 have been rented froM the owners, and the rooms were opened as a club on Tuesday even- ing last. The boardroom has been converted into a bil- liard-room, for which itis admirably adopted, and the committee room adjoining makes a comfortable reading- room. There is a comModious lavatory attached. As the club has been formed for the working-men of the town, it is not deemed necessary to have the rooms open the whole of the day, and the hours fixed are from five to eleven in the evening. The subscription is fixed at the small sum of 4s per annum. Mr. Joseph Morrison, who has taken a prominent part in the formation of the club, is chairman of the committee, and Mr. Frank Cave is the hon. sec. _ .

Ferarwcarrn PARISH. CHURCH. —On Sunday special choral services in aid of the fund for supplying the choir of St. Luke's Church, Farnworth, who igve their servicns ' quite voluntarily, with • new books, and renewing old ones, and other appliances, was held in that place of worship. In the morning the Vicar occupied the pulpit, the Rev. C. W. Wooll„ M i :A., of Ditton, assisting n the service. The musical portion was very beautiful and most efficient. The processional hymn was ",Onward, Christian soldiers'," the other hymn being "Angel voices ever singing." Dyke's "Te Deum " and Garrett's "Nicene Creed" were also sung. The anthem, "The Wilderness" (John Goss), was tastefully rendered by the choir, under the able conductorship,of Mr. Watts, the bass solo being taken by Mr. J. R. Lea, the tenor recitative by Mr. Warburton, and the trio by Miss Bond, Mr. War- burton, And Mr. J. R. Lea. The communion service was also choral, the hymn during administration being "Hear, omy God." The " Sanctus" and "Gloria in Excelsis " were both sung, the solo in the latter being taken by Miss Fogg. The service concluded with Dr. Stainer's sevenfold Amen. The pulpit in the evening was occupied by the Rev., S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. : Paul's, Warrington, and the musical potion was again very efficient. On both occasions there were good con- gregations, especially in the evening, and the collections were eminently. satisfactory. div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monhly meeting was held at the Town llall on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Messrs. S. C. Beclvett, E. Imisun, F. A. Lake, and Dr. McDougall; G. Moss (clerk.)

I , , , SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The 'School Attendance Committee reported that 29 parents were summoned to attend.before the committee on the 12th October, and 22 parents or other representa- tives attended. Suitable warnings were given; It was also recommended that Visitor Howard's salary be ad- vanced from £7O to £75 per annum. Such advance to commence on December Ist. At a meeting held on the 25th October 21 parents appeared before the committee, . and in a number of cases it was ordered that proceedings 'should be taken before the magistrates.—The Clerk re- ! ported that the Guardians had held a meetingin that room during the month to receive applications from poor parents, who are not paupers, for school fees to be granted. Fifty-one cases were heard and fees were granted in 44 cases for various periods. During the month the visitor had served 261 notices, many of these having resiilted in improved attendance. The gross average attendance for the month was 2.361, as against 2,501 for the same period last year. The decreased average was caused by the epidemic of measles, but he believed the disease was now abating, and the Board might hope for a better state of attendance.
The rii—inutys were pasi,:ci: _

On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, accounts amounting to 06 N. 7. were passed for payment.—On the motion of Mr. Imison, seconded by Mr. S. C. Beckett, it was resolved to amal- gamate the various committees into one committee to be composel of the whole of the members of the Board and designated as the "General Purposes Committee."'

The balance in hand on the 29th September, 1886, was £B5 1,7 s 3d, the grants from the committee of the Council on Education—was £274 2s 2d,the payments to the, Board by the rating authorities was £950. School fees amountea to £154 12s 11d, and other small items brought up the receipts to £1,523 19s 88: The expenditure amounted to £1,417 8s 4d, and included £273 3s 4d; salaries of officers of the Board; £9B 6s 2d, legal and other expenses of adminis- tration; salaries of teachers, £477 6s 5d • lighting, clean- ing, and repairs to building and furniture, £llB les 4d; contributions towards the expenses of industrial school, £26 2s ; the repayment of principal .of loans, £lB4 9s ; and interest on loans ma: There was a total balance to the credit of thellbard of £lO6 Us 4d.—The Clerk re- marked that ~these accounts were really fox 13 months, because there were only 11 months in last year's state- ment: Mr. Rigby made up the accounts to the end of August.

div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ACTION lIIROUGII FAMILY DIFFERENCES.

A special sitting of the St. Helens County Court was held on Saturday, before his Honou; .ludge Thompson and a jury, ,to conclude the,hearing of the action brought by Mrs. Sarah Hallett, of 21, Muspratt-street, Widnes, to recover £25 compensa- tion from Mr. Hugh Stubbs, of Dale-street, Man- chester. and Edward Mai tley, of Victoria-road, I Widnes (as agent for the former), for wrongful seizure, and an equal amount from her husband, George Hallett, for unlawful detention of certain household furniture and effects. She alQo applied for an injunction to restrain her husband from sell- ing or otherwise disposing of the goods. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff; Mr. Edge, barrister, of Manchester, was for Stubbs and Martley ; while Hallett was unrepresented.—Mr. Riley stated that the plaintiff married the defendant Hallett after the passing of the Married Women's Property Act. At that time she was, as the administratrix of her former hus- band, possessed of certain household furniture and effects, which did net pass to the defendant by at of marriage. Altogether she had a nice house of furniture. as well as some money in the bank. Since the marriage the plaintiff had purchased out of moneys in her hands' as administratrix, and out of moneys earned by her in the separate business of a dressmaker, additional furni- ture and effects. Mr. and Mrs. Hallett were in May,last living in Muspratt-street, Widnes, which had been pur- chased by Stubbs from• the former owner. There were ' certain arrears of rent owing to the former owner, but the .sale of a house conferred no right of distress upon a new owner. Mr. and Mrs. Hallett had a disagreement, and the tatter, rather than allow her home to be recklessly broken up by her husbandi wrote a letter to Mr. Hartley stating that Hallett was "at his old game again," and informed him that she would rather the " things " 'went for an honest debt than that they should be disposed of by her husband. Directly afterwards the bailiffs came with an execution. Mrs. Hallett pointed out what things belonged to her, but all the things were taken, one of the ' bailiffs assuring Mrs. Hallett that what belonged to her would be returned in the evening. Stubbs and Martley subsequently sold a portion of the goods, the residue be- ing handed over to the defendant Hallett, who refused to return the prolierty in his possession. The plaintiff hav- ing been examined and cross-examined at length, it was agreed that the jury should be discharged, find that the matter should be placed in his Honour's handkfor arbitra- tion. The jury was dismissed, and the judge, counsel, advocate, and plaintiff adjourned to an ante-room.—On returning into court his Honour said he was quite certain that the verdict would be against the plaintiff, for she really had no claim against Stubbs or Medley. And if the verdict went against her she would be called upon to pay the costs. He had taken into consideration all the circumstances of the case, and' he ordered that there should be a non-suit as against Hallett and judgment, in favour of the other defendants, each side to pay its own costs.

The Chairman, in his opening address, said he had sometimes been .cast down whilst thinking about the progress which was being made in rnissibnary work. It was not going at the express speed they would all like to see, but they must remember that they were in the hands of God. They ought all to be workers in the good cause and they ought to join together to do something for the salvation of souls. Sometimes he had asked him- self whether they were doing their duty as Wesleyahs, whether there was a lack of workers and of efforts to spread the glorious Gospel of Jesus, and he could not but conclude that there were plenty ready to work if they only saw with full force why they should work. He should like to hear the sounds and cries that used to be heard in St. Paul's Chapel at such gatherings. They must remember that the Word of God was quick and powerful, and although they might be afraid that it was not working as it used to do, still it was the same power, and if they only did their duty and looked to God for help through the holy spirit, he believed they would be able to do more in the cause of missions. (Applause.) The Rev. 0. Davies then spoke, and gave an encourag- ing view of missionary enterprize. He said the mission- ary map was year by year decreasing in blackness, and th rosy colour was increasing. (Applause.) The Rev. A. H. Male deliyered an exceedingly inter esting address about !us' work amongst the soldiers in Egypt. There were, he said, people who looked upon soldiers as the scum of society, but in soldiers he had found the finest attributes of a man. He thought the soldiers had earned from them some kindly Christian sympathy. (Applause.) The customary votes of thanks concluded the pro- ceedings.

RUNCORN BOARD OP COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. J. Dobson presided, and there were also present—Messrs. 11. J. Grice, W. nankin- son, 11. White. W. Mellor, P. Smith, F. A. Lake, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor.,, and Dr. McDougall (medical - officer).
HIGH DEATH RATE.

The Medical .oflcter of Health reported that the ffinn- ber of deaths registered during the past month amount to 48; of these 19 were due to measles, 4 to typhoid fever, sto heart disease, 2 phythsis sto consumption of the: M bowels, 2to teething, 2 to inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain, 2 to bronchitis, and one each to inflammation of the lungs, cancer of the liver, convul- sions, paralysis, and to diseases of uncertain origin and one to chronic rheumatism. Of the above 48 deaths, 27 were children of two years or under. The deaths showed an average death rate for. the 12 months of 33 and a fraction per thousand of the estimated population. He regretted to have to report an increased death rate from measles and typhoid fever.—No comments were made on the report. • ,2*-ENV _

THE VIOINVY ON THE BOARD.

• The Secretary read the following letter from Mr. Richard Morris :—" Will you please convey my thanks to the Board of Commissioners for voting me to the vacancy on the Board by the removal from the town of Mr. Robert Shaw. In the report of the proceedings of the meeting, I saw that directly after my appointment Mr. Timmins informed the Board that he had received a letter from the sectetazy of the Manchester Ship Canal Company that they intended to appoint their own official in the place of Mr. Timmins. No doubt had the Board been aware of this before filling up the vacancy, Mr. Timmins would have been elected instead of myself, as Mr. Timmins,' from his great experience, must be a valu- able member of the Board. I have great pleasure in the interests of the town, in resigning the position to which the Board have elected me, and I trust Mr. Timmins may be appointed. I hope, at some future time, to have an opportunity of gerving my fellow townspeople on the Board."

Mr. Smit said he was not present at the meeting when Mr. Morris was elected; and he inquired whether it was customary for such an important matter to be de. cided without giving notice. The Chairman replied in the affirmative, and then Mr. Smith asked was it usual to elect a gentleman to the Board who had never been before the ratepayers. The Chairman said it rested with the Board to appoint :whom they thought fit. The Law Clerk explained that the Board were com- pelled to fill up the vacancy within a month, and if the appointment had been deferred to that meeting it would not have been within the month.

Mr. smith: It is evident the Board have been very pre- cipitate in the matter when they have oleeted a gentle- man who declines the position. The Chairman: There has been no precipitancy in the Matter. We have gonii according to the standing orders.
Mr. Mellor said he protested against the appointment at the last meeting. He thought there ought to have been a special meeting for the purpose. The Chairman: That has not been the usual course.
Mr. Mellor: That is no reason why it should not be done.
- In reply to Mr. Lake, the Chairman said there had not been a reply from the Ship Canal Company with regard to Mr. Timmins.

_ Mr, Smith remarked that the Board had taken action upon a private letter addressed to Mr. Timmins, and as the Manchester Ship Canal Company were entitled to two members, irrespective of the ratepayers' opinion, he. thought it was rather cheeky of the Board to dictate to them.
as- resolved to. accept the resignation. Messrs. Lake, Smith, and Mellor voted against. Mr. Grice gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the appointment of Mr. Timmins. .
TRE DANGERS OF THE FAIR.

Mr. Hankinson said it was now Runcorn Wakes times and he wished to know if anything could be done to pre- vent or mitigate the likelihood of accidents occuring at the swing boats. It was a very lamentable thing when they heard of a young man being lamed or killed, which had been the case in Runcorn. Could not the Board make some restrictions as to the boats.— The Chairman said the Board had done all they could to- prevent these accidents. Bills warning the public had been posted in various parts of the town, and the market inspector had exercised all the care he could, but people were/4o reckless in these matters that it was difficult to prevAnt accidents occurring.—Mt. Hankin.son : Persons who are drunk ought not to be allowed to get into the boats.—The matter then dropped.

THE WATER SUPPLY. Mr. Linaker asked for a cheque of £l2O on account of the Parliamentary proceedings with regard to the Liver- pool water scheme. The total amount of the bill would be about £l3O or £l4o.—The cheque was drawn on the proposition of Mr. Hankinson, seconded by Mr. Whit-, thker.

His Honour Judge Wynne -F-fofilk-es—disposed of the followiug business at this court, on Tuesday : One adjourned judgment summons, five original judgment summonses, two adjourned plaints, two default sunimonses, and 137 original plaints. The only case of public interest was one in which Mr. A. Linaker (Messrs. Linaker and Linaker), appeared on behalf of Thomas Forster, farmer, FreaLsham, in an action against John. Whitby, farmer, Cromer's Lake, Frodsham, defended by Mr. J. Barton. The sum'in dis- pute was £B9s for 32i cwt. of hay, alleged to have been sold by the plaintiff to the defendant., at the rate of £4 per ton.. The defence was that Whitby, at the pliintiff's request found a customer for the hay, in the person of S. Cox, of Greenway-road, A few days after the sale took place, the effects of Cox were disposed of by auction, and Luke Holmes gave evidence that the defendant asked him if he could not pay for the hay. He replied in the negative, and he subseqfiently heard the defend- ant threaten to have Cox locked up. John Frodsham, accountant, corroborated. A ticket from the weigh office stating that the hay was from Forster to Cox was produced, and Mrs Whitby swore that the plaintiff had told her to take no notice of a letter from Messrs. Lina- ker, as he had,not instructed them to write.—His Hon- our gave judgment for the plaintiff, stating that he mu.St believe the evidence of the independent witnesses, Holmes and Frodsham.
