div.head: MYSTERIOUS.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS.
Tin ALARMING NATLRE OF UNSEEN DANGERS ACCOUNTED FOR.

"I fear no evil that I can se," exclaimed Napoleon, aniil his acts proved the truth of his philosophy. He ,conlcl face danger in every form; but the sunken -road of Waterloo was an unseen foe greater than the armies around him. This same principle seems true with most people. We fear the unseen; we dread the unlenoven ; we shrink from that which possesses the power to harm. In the midst of so much mystery and so many unseen dangers we naturally feel a sense of awe. We wonder if some small portion of the human machinery should get out of order what the result would be; and we fear dis- aster from powers we cannot comprehend. It is natural we should do so? It is teasonable we should ask what the result would be if the million tissues of the lung-s, liver, or kidneys should become disordered. A slight excess, a careless attention to the details of health, ap- parently does no harm ; but it none the less undermines the life. It is a draft upon vitality which must be hon- oured in the future. But our own neglect is by no means all the unseen in- juries that come to the human system. There are a thousand evil influences all around us at war with our lives. They are inhaled into the lungs, and poisonthe blood; they are absorbed through the skin and foster disease; they are devoured with the food, and corrode the most important organs of the body. The man or woman who possesses the power to counteract all these evil influences has obtained a secret of untold value. The lungs, heart, liver, and kidney's can very easily become weakened ; and how? By these very abuses and strains that are constantly brought to bear upon them. It is necessary to guard these organs, and preserve their proper tone at all times. A friend of mine, a prominent gentleman, residing in the West End, felt unusually tired one day, but suppos- ing it to be caused by over-exertion; he gave it little at- tention. The next day he was not so languid, but his head pained him. This he attributed to indigestion, and , took no further notice of it. Matters went along in this way for several weeks, the headaches and languor in- creasing, accompanied by certain dull pains in various -parts of his body. He was not wholly insensible to these troubles, but, being closely occupied, he heedlessly overlooked them. There finally came an intense pain in the small of the back; his ankles became swollen to - twice their natural size, and life seemed one intense pain. A physician was called, who pronounced it Bright's ' disease of the kidneys. Now, had any one warned my friend that the symp- toms that had troubled him so long arose from the kid- neys, he would have attended to them at once, but he did not know it. Many men and women to-day, in every part of England, are suffering, substantially, as did my friend, and from the same cause, and they should know what it means. It means present discomfort, future un- happiness, and premature death, unless attended to promptly, and treated rightly. The only discovery, which has ever been made in the scientific or medical, worlds that is a certain remedy for all such troubles is "Warner's SAFE Cure." Made from a tropical leaf, whose properties, like Peruvian bark. are known and in- valuable, it acts at once and naturally upon the organs which produce these distressing troubles, carrying health to the entire system, While the most serious evils which afflict man and womankind are those which arise from disordered kid- neys, they are diseases which can be controlled if taken in time. The truth is that they are "unseen evils," and the prifnary danger arises from the fact that the symp- toms they manifest are not recognised, but are attributable to some minor disorder, which, by being considered slight, is permitted to fasten itself upon the system. That more than one-half of physical disorders arise from impaired kidneys is a settled fact, and that theirdisorders can be prevented by using "Warner's SATS Cure" is equally true. Thousands of people, including prominent physicians, scientists, and divines, who have known of its wonderful powers, indorse and recommend it. Chemists throughout the world sbll it; and the op- portunity for thus obtaining its benefits are brought near to every one. It will solve the mystery of good health, and keep back the day on which comes "thegreat mystery."

DISPUTE BETWEEN NEIGHBOVW3. Mary BleaSO was charged with having unlawfully used threaas to Harriet Miller on the 24th September. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant and Mr. P. Davies for - the defend- ant. Both the complainant and the defendant live in adjoining houses on Knutsford-road, and it appears that there has been some dispute as to the use of a well. It was alleged by the complainant that both of them as well as another neighbour had an equal right to the well, but that Mrs Meese was in the habit of emptying the welts° that the others could not get water. She had also made an attempt to strike the complainant and threatened to push complainant down the well. The summons was ultimately withdrawn on defendant un- dertaking to pay the costs of the sununons and promis- ing not to molest the complainant further. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Henry Norcott and John Rutter were charged with having on the 3rd October, at Stret- ton, assaulted a young Irialiman named Michael Grif- fiths. Complainant stated that the defendants threw him down with a rope and said they would hang him. The ease was dismissed. ASSAULT ON A YOUNG WOMAN. John Halliday, a young married man living at Whitley, was charged with havin. assaulted a young woman named Ruth Thomas, at Little Leigh, on the 13th October. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defendant. Complainant said that on the day in question the defendant came to the door and asked her Rile could sell her a sewing machine, and she replied thathe could not. He then said" If lean- not sell you a machine can I sell you a young man." She replied"No," and he in answer to his inquiry " Why ? " she said she was better without one. He then came into the house, pushed her up against the wall; put his arm round her and kisSed her two or three times. A witness having been called by complainant, Mr. Davies said the case was a totally different, one to what he had been in- structed it was. He understood that all defendant had done was to attempt to kiss the complainant outside the door of the house. He could only blame the defendant for instructing him in the way he had done. The Chair- man said that was a most disgraceful case, and defend- ant would be fined £1 and coats.

FOOTBALL IN TAB STREETS.—Arthur Bowdon, William Santlev, Walter Johnson, and Ernest Roach, boys, pleaded guilty to having on the 25th October played football in Ashridge-street to the annoyance of.passen- gers.—P.C. 243 said he had received many ,complaints with regard to this practice, and the local authorities had published bills with the object of putting a stop to it.—Each defendant was ordered to pay 3s 6d costs. LICENSING MA'rrllll.S.—Thomas Finegan was granted permission to sell at the Boathouse Inn, recently occu- pied by Samuel Spann. Samuel Spann received permis- sion to sell at the Royal Oak Inn, St. John-street, lately occupied by Frederick George Lan,gley. Permission to sell at the Grapes Hotel, Halton-road, was granted to i Edwin Field_

The tries were obtained by IT. P. Williamson, P. Williamson, H. Webster (three each), J. A. liewley (two), and W. R. Hannah, Fr. N. Linaker, G. R. Williamson, E. J. Howley (one eaniV. H. Webster kicked the goals. , WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. FRoDsMAM.—ThiS match was played at Frodsham, and after a rough aameeended in a draw. The home team kicked off at 46para, Law- , :On charging the ball down. The visitors' farwards took the ball with a dribble to the line and the home team were forced to touch down. After the drop-out a scriminage was formed near centre. The-visitors' forwards broke through, and taking the ball' with a dribble the home team were again forced to touchdown. The home team dropped out again and the visitors fall- ing to return the home team broke through to, the line, Astill kicking dead for the visitors. Astill dropped out and the visitors following up, a scrimmage took place in the home 25. Dauber here received a pass a.nd got over, but the point was disallowed. Another scrinanage was formed, and the ball becoming loose, Stevens kicked a goal from a flying kick. This was also called back, and knother scrimmage took place, from which Graham get- ting the ball, got over for the visitors, thakick at goal just failing. This brought about half-time. At the change of ends Lawton kicked off for the visitors and a good return being made, a scrimmage Was. formed in the visitors' 25. The home centre hare received a. pass and got over for the home teath. The kick at goal failed. Nothing but minors were scored after this, and at the call of time the score was—Wanderers 1 try and 4 minors, Frodsham I try and 4 minors. SAINT PAUL'S v. WYCLIFFE (Ist Teams).—The above teams met on Saturday afternoon when a good game was expected, as Wycliffe appear to have greatly improved, whereas it was all in favour of the Saints, who played with great dash, their passing and tackling beating all efforts of the Wycliffe team to score. The game was commenced by Emma kicking off for the home team at 3-30 against sun and wind. The ball was rushed up by the Saints, which forced Wycliffe to concede a minor. After the drop out Wycliffe, who seemed to pull them- selves together, rushed the ball down the field and thus compelled Marriott to touch down for the home team. After several minutes play the Saints' forwards took the ball at their toes, and ably Seconded by their backs, gained the first substantial point through the Wycliffe back failing to hold the ball. Warburton failed at goal. Hamer, who had been playing a 'good game for Wycliffe, kicked out, but the ball was charged down by Emaon, and after cc series of scrimmages on the Wycliffe lines

the ball was passed to Warburton; who after a short rim transferred to McCue, the latter succeedim," in dropping a splendid goal. After this to the end of the game all play rested in the Wycliffe quarters, resulting in a suc- cession of tries and minors. For the home team all

played well, whilst the passing of Williams at half and Warburton at centre were much admired. For the visitors Hamer and Haynes played the Nit. Result— St. Paul's, 4 goals, 3 tries, and ten minors, Wycliffe 2

minors. WIDNES v. ROCTIDAT.E Sr. CT.EMANT'S.—PIayed at Wid- nes on Saturday, before 2,000 spectators. Both teams were strongly represented, though Parkinson, Howard, and Fogg were absent from the Widnes ranks. The game was well contested throughout, and at the Close Widnes were declared victors by one try and twelve minors to nothing. A game of seventy minutes was played, a start being effected at a quarter to four. Play settled in the Rochdale quarter, and in a few minutes Morris made a splendid drop at goal. The oval missed its makk, but Morris dashed after it and succeeded in obtaining a try, but the major point was not obtained. The rest of the game was monopolized by the Widnesiansscoringminors. Morris made several fine drops at goal, but each time he failed, and the rest of the players, though they frequent- ly penned their opponents to their goal line, could not score anything tangible. Of the Widnesians Farrell, Morris, Wilkinson. and all the forwards played a fine game; and James Rangeley and Shepherd did well for the St. Clement's. Teams :—Widnes: S. Bingham, back; Plumpton Barker, and Morris, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wilkinson. half backs; Smith (cap- tain), Kiddie, Hardman, Hughes, J. Bingham, T. Pen- nington, Gandy, Woods, and Barber, forwards. St. Cie-, ment's : John Rangeley, back; James Rangeley, Pratt (captain), and Shepherd, three-quarter backs ; Heywood and Richardson, half-backs; Oddie, W. Waugh, J. Waugh, 13. Ride,haugh, Ramsey, Whitehead, Dix, Peel, jand Clegg, forwards. Referee, Mr. R. WilcOck, Liver- pool. WARRINGTON T. MANCTIESTER RANGERS "A " TRAMS.— This fixture was played at Rusholme, Manchester, on Saturday, in fine weather. The visitors were only weakly represented. but nevertheless proved successful. The Warrington captain won the toss, and two 35's being the time agreed upon to play, Vickers kicked off for the Rangers at 3-30. A smart run by Antrobus and kick by [ Appleton took play to the home full back, who relieved by sending the oval into touch. Parlane now put in a good kick to Sanson, this player having 'his return charged down, but he managed to secure the ball, thereby averting any danger. Some very good passing between Antrobus, Randalls, and Appleton was now witnessed, [ the ball eventually going into touch in the Rangers' quar- ters. The Warrington forwards broke away from the [ scrimmage and took the ball over the line, but it was kicked dead. Appleton returned the drop out into touch. [RitsOn here put in some good work, but Daniels saved by lkicking into touch. Hackett, Randalls, and Jones drib- bled to the line, where Whittle got hold; from a scrim- mage and passed to Evans, who transferred to Appleton. this player taking a drop at goal which was charged down, but Jones securing the ball grounded it over the line. Antrobus took the place, and made a good bid for [ goal, the ball striking the cross bar. After the drop out, Hackett, Jones, and Eyes dribbled to near the line, Parhne having to towhdown. Antrobus returned the drop out, and Parlane punted to Whittle, who put in a nice run and passed to Appleton, who kicked over the line, the ball going dead. Some grand passing between Whittle, Antrobus, and Evans and good runs by Daniels and Appleton, caused the home team to concede two minors in rapid succession. Graham dropped out, San- son returning into touch, and from the line out Hackett made a strong run, being collared on the line by the full back. The Rangers' forwards worked the ball out of danger to mid-field, where Antrobus got possession and made a short run, and when tackled by Pownali passed to Daniels, who dashed past all his opponents and gained a splendid try. The place kick was a failure. Vickers kicked off, Unsworth returning. The Rangers now in- vaded the Warrington territory, where some severe scrimmaging took place. Antrobus, however' finally got possession, and made a grand run, but was brought down by the full back, Graham having ultimately to save by touching down. Half time was now called, the score standing—Warrington 2 tries and 6 minor points to Rangers nil. On resuming, Whitt4e kicked off, and Eyes dribbled to the Rangers' 25. On the hill becoming loose Appleton got hold, and made a beautiful run in, Randalls failing at goal. Holmes charged down the kick-off, and Molvneaux, Eyes, and Randalls dribbled to the line, forcing the Rangers to concede another minor. Imme- diately afterwards Ritson was allowed a free kick for off- side tackling. but Jones returned, and from a scrimmage in the home 25 Antrobus passed to Evans who dropped a splendid goal. Whittle afterwards threw to Evans, who passed to Appleton, this player putting in a good kick, the ball going dead. After the drop out, Moly- neaux got away with a nice dribble, Graham saving. Whittle next twice made his mark, Randalls' kick being charged down on the first occasion, and on the second the forwards dribbled to the line. Evans here missed a pass, and the Rangers taking advantage, Galley and Myers dribbled down the field, but Sanson got the ball away, Eyes pushier,' Kinder in touch before he could get far. From passes 'by Whittle, Appleton succeeded in running in two grand tries, the same player kicking a goal from one of the places, and, on time being called, the score stood—Warrington, 2 goals, 4 tries, and 10 minor points, to Manchester Rangers nothing. Teams: -.—Warrington: Full back, D. Sanson; half backs. Whit- tle (captain) and Antrobus; three-quarterbacks, Daniels, Evans, and Appleton; forwards, Molyneaux, Thotnley, Jones, Hackett, Randalls, Jones, Holmes, Unsworth, and Donohue. Manchester Rangers: Full back, Kinder; half backs, Pearson and Ritson three-quarter backs, Graham, Parlane, and Langford; forwards, Vickers, Unsworth, flelin, Tysecke, Goldschmidt, Frost, Pownall, Galley, and Myers.

was enabled to make a grand run to the home team's territory. Sabin tried hard to get apraybut the " wire- pullers' " tackling was too safe: 'Barnes replied back to centre field, anti Speakman was next conspicuous by a grand dribble through the opposing backs close tothe visi- tors citadel. A mull by Barnes enabled the Rangers to save by conceding a minor. Jolley returned the drop out, and Fair Turner took the leather to the lines. From a subsequent scrimmage formed here, Speakman passed nicely to Barnes, SOO, in turn transferred to Massey, that player being pushed in touch on the line. The home team's efforts were, however, shortly afterwards rewav tied, for from the line out, Fair Turner secured posses- , sion, and safely grounded the leather over the line. This successful piece of play raised the enthusiasm of the spectators to the highest- pitch, especially when Speak- man safely piloted the leather over the tar. Harry Hasellrain reeommenced operations from the centre, and notwithstanding their reverse the visitors played up with renewed vigour. for a moment threatening the Warrington goal. The home team by a combined drib-: ble, in which Frank Turner, Littlewood, and W. Dillon were conspicuous, relieved to quarter flag, Harry Rad- cliffe saving his charge in grand style. Massey next put in a good kick to the visitors' backs, but a poor re- turn was made, and play settled down in the Rangers' territory. From a series of scrimmages formed here Harry Haselham, Mee, and Taylor broke away. Barnes saving what appeared a chance of scoring. The play was removed back to centre, and reliant) got in a kickto Nevins, who safely returned into touch at centre field. Warren tried hard to get away but was well tackled by Sabin, and shortly afterwards Frank Turner, Littlewood, and Povey broke Sway with the ball at their toes, re- lieving to the yisitors' 25. From some loose play which followed, the Rangers were forced to adopt the saying clause. Harry Ha.selham dropped out, and play was taken to the home team's quarter. Barnes smartly col- lared Sabin with the leather in his possession, which was soon afterwards followed by a fine shot at goal by the visitors' captain (Herbert Flaselham), who all but scored, Massey running the ball out to the quarter flag. Sabin made a good run through the midst of his oppon- ents, but Barnes was too much for him, and brought him quickly to grass.. A splendid shot at goal by Mas- sey from the touchline, the ball going a few feet out- side the posts, brought about halftime, with the score— Warrington, one goal and three minors to, Manchester Rangers nil. Harry Haselham re-started, play settling down in neutral ground. Jolley secured possession, and made the run of the day: commencing at his own quar- ter flag he was not brought down until be reached the visitors' lines. A movement was next started, in which all the home teamwere prominent, their passing at this juncture of the game being splendid, and they were fin- ally rewarded by Warren planting the leather over the line close to touch. Speakman failed at a difficult place. Harry Haselharurestarted, and some excellent give-and- take play ensued in the course Of which Massey had to retire owing to an unfortunate accident. Warrington; considering they were a man short, still played splen- didly, and kept up the attack on the visitors' citadel. From some loose play which followed. Frank Turner passed to Barnes, who Promptly dropped the leatherover the bar from the midst of the 'Rangers. The signal to start from the centre was received with loud applause as very few knew how the bait had got over, the bar, and it was not until Barnes emerged from the Midst of his opponents that they knew he had added another dropped goal to his already long list. Speak/n/1a saved a rush of the Manchester forwards in grand style, and from a scrimmage formed at centre field Povevdrib- bled well along, Hamblett chicking his career by kicking the leather in touch. Warren passed to Barnes who got in a good kick to the Rangers' lines. The visitors now rallied, and taking advantage of a bad pass to Jol- • ley they were enabled to relieve to the quarter flag. Mas- sey (who had returned to his place), saved this rush. Warren got away from the pack, and passing to Barnes, 'that player handed over the leather to Jolley, who was put in touch before he became dangerous. Massey over- ran the hall when a .chanee of scoring seemed possible, only a touch-in-goal resulting. Mee dropped out, and a good pass to Sabin was spoiled by Jolley tackling before he could get away. Barnes wa.s next brought down on the line, the visitors oonceding a minor. From now to Icall of time both teams tried hard to score, but without avail, and after seventy minutes' hard play the Warring- tonians retired the victors in a grandly-contested game by 2 'goals;l try, and 5 minors to Rangers nil. The match was a fine exhibition of Rugby football, and'geldom has there been seen at Warrington such a fast and exciting game. On behalf of Warrington the full back, Nevins, had little to do. The three-quarters played a grand combined game, their passing, kicking. and tackling leaving nothing to be desired. It would be folly to make choice in the halves, as both played in their best form. It is also a hard task to make special commendation in the forward ranks, but it may be said that navvy's play was particularly praiseworthy. Of the visiting backs Sabin was undoubtedly the best, and he. received valuable assistance from Taylor and Harry Radcliffe. In the forward division the brothers Ilasel- ham, Pollard, and Mee were the most conspicuous. The teams were as follows—Warrington : Full back Nevins ; three-quarter hacks, Massey, Barnes (captain), and Jolley; half-backs, Warren and Speakman: for- wards, Fair Turner, R. Littlewood, Hayes, F. Turner, W Povey, T. Davies, H. Dillon, Cragan, and W. Dillon. Manchester Rangers: Full back, H. Radcliffe; three- quarter backs, Sabin, F. Radcliffe, and A. Hamblett; half-backs, Taylor and Parlane ; forwards, Herbert Ha-selham (captain), H. Haselham, Mee, Pollard, Barrow H. Hamblett, Wilson, A. McDougall, and D. McDougall. Referee Mr. Trevor Smith.

Hughes won the toss, and elected to play downhill, Chambers kicking off. The return by Davies was charged down, and play settled in the Runcorn 25. Jones had a chance of scoring from a neat pass by Perry, but the Old Bi-gs could not get through, and W. Hughes ultimately relieved his lines by dribbftg to centre. Perry and Hickson, by meantli of a clever passing run, again got to tho visistors' 25, where somelbose kicking between Hickson and Davies resulted in Runcorn's favour. Andrews next got away neatly, and transferred hostili- ties to the home 25. Speakman now got a neat throw from Hughes, and passed to Cawley, who made a huge punt, and 'Vaughan touched down. Upon resuming, Speakman made a very long pass to' Davies, but the latter was grassed by Wood when getting well away. Forward play was the most remarkable feature of the game at this stage, and the superior weight of the home attack was • gradually beginning to tell. Brodie and Chambers got away together, but Spealtaran,' by taking an opponent's pass, ramtralised this effbrt. The home captain was again prominent, coming through finely and tackling Cawley. Tall kicking between Perry and Cawley finally resulted' in the oval going into touch in the home 25. After momentarily visiting the time line Runcorn were forced/ on the defence, Cawl4y having spoiled a grand opening-by passing forward. Wood got well away and passed' to Perry, who continued the movement and threw to Jones, the last-named scoring near touch-in-goal, Hickson failing at the place. A good run and kick by CawleFlanded the leather to Vaughan, who mulled the catch and touched down. A scrambling 'nit, of play in the home 25 enabled Wainwright to pass to Gatley, who ran and passed to his captain, H. Hughes., the latter dropping a neat goal. Play continued to be even and exciting, the home team having slightly the advantage. • A minor, from' a big kick- by Perry, was soon followed by a rusho on the Runtern line, where Perry, from a pass by Wood, ran in neatly under the goal pests, but Hicksortfailed at an easy place, and the teams crow. .dover with)the score in Runcorn's favour by 1 goal and 2 minors to 2 tries and 1 minor. Upon re- starting (W. Hughes kicking off) Speakman put in a , strong run, but by a great dribble the itorne .team got to the Runcorn 25, where. Perry threw away a splencrld chance. The same player' soon retrieved, however, and pickim,oup in grand style; passed to Jones, who ran in smartly; but Hickson *fer the third time failed at gad. The home team continued to have the.bast of the argu- ment, and were soon again in the visitors' 25, where Perry dropped abortively at goal. WOod. pluckily running the hall out. A grand run in by Jores received the re- feree's veto—certainly a near thing--and then Hickson dropped a goal, a dead ball resulting, a similar point accruing immediately afterwards. A grand bit of play by H, Hughes, who tried to place hils side on attack, al- most resulted in Davies getting in, but beyond a minor point to each side nothing more was scored, and the game remained drawn with the SCCAT• :—Runcoin. 2 goal and 3 minors t Old Boys, 3 tries arid 5 minors. The home team suffered by the absence of Ashton, whilst Nevins was given a trial at full back, but he had little work to do. On the visitors' side Wilson and Jones were absentees. Both teams had now settled down to work in real earnest, and give-and-take play followed, until Jolley got away with a good run to his opponents' line, Meo saving by punting into touch.. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The Warrington first team, though it has been narrow- ly defeated in both its contests away from home, is still invincible on its own ground. The match last Saturday with Manchester Rangers was everything that could be desired from a spectators point of view, being a fine open game, played in an intelligent manner, and free from any sort of roughness or bad feeling. The Rangers have a reputation for open play, and two orthree times during the game. they indulged in some•very effective passing tactics, but notwithstanding this the home players Were decidedly superior behind. Their play in- dicated better orgignisation, and, though once or twice there was a little want of judgment in passing, it was • evident that the beat team won.

The post of, full back in the Warrington team is no sinecure, as Ilitxton'must have experienced by this time. Last week Nevins Wati given a trial, and it is only fair to say that he did the little he had to do well. Bit there can be doubt that Warrington suffered last season from the frequent changes of full back, and it is a thing to be avoided if poisible. Like every other player in the team, the full back Will make his mistakes; but certainly there are plenty of people who think that, taking him all round, Buxton cannot very well be improved upon. The " A " team of the Warrington Club are threaten- ing to pile up a phenomenal record. So far they have won every match they have been engaged in, and some of them in a ridiculously easy fashion. Their style of , play is full of dash and spirit, and splendidly oln- bined.

div.head: 'THE HART CASE.
div.p: 'THE HART CASE.
COUNTY CaURT ACTION:

- - - _ His Honour Judge Ffoulkes held a spacial sitting at the Warrington County Court, on Saturday, to hear the case of Hart against Thornton, which has caused so much interest in Warrington and the locality. The court-room was crowded, and some difficulty was experienced in keeping good order. Mr. Wharton. barrister;. Manchester, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland, barrister; Liver- pool, for the defendant: In stating the case to his Honour, Mr. Wharton said it was an issue sent for trial from the High 'Out. It was an action for ' the return of an office• copy of a will of Martha Hart, deceased, formerly of Latchford, Cheshire, dated 1829, which was proved in the Cbnsistory Court at Chester; for the return of an original' will of the said Martha Hart, and also of a bundle of papers, including certificates of births. marriages, and deaths. Plaintiff—Edward Hart, a nagger and slater—also claimed £5,000 as damages for the de- tention of these documents by the defendant, who, is an insurance manager. About twenty years ago; counsel said, a member of the Hart family, whose name was Martha, Hart, but who went by the name of Lady Hart, died and, left a will, which seemed to have been• preyed at Chester in April, l'S3O, she having died in 1829. An office copy of that will was one of the documents which they allegol wr.ks. in the possession of the defend- ant. But in additiOn to that there was in another will --said to be the original will of Martha Hart—which was duly signed and attested, and which left the property to the Hart family,whereas the will of which they de- manded an office cop had been duly proved and left the whole of the property to one Triphena Tun.stall, who was.now in possessidn. This will in respect to which they now claimed had been handed down from one rnem- b3r of ;he family to another, until it eventually mine into the hands of William Hart some eleven years ago. This man was the husband of Sarah Hart, and she was the person who would be entitled on the death of her husband to the estate and effects, whatever they were. She died without any will, and the present plaintiff ad- ministered to her estate for the purpose of bringing the action. His Honour : It was in the possession of Wm. Hart, then he died; what became of the will.— Mr. Wharton said that William left a will, which was made by-defendant, who had assured the Harts that it was only a. question of time and money to enable them to obtain possession of their property. The will was pre- pared by the defendant on the 21st September, 1875, and in it William Hart bequeathed all his real estate property of which he died possessed to his wife 'Sarah, and ap- pointed the defendant executor, but it remained in the hands of Thornton until some Proceedings took place in the police court net long ago, when he was made to pro- duce it. William Hart was only a labourer, and it was a remarkable thing that Thornton should make the will of a man who had not a penny piece, and make him de- vise all his real estate •to his wife, and appoint him executor. The meaning of it was that the defendant had an idea that this property could be recovered, and

• believed it would be, and that, therefore, as executor, he • *mild have eVentually a large property to deal with. 'About eleven years ago defendant obtained some certifi- cates and information, and gave advice as to the will, in order to recover the property, leading the Harts to be- • lieve that they could get it. This wil,l was .preserved, and kept, with a bundle of certificates, on the top of some articles of furnibure in the kitchen of W. Hart's house. One evening about the period mentioned, while the family were together, it was alleged that defendant walked into the place, and, recognising the papers, took them up, and said he wanted the documents to make copies, because they were very valuable. The family protested against his taking them away, but he went off with the papers and promised faithfully to return them. From that day to the present he had never returned the documents, and had made all sorts of excuses. Defend- ant, who had been in very low circumstances suddenly rose to opulence' and he (Mr. Wharton) could therefore understand a rich man going into this matter if he was to have Latchford House and part of the property in the 1 vpssession of the Tunstalls. What they Niranted was not so much the daniages as the papers which, it was per- fectly clear, defendant had never returned. Evidence in support of the plaintiff was then called. Annie Hart, wife of Edward Mixt, 49, Old-road,Latch- ford, said that on several occasions she had heard the de- fendant speak to William Hart about the property at her father-in-law's house. She had frequently seen the will of Martha Hart, and uSed to read it to her father-in-law.
According to the will, the property, she said, was left to Harts and Harts only, and there was no mention in it of the name of Tunstall. She remembered the defendant

coming to the house about eleven -yea; ago; after she had been interrupted in reading the will. The document was placed on some draweis, and Thornton, on seeing it, took the bundle in his hand, and, saving that he was going to make copies of them,took the iloCuments away. There were in the room at the time, besides herself, Mr.

and Mrs. Hart, Edward Hart, and Ellen Payne (once a Miss Hart), and all saw the defendant take the will and papers away. William Hart, who was then paralysed, frequently asked his wife to obtain the papers from the defendant, as he felt very uneasy about them, but Thornton would never return the documents.

Ellen Payne, wife of Samuel Payne, 7, Gaskell-street, a sister of the plaintiff, also deposed to the defendant taking possession of the bundle of papers and will about about eleven years ago. At that time Thornton wore shoes and trousers belonging to her father. (Laughter.) —Mr. Mulholland: May I ask what this applies to— it may have been his fee. (Laughter.)—Witness also spoke to defendant having been asked to produce the papers. John Broadhurst, of Kensington, Liverpool, who was in 1836 employed in his father's shopin Manchester-road, Warrington, deposed that in June of that year, he heard Thornton, when in the shop, state that he had all the papers that would be required to get the property for the Harts,' but it was not likely that he should give them up without being paid for them. Defendant said that he had them between his finger and thumb, but he should want a large sum of money besides Latchford House. Samuel Payne, husband of witness, Ellen Payne, said that in June, 1886, he asked Thornton about the Hart estate, and Thornton Aid he had all papers in his pos- session that would be required to recover the property. He had an agreement, he said, to show that if he got the property for the Harts.he should have Latchford House, but he should want something more, say about £3,000. and the house. • Further evidence for the plaintiff having been given witnesses were then called for the defence. ; Mr. J. L. Whittle, deputy town clerk, f said, that in 1871 he was clerk with Mr. G. T. Moore, the then town clerk, and remembered Sarah Hart, wife; of William, Hart, coming frequently to the office in the matter of Martha Hart. deceased. There was a bundle of papers left at the office' and he believed a will, or a copy of a will, but, he could not say if Mrs Hart left them. These papers were in Mr. Moore 's 'possession for many years. George Townend Moore, solicitor's clerk, gave similar evidence.—Harry Lloyd Price, accountant, Manchester, produced documents as part of the estate of ,James Townend Moore, relating to the Harts and Tunstalls.— Archer Brown, a builder's clerk, and Henry Dutton,. clerk and son-in-law to the defendant also gave evi- dence. The defendant was then called. He said, he first had dealings with the Harts some 26 or 27 years ago, he being then about 21. He was (waged by Sarah Hart in reference to some money and property belonging to her, but which was in the possession of Tunstall. Wit- ness then commenced looking for inscriptions in grave- yaris to prove the title of the Harts to the property, and afterwards got several certificates of births, marriages, and deaths. As he got the certificates he gave thent`to Sarah Hart, and he had not seen them frqm that time un- til the present. He also made two joneneys to Chester,. and got an office copy will. Ho could not say whose will it related to, but he gave it to Sarah" Hart. Sarah Hart told him that she had no +confidence in her children, and that was the reason why she asked hina to draw a will for her, which he did in 1875. Witness emphatically denied that he at any time received or took away any bundle of documents, as had been described, from the house of Hart. He had not in his possession an office copy of the will of Martha Hart, dated the 28th April, 1829, nor did he know any one who had. He had never seen or heard of any original will of Martha Hart except the one in Chester. Witness , never could trace how the Harts claimed the Iproperty,' and he never knew they were claiming under any different will to the ode in Chester until quite recentlY. He denied having said in Broad- hurst's shop that he had the papers- that entitled the Harts to the Latchford estate. His conversation. with Broadhurst was, that the Harts 'imagined that they had an estate, and that he had been sorne•years ago, engaged in securing a copy of a will and several registers for them. He had never said that he had documents which would enable these people to regain.this property. He also told Broadhurst that he had the papers—meaning that he had papers when he was employed by Sarah Hart. When Payne and his wife called upon him: he told them that he had succeeded many years before in get- ting several certificates, and that he had given them to , Mrs. Payne's mother at the time. Whenever any demand , was made to him forany papers he told the Harts that he had none. Then in October they came and disturbed his place, and it was a good job he went another way home that day. (Laughter.) Another time they assembled in Padgate, determined to throw him out of his carriage as he passed along. After the action was commenced,, some interrogatories were servedupon him, to which he replied on the 17th October last, and, pending the pr&sent case, a summona for perjury was taken out against him. He I had answered the interrogatories to the best of liis.know- ledge. After counsel on both gides had addressed the Court, His Honour summed up, and pointed out that there was a discrepancy in the statements of Annie Hart and Ellen Payne as to the taking away of thewill by the de- fendant, which he considered of some consequence. One clearly made out that the will was rolled in the.bundle, while the other said the document was not, and from the evidence of these two persons he could not say that he was satisfied that there was among the bundle such a, will as that spoken of. As regarded the conversation between Broadhurst and the defendant, he thought the former, being an uninterested party, might easily misun- derstand the statement of Thornton .as to thepossession of some papers having reference to the estate which he had obtained some 20 years before. Why should the de- fendant take away the papers if he was interested in the matter? He ought to be the last person to withhold any documents. Looking at different parts of the evidence for the plaintiff, he did not think that any documents had been taken away by Thornton, and he therefore gave judgment for the defendant, with costs.

- - THE, CASE BEFORE THE MAGISTR'ATES. At the Borough Court on Thursday,. before Major Litton in the chair) and several other magistrates, Henry Thornton, the defendant in the case of Hart v. Thornton, appeared to answer a summons charg- ing him with having, on the 14th of October, 1887, committed wilful and corrupt perjury in certain affidavits in answer to interrogatories, which he made upon oath in a certain cause pending in the County Court between Edward Hart, plaintiff, and • Henry Thornton, defendant.—Mr. Wharton, barris- ter, appeared for the prosecutor, and Mr Mulholland, barrister, defended.—Mr. Mulholland, at the commence- ment of the proceedings, called attention to the wording o4he suin.rnons, which charged the defendant with committing perjury in connection with,an action "now depending in the County Court." That action, he said, was no 'longer depending, as on Saturday the County Court judge had the matter before him, , heard evidence, and decided that the perjury was ; the other way. Were the magistrates, he asked, now going to meddle with the decision of the County Court judge ? He thought that the case should not be pro- ceeded with.—After further conversation had taken place on this point, Mr. Wharton urged that there was a great distinction between the issue before the County Court judge and the trial of that day. Perjury might have been committed in the minor details that did not vitally affect the issue before tho County Court, but which that Court could deal with.--Mr. White (magis- trates' clerk) It may be alleed that a similar perjury was committed at the trial,which gained the case for the defendant..—Mr. Wharton : That is so. The Bench decided that the case should be proceeded with, and evidence for the prosecution was then called.— Mr. Martin Lyons produced an original affidavit sworn in the promedings, and Mr. Ridgway (solicitor) deposed to administering the oath to Henry Thorntotn.—Annle Hart and Ellen Payne gave evideneesimilar to the evidence they gave at the County Court on Saturday.—Samuel Payn deposed to defendant saying to him that he had all the papers, and thatthe Harts ought to be riding in their carriage, but as things then stood he should require something besides the house at Latchford, say .23,030 and the house. He did not ask Thornton for the will, but for information.—Thomas Hart, labourer, Stamford- street, was also called, but nothing material was elicited for the prosecution. Mr. Mulholland ; •Are you a poacher? Witness : I have been, but Ido not do it now. How long is it since you did it last? Twelve months since. Bow long have you been in gaol? I cannot tgli exactly.—Edward Hart, the prosecutor, also stated *at he was in his father's house when the defendant came in and took • the papers away, saying

that he wanted them to make copies of them.— Mr. Mulholland: Were you told 1)3, your counsel and solicitors that you had no case whatever, and you re- plied that you wanted to gre ou for the purpose of injur- ing Thornton ? Witness: never never said that at all.—Mr. I Mulholland: If your counsef told Mr. Percy' Davies that in the railway station on Saturday night—Mr. What ton (interrupting) :1 Which ho blulholland Would that be true P—Witness,r I did not say that..—Mr. Mulholland said Mr. Percy Davies was in a position to swear it, and Mr. Wharton said Air. Davies could swear what he liked • it was not trne.—John Broadlaurst then spoke to Thornton' telling him that he had every- thing between his finger and thumiN but that he should require something more than Latchford House. At this stage of the proceedings, Mr. Southain, solicitor, Manchester, was called to produce the original inter- rogatories. He proved making the interrogatories to; de- fendant, but could not produce them. It then tran- spired that through a mistake notice had been sent to the defendant's solicitor to produce the wrong document,. and counsel for the defendant now declined to produce the original interrogatories.—Mr. White: The case can- not be dealt with without the interrogatories 'being'pro- duced.—Mr. Mulholland: They should have come here prepared to prove the case.—Mr. Wharton: It only means coming again with another summons. It is perfectly true notice should have been given to produce the inter- rogatories, but by mistake notice was given for the answers to interrogatories.—On the advice of their Clerk, the Bench ruled that the case had not been made out, and it was understood that it was open to the pro- secutor to take out a fresh summons if he so desired, and arrange for the production of the proper document.

THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. SMUT-EAST WARD ELECTION. The only contest in connection with the munici- pal elections in Warrington took place in the South- East Ward on Tuesday. The carididates for the two vacant seats were Mr. R. W. Marsh (C), a re- tiring Council/or, Mr. N. B. Percival, the nominee of the Ratepayers Association, and Mr. S. Barlow, who came out as an independent. It was generally anticipated that Mr. Marsh and Mr. Percival would be the winning candidates, and in fact, Mr. Bar- low's candidature might, perhaps, be regarded as more of the nature of a protest against the " ar- rangement " by which it was sought to fill up the vacancies without a reference to the rate?ayers. In the South-East Ward there are 1,211 'persons entitled to vote, and there are two polling districts, No. 10 and No. /I. The polling booth for district No. 10 was the lower room of the National School, Church- street, for voters on the burgess roll from 4,422 to 5,065 (both inclusive)' for division one, and from 7,081 to 7,137 for division three. The polling booth for No. Ii district was the Parish Church School, in Lower Hank-street, where voters on the burgess roll recorded their v-otes as follows :—Division one from 5;066' to 5,524 and division three from 7,138 to 7,1::. The preMding officer at the polling booth in the National Sehoolroom was the Deputy Town Clerk (Mn J. Lyon Whittle), and the poll clerk Mr. , Stanley Wilson ;- while at the Parish Church School in Lower B'ank-street the presiding officer was Mr. Spencer iirallhead, and the poll clerk Mr. T. Wall- head. The poll opened at eight o'clock in the morning, and was continued till eight o'clock at night when the booths were closed and the ballot boxes conveyed to the Town Hall where the papers were counted. The contest was the reverse of an ex-Citing one;. and at no time during the 'day did there seem to he any great interest taken in it. Mr. Marsh and Mr. Percival had each engaged commit- tee rooms in Church-street near to the police head- quarters, and vehicles of 'various sorts were en- gaged in bringing up, their supporters. Mr. Harlow conducted the contest on what he termed the "purity ticket," discarded all the usual para- phernalia of am election, and eten dispensed with the "canvassing business," with which he expres- sed himself disgusted. According to his address he "relied simply upon the intelligence and judgment of his fellow ratepayers to record their votes as they might deem advisable."' Apart from the ad- dresses of the candidates which appeared in our advertising columns- lhst week, there was not a great deal of election' literature issued: The Rate- payers' Association issued' a. placard asking all the bargesses "anxious. ler the welfare of the town and for a more' economical' expenditure of public monies" to vote-for. Mr. Percival, the nominee of the Association; and' the placard also set forth that the Association had unanimously decided not to sup- port Mr. Barlow' S candidature, In reply to this Mr) Barlow issued' a inanifestoe in which he "re- jected' with scorn "'the insinuations of the Associa- tion, and said that he had' "told the members that their selection of candidates was bad." In conclu- sion, M. Barlow said' lie should 4. come up smiling" whatever the result, but he felt a certain curiosity as to the upshot of what he considered was the right course to take. Mr. Marsh, on his part, des- cribed himself as' the "approved candidate. of the COnserrative, LRPeral; and Ratepayers' Associations," ann he alto put forth in prominent type the fol- lowing extract from a letter. written by Mr. J. Crosfleld to Mr. J. White, viz:, "I agree to and con- film the, arrangement you have made respecting the municipal seats, and t was glad to hear that Mr. Flood' and Mr. A. Brown having retired, there will be no contest in- any, ward." Promptly at eight o'clock the polling booths were closed and the boxes conveyed to the Town Hall, where the counting was at once begun under the superintendence of the Mayor. About nine o'clock the Mayor, accompanied by the Town Clerk. the Deputy Town Clerk, Mr. .S. Barbw, and others, came to the front of the Hall, and announced to the small group of persons who had assembled .th 4 the result of the contest had been- as follows : N.. B. PERCIVAL - - 496 R. W. MARSH - - - 476 S. BARLOW - - 164 Mr. Percival and Mn Marsh were consequently declared elected. The 'announcement was received with applause and laughter Mr.BArmow then cammforward and said that it was of course,quite understood, and he understood it from the first, that he should be the defeated candidate inasmuch as he had not all the usual appliances for the conduct of ainunieipal election. But he could say this, that he had not asked a single man and had not employed a single man in reference to that election. (Hear, hear.) He was heart and soul for the benefit of his native town, and he hoped that whatever course the gentlemen who were elected' took they would caress much for the borough as heclid. With regard to their Mayor he must say that he was ,m capital Mayor and he (Mr. Barlow) hoped they would never get a worse Mayor. (Applause.) That was one of those occasions on which they should express their opinions, and, although. he had not the slightest doubt that the gentlemen wholad been opposed to him would try to do the best they could, he believed he could have done better. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He did think that the Corporation of this town was not governed eco- nomically—he said that advisedly, straightforwardly, and honestly. He was not deterred by what had taken place for he had had nothing to help him but his own honesty of purpose and the fact that he was about the , largest ratepayer of ttny of the men who sat around that great table behind their backs. Whether he was their I representative or not he would help forward the move- ment for reducing the ratas to what they ought to be— about ss. in the £. Thok men who had ',been elected , against him were no doubt good men, but he was afraid they would be good for nothing. (Laughter.) Howelkr, he was very much obliged to the Mayor and the officials for the very kind and courteous way in which they had received his candidature, and he was also obliged for the kindly way in which he had been met all round. On some future deeasion he would be there (pointing to the Council Chamber) and they might rely upon it that he would make it hot fel.- the Corporation. (Laughter and applause.) If they went wrong he would watch them very carefully. (Applause and laughter.) Mr. H. J. LONOTON, then returned thanks on:behalf of Mr. Percival for.having placed him in that honourable position of the head of the poll. (Mr. Barlow: "where is he"? and laughter. ) It showed that a man independ- ent of party, but who came forward in the true interests of the ratepayers would have his platform supported. (Hear, hear.) For the Ratepayers' Association it had been a glorious day, and it was an augury of victories:to come. (Applause.) Mr. Percival had met with the greatest courtesy at the hancfs of his opponents,,Mr. Barlow and Mr. Marsh, and he was greatly obliged to his supporters for their glpport. (Applause.) The proceedings then ended. MR. BARLOW AND HIS SUPPORTERS, A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. S Barlow was held on Monday evening, in Mr. Nay- lor's Temperance Hall, Howley Quay. There was not a very large attendance. Mr. Rigby was elected to the ch air, and the candidate was also supported on the platform by Mr. W. Diggle. In addressing the meeting, Mr. BARLOW said that he had been charged with being ambitious, and with being condemned by the so-called Ratepayers' Association, who deeply deplored his candidature.' It was owing to himself and Mr. Diggle that that association was formed, but he and Mr. Diggle were independent gentlemen, who did not care for any asso- ciation, political or otherwise, as their wish was to reduce the corporate expenditure, and look after the interests of the ratepayers without any regard to party. In his opinion this question of reducing the rates was of more importance to the people of Warrington than the selec- tion of a Parliamentary representative. Party representation in municipal matters was, he main- tained, the cause of the high rating of the borough. He had been asked how he would fulfil his promise of saving £l,OOO in rates to the borough. Instead of £l,OOO he could save £2,000. (Mr. niggle: That's better.) Mr. Barlow proceeded to show how by cutting down cor- porate salaries he would reduce the rates. Mr. W..

[Mr. Dlt;gle : Give him four.] He had not a word W say aganvt Mr. Chorley, who was a good borough trea- surer, but he thou alit his salary might be reduced fn to £4lO. When working-men's wages were going down, the salaries of these officials should also be re; duped. FREE LECTURES. Sir,—The Warrington Museum and Library Committee did an excellent work last winter when they organised the series of free lectures, and it is to be hoped that they are contemplating something of the same kind for the present winter. The lectures, I believe, were free in a double sense—they were free to the audiences, and they wire freely given by the lecturers. It cannot be denied, therefore, that the lectures were cheap at the money; but still while some of them were allthat could reason- ably be expected, there were others compounded of Itther poor stuff, more fit for the filling—up of the I programme of a Mutual Improvement Society than for the attraction and instruction of popular audiences. Now, I notice that the Widnes Free Library Com- mittee has applied for and secured the sanction of the central authorities to spend Dart of its in- come in the promotion of free lectures. Would it be iafra. dig, for the Warrington Committee to follow this laudable example? lam sure that by the expenditure of an insignificant sum of money they might supplement the best local talent with some outside help, and arrange a series of really good and useful lectures.— Yours, &c., • Warrington, Nov. 3, 1887•
R. S.

MR. WHITHAMS DEPARTURE. Sir,—The meeting reported in your paper to do hon- our to Mr. Henry'Whitham, on his departure to America, is to me sorrowful reading. It is a repetition of the old and shocking story, that of killing the prophets, and then with a flourish of trumpets building and adorning their sepulchres. There was a touch of remorse, I see, in one or two of the speeches at the neglect and indiffer- ence shown to this "honest man, big and compact in virtue," over his long career—estimable, patriotic, and suffering throughout. Warrington should have cher- ished him and honoured him as a true and noble citizen, while he did yeoman's service for it yet note, while practically casting him out, he is asked to continue his generous services to the town by giving its people all the information he can send them about the land of promise to which he has gone—seeking that salvation from semi- starvation here which is afflicting large masses of the people. Mr. Whitham possesses the virtue of magnani- mity; and instead of resenting the " heathen " treat- ment he has received, he will forgive -and show his warmth of heart and love of humanity by doing what he ...can still to serve Warrington.

It so falls out That what we have we prize not to the worth, While we enjoy It; but being lack'd and lost. Why then we rack the value, then we find The virtue that possession would not show us Whilst it was ours.
London, October 31.

THE GAMES AT RUNCORN FAIR: Sir,—With your kind permission, I am desirous, by means of your valuable paper, to draw the attention of the authorities to the evils that are so often permitted on the fair ground. I would like to ask why these itiner- ant swindlers, with their modern methods of gambling, are allowed to make these invasions on the unwary of our town and neighbourhood? Are there not sufficient temptations to the rising generation in the shape of bil- liard rooms, cards, dice, &c., that these utiprincipled bipeds must be allowed to pursue their nefarious means of plunder with such impunity lam a parent, and I write this letter at the solicitude of other parents whose children have been fleeced, time after time, of their sav- ings by these pernicious games that are placed before the eyes of the inexperienced in so tempting a form. I venture to think that if any of our authorities will trouble themselves to watch the proceedings they will agree with me that the games of love in a tub, &c., &c., are most fragrant breaches of the Lottery Act, and, as such, ought to be suppressed. A very few years have passed since the Lottery Act was enforced, and all gam- bling by means of timing was prohibited; but the in- ventive faculties of the fraternity seem to have no limit, for no sooner is one mode blockedthan othersarebrought about which are (all of them) manifestly greater games of cbaiice than turning was. Hoping you will kindly grant space for this letter, I remain, yours, Sm., A PARENT. Runcorn, Nov. 2, 1887.

THE KNIGHTS OF LABOUR. Sir,—Being one of those who believe that the interests of the wage-earners, as opposed to the interests of the aristocratic and plutocratic classes, can best be advanced and secured by strong and vigorous combination, I was particularly pleased to see it mentioned in the news- papers the other day that Mr. Powderly, the head of the Knights of Labour of America, is aboutto visit England. Started about 1869, as the Outcome of a labour move- ment amongst Philadelphia weavers, the Knights of Labour orgarusation has already attained a power and influence in America such. I should think, as no other labour organisation has attained in any other country. It is broader-based than any kindred society that we know of, as not only males but females also are admitted within its ranks; and, in addition to wage-workers, manufacturers, employers, and farmers are allowed to become members, subject, of course, to their willingness to promote the objects of the order, and conform to its regulations. The persons excluded are lawyers, profes- sional gamblers, stockbrokers, and all who make, sell, or derive any part of their support from the sale of intoxi- cating dnnk. For my own part, I sincerely hope that the result "of Mr. Powderly's mission will be the estab- lishment of branches of the order of which he is the head in every centre of population in England. The working people of England would then have at their command an instrument for the improvement of their condition such as they have never had before. ULYSSES.
-- LONGFORD WORKS, &e. Sir,—lt is to be regretted that Alderman Crosfield was not present at the Council meeting when the Sanitary

Committee had on their minutes the order for a cistern— when I raised the question—whether the gentlemen pre- sent at the luncheon stated what was correct or not. If correct, then the cistern was not required, but no one answered the question. If he had been presept, he would have had a good apportunity of stating his views on the work of the Sanitary Committee. If the public are to infer from the statement in the let- ter that the value of the manure is great because of the process, allow me to say it is not correct. The cause of the value is that the ashes, &c. are not mixed with the excreta. As the chemi et at Manchester said, to treat the contents of the pails collected at Warrington was a great deal easier for working than as they were collected in Manchester. The plant at Warrington is the most unsatisfactory one I have seen, either at Rochdale, Manchester, Birming- ham, or Stafford. At Longford the material has to go in three machines ; Birmingham, one only; Stafford, the same as Manchester, uses only one machine; but it is not so complete as Birmingham, which has the most effi- cient plant for working a large quantity. Stafford has a neat plant, which has been,working since 1881. In 1883 they were as far advanced in the manufacture as the I Warrington people are to-day. ' Alderman Crosfield cannot duplicate the plant. If any- thing more is done, it must be at No. 2 Works; and, be- fore I should agree to spending a further sum, I should advocate the Longford works being closed. The ar- rangements of the works is as unsatisfactory as it is pos- sible to be. There are none so defective as the Longford works.—Yours truly, Warrington, Nov. 4, 1887.
FRANCIS DIXON.

THE BISHOP AND THE CURATE. Sir,—No doubt you will be conversant with the case of Mr. Twist, for some time past curate at the Warring- ton Parish Church, who, while heartily snubbed by the Bishop of the diocese, seems to have found much favour in the eyes of the parishioners and, also, be it recorded, in the critical eyes of that somewhat testy individual, the Rector. It is not my desire, sir, to enter into the merits or demerits of the case as it stands; to grumble at the action of the Bishop, or to offer sympathy to Mr. Twist, who, I understand, still remains in the parish. The moral of this case, as it appears to me, points to a disgraceful condition of things in connection with the Established Church itself. A curate' who jumps into the good graces of innumerable friends and gradually be- comes the prop of the Rector in his old age, ministers in the parish for some nine months. When the time comes for him to be duly licensed to the curacy, Bishop Rvle refuses his sanction, to the great astonish- ment of Warrington. A memorial, signed by the officers of the church, and another memorial—a stupendous one—signed by some thousands of the parishioners, both praying the Bishop to re-consider his decision, are of no avail, and there the matter rests. It is presumed that Mr. Twist has, in some way or other, brought this upon him- self, but as yet I have been unable to find a single per- son who knows what his fault has been. Thus, we have one man, supported in his action by the rules of a State-aided Church, obstinately running counter to the wishes of this large number of people, who have to stand by and see a man punished, not knowing what his pun- ishment is for, and not knowing whether or not it is just. Don't you think, sir, that it would be greatly to the advantagea the Church itself, if such fetters of authority as these were thrown off, and her adherents had some voice in a question so important to them as the choice of a spiritual adviser? Many of the people who signed the memorials which did so little good will no doubt think that what has happened forms an argument in favour of
