div.head: MR. BRUNNER AT LIVERPOOL
div.p: MR. BRUNNER AT LIVERPOOL

On Thursday afternoon a luncheon was given at 1 the Junior Reform Club, at which Messrs. J. T. ' Brunner and Philip Stanhope, M.P.'s, were enter- tained as ghests. Mr. A. J. Arnitt Dear presided, there being about a hundred members of the club present. Subsequent to the luncheon, he Chairman intro- duced the ghests, observing that Mr. P. Stanhope, who was member for Wednesbury, had always taken a deep interest in the complicated affairs of Ireland and the policy pursued with that country, and he hoped Mr. Stanhope would be enabled to do the Irish people some good by his study of their affairs. He thought the members might congratu- late Mr.Brunnerupon his narrow escape at Mitchels- town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner seemed rather inclined to laugh at the matter, but he (the chair- man) thought he had really had a narrow escape, and that he had run a considerable risk in going to Mitchelstown. The Chairman went on to speak of Mr. Brunner's splendid majority at the late North- wich election, and of the great and welcome sur- prise it was to the Liberals throughout the country. Mr. Rrunner, who was cordially received, thanked the members for their kindness, an I, in refer...mg to his election, said he had been given great assis- tance by some of the members. who had worked for him during the contest. Vitt iOllB reasms had been erroneously given to account for his success, but he held that the true reason was to be found in the question of liish policy which was at stake. (Ap- plause.) If the members would allow him to ten- der them some advice, he would ask theca to study deeply the affairs of Ireland, and• it they had time he would advise them to make their inquiries in Ireland itself. (Hear, hear.) They must do what they could to bring to an end that Government which had so badly managed Irish affairs, and which was still mismanaging them. (Applause.) It was but a week or so ago that the Government had sought to put into prison the journalists in Ireland who were most beloved by the people; this they attempted under what they called the Press clause of the Coercion Bill, but everybody knew how ludic- rously they had failed. (Applause.) Not long ago they broke up a meeting at which Mr. Stanhope was present; they batoned and shot the people at Mitchelstown in the endeavour to introduce a re- porter to the meeting, and only six day.; after that, to use the words of Mr. Balfour himself, they sub- mitted to the indignity of asking permission from the promoters of a meeting at Bandon to put a re- porter on the platform. (Applause.) They had sent the bravest little girl in Ireland to prison, with the result that she had got two gold watches. (Ap- plause.) The police batoned the people for hours whenever they came together to hear Mr. Blunt. (Shame.) All over the country, wherever men were being sent to prison for opposing the Tory Govern- ment, the people were more determined; and yet Mr. Goschen said that the Crimes Act was quietly doing its work. What the Government had brought about in the last few weeks was a sham and a farce, and not government at all. His advice to them was that in opposing the Tory Government they should protest, protest, and protest again. - (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. Philip Stanhope, M.P., who was well received, also addressed the meeting.

. MEETING AT THE REFORM CLUB. On Thursday evening Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, and the Hon. Philip Stanhope, M.P. for Wednesbury, were the guests of the members of the Liverpool Reform Club at a house dinner given in the club. Mr. Malcolm Gouthrie, the president. occupied the chair. The Chairman, in giving the toast of "The. Liverpool Liberal party," coupledvrith the name of Mr.IT Brunner, M.P., said they had met that night for the purpose of congratulating Mr. grunner on his success at Northwich. He concluded by offering their hearty congratulations to Mr. Brunner, not only for the success which he achieved at Northwicir, but for the important work he had under- taken since his election. (Cheers.) The toast was heartily received. Mr. Brunner, who was received with loud cheers, in responding to the toast, said Mr. Chamberlain had de- scribed his action in condemning the police at Mitchel- stown as an impertinent absurdity. When he read this statement in the newspapers, he asked the Liberal Akio- ciation of Birmingham to give him an invitation to a meeting there. They had not the courage to do so, and he took the liberty of going without an invitation, and he was told that his reception was better than that accorded to Mr. Chamberlain in his own town the night before. Alluding to Mr. Chamberlain's speech at Isling- ton, Mr. Brunner said it seemed to him, as the result of life-long observation, that the most marked character- istic of Toryism was fear of the peopie—(hear, hear, and applause) and never had that fear been so completely shown as in Mr. Chamberlain's speech. The action of the Liberal party in this century had steadily aimed at the reduction of the number of the discontented. In spite of the loss they had suffered they would go on in that work, and he saw with prophetic vision that the day would come when-Citizen Joseph, as the revered and venerable leader of the National party, would be denouncing with great fervour, in the House' of Commons, Mr. Champion, the last discontented man. He did not know what the occasion would be, but it might be that Citizen 670 might be grumbling about the ill-management of the free distribution of orchids at Highbury. (Great laughter.) Mr. Chamberlain had recently said that if once the people of England came to the conclusion that the Liberal party were Home Rulers because they were Liberal, the game of the Liberal Unionist party would be lost. He believed that was so, and he believed that the Home Rule policy that they had now as a united party adopted, was the latest develop- ment of the Liberal principle. The discussion of Home Rule had taught them to open their hearts to the poor and suffering in Ireland, and it was only by studying the condition of Ireland that they had arrived at that point. He had found in Ireland amongst all sections of the people a deep-seated desire that Ireland should be allowed to make a new start. This was exhibited not only

amongst the prominent citizens, but amongst :quiet people, the farming classes, and even amongst the com- mon people one met on the roadside. (Hear, hear). Mr. Davitt lsad pigeon-holed many schemes for the ameliora- tion of the people. Mr. Parnell and Mr. Dillon, both in public and in prilate, had spoken of their desire to pro- mote temperance reform in Ireland, and he heard Mr. [ Parnell say at the close of some interesting conversations he had had with him, with the deepest sincerity, his ardent wish to be the author of a scheme of technical education for Ireland. (Applause.) They did not as a. rule look upon Ireland as a possible country for manu- facturers, but he would like to give the authority of Sir Lyon Playfair, who had pointed 'out that there was no place in Ireland where coal need be as dear as it is in London., that there was no civilised country which had a greater water power area than Ireland, and that there was no spot in Ireland which was more than sixty miles from navigable water. (Hear, bear.) And Sir Lyon Playf air said that he knew no population which was so quick to learn a new trade as the Irish. (Applause.) He had been at a meeting in Ireland at which the most prominent speaker was Mr. O'Brien—(loud cheers)—was it not a significant thing that the name of a felon should be cheered in that room—(renewed cheers)—and he had some interesting conversation afterwards with Mr. Devitt on the subject of Archbishop Walsh's proposal that the landlords and tenants should appoint from amongst themselves representative men, and endeavour to come a satisfactory and friendly conclusion with regard to , the questions at issue between landlords and tenants. Let them believe that the responsibilities so soon to be put upon the shoulders of the Irish people—(hear, hear) —would raise all the good and restrain all the evil passions amongst them. Let them hope that the English, Scotch, and Welsh nations would have before long by their side a fourth nation bound to them by the instincts •of self-preservation, by the friendship produced by con- stant intercourse, and also by the memory of a gracious act of goodwill on their part. (Prolonged applause). Mr. E. X. Muspratt, in proposing "The, House of Com- mon," said, speaking of the Coercion Act, that many of them thought that this action of the Government was not likely to hurt them. He maintained if they allowed this act of injustice in Ireland to take place without re- buke, they would suffer for it in this country. The Tory Government were disposed to suppress freedom of speech and freedom of meetings in this country. Had I, not they begun already in London to suppress meetings [ and make impertinent inquiries with respect to meet- ings. Had not they hinted that if the people of England I did not mend their ways, they would have the same police interference with the liberties of speech and liberties of the Press as they had in Ireland. The Tory party, as they were all no doubt aware, were in- capable of originality. The Liberal party—with all due deference to Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Harlington, he said the jAberal party—met at Nottingham, and laid before the country a programme. No membei of the Government had spoken since that time but that eccen- tric friend of the Government, Lord Randolph Churchill. He had given out a programme alifiost identical with the Liberal programme. They need not, however, think that the Tory Government would agree with this un- authoritative utterance of Lord Randolph Churchill. They must work together, and would find, he was sure, that if another election took place, they would be in a con- siderable majority. , Mr. Stanhope, who was cordially received, responded as a Radical member of the House of Commons.
THE CHARGE AGAINST A WAR- RINGTON ENGINEER.

At the County Quarter Sessions. at Liveryool, on I Wednesday, James Proctor Jones, described as an engineer, crf Warrington, was charged before Lord Derby and other magistrates. with having, at Wid- nes, on the 23rd December, 1:46, obtained the sum of £7 by false pretences from William Leatherbarrow, with in- tent to defraud. Mr. Shand, barrister, appeared to pro- secute, and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington) appeared for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Shand said that he thought he was justi- fied in offering no evidence against the defendant. At the time the proceedings were instituted, Mr. Leatherbar- row, the_prosecutorl was under the impression that a lathe had been obtained, or a certain sum of money had been obtained on a statement made by the defendant as to the amount he had paid for the lathe which he pur- chased at Bury. The amount he stated he paid was £22 10s. The lathe was bought at an auction, and it was subsequently found out by Leatherbarrow that only £lO had been paid for it, and they believed ifben he stated that lie had paid £22 lOs that he had cibtalned a further sum of money from them by false pretences. It subsequently turned out that the defendant purchased, on the same day, in Manchester, some tools and shafting I which made the difference between the £lO and the £22 10s. 'He (counsel), having seen the receipts, felt it would be a hard thing if any proceedings In a criminal court were taken against Jones. Therefore, he did not think he should be Justified in offering evidence against him.—Mr. Mulholland said his client was a respectable manufacturer, and a charge of this character had never before been preferred against him. He had now demon- strated the absolute truth of the statement he made at the time he got the money, and had satisfied Mr. Shand. They had demonstrated that they did pay the actual sum of money which they represented was paid at the time. The case would never have come before the court that day if the application he made to the court below had been acceded to, namely, to adjourn the case to en- able them to bring a man from Manchester who sold the supplementary articles. The magistrates, in the exercise of their discretion, on the advice of their clerk, refused the application, and the case had now come before his lordship. He hoped it would be admitted that defendant left the court without a stain upon his hitherto unstained character.—Lord Derby (to the jury) : Under the ircum- stances, and as no evidence is offered by the prosecution, you are, of course, bound to acquit the def;endant.—De- fendant was then discharged, his Lordship remarking that there was no imputation on his character.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 5, 1887.

death rate from all causes was equal to 17.4. Since the last meeting an epidemic of whooping Cough had bioken out at Padgate, Woolston, Fearnhead, Houghton, and Croft of a severe type; and although two cases only had yet proved fatal, there were many more seriously ill. The disease had been produced by atmospheric influences over which the Authority had no control. SURVEYOR'S REPORT,-Mr. Owen reported that during i the month the following drawings were submitted and 1 might be approved: Messrs. 4. Bridge and R. Allen, 41 cottages, Glazebrook -; Mr. W. Barlow, additions tq house, Winwick-road. The borough surveyor (MO Longdin) haying called his (Mr. Owen's) attention to the fact that there was both a Price-street inside the borough as well as one immediately outside the borough, and hav- ing asked whetherctilat Authority should object to the name of the street being changed to Selby-street, with whic'h street it. is in direct continuation, he replied that he thought no objection would be made if the Corpora- ' tion would provide filename plate and have the numbers lon the doors altered. Mr. Longdin had since written to say that he thought his committee would provide the new name plate and have the numbers altered.—The report of the Surveyor was adopted, and it was agreed that the street referred to should be re-named Selby-street. This was the principal business. FRODSHAM.

ASSAULT AT KINGSLEY.—At Edclisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Robert Briscoe, was chargedt with as- saulting Thomas Harvey at Kingsley on the 28th October.—Prosecutor said on the date in question the defendant came to him and began insulting him, and afterwards struck him several times.—Fined 5s and costs. _ _

CONDBIIT.—On Friday and Saturday evenings a con- cert was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, by the scholars of the Union Church Sunday School, Frodsham Bridge, assisted by the choir, the pieces rendered being those contain&l in the cantata entitled The Indian Summer." Most of the choruses and songs were given fairly well, but the piece which calls for special mention was the duet "Sweet Sister Fay," by two young girls, who took the character of fairies, and this was deser- vee'y encored each evening. The accompanist was Mrs. T. A. Rigby, of Overton. The platform had been pret- tily decorated. From the ceiling Chinese lanterns were suspended, these adding greatly to the beauty of the scene. CoNcincr AT KINGSLEY.—On Friday evening a miscel- laneous concert was held in the National Schoolroom. The artistes included the following :—Miss Harrison, piano- forte solo; Mr. Turnbull, • The Yeoman's wedding song" and "The warrior bold " ; Miss Hall, "The broken pitcher" and "Let me dream again," both of which elicited encores; Mr. T. Cole, humorous readings, "Woman's rights " ; Mr. G. Clarke' Manchester, "Father O'Flynn " and "The agricultural Irish girl " ; Messrs. TurnbuU, Jones, and Holland (trio), Hark to! the rolling drum " ; Mx. C. H. Ilibbert, pianoforte solo; Mr. C. E. Hitihen, "It's just as ,well to take things in a quietsorV of way." ,The comic portioli of the programme was well sustained by Dr. Bubidge, of Liverpool, and Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington. Mr. 0. H. Hibbert, Frodsham, was the accompanist. The proceeds of the entertainment will go towards defray- mg the expenses in connectionwith the Kingsley Cricket Club. AN EXTRAORDINARY FREAK AT HRLSBY At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Spruce and George Spruce were charged by Henry Res- wick with having on the 28th October, at Flelsby, dam- aged a window and lock, to the amount of 18s. the property of the Marquis of Cholmondeley.—Mr. Flet- cher, who prosecuted, said it seemed to have been an, unaccountable freak on the part of the two defendants. It appeared they were passing the house when a spirit of ;mischief seemed to have seized them, and they forced their way into the house. The defendants had admitted the offence, and had been to the agent to ask him to for- give them. All that the agent wanted was to make an example of these men so as to prevent a recurrence of the mischief.—Cornelius Lovell deposed that he heard the defendants say there was a cat in the house, and it had been there for a fortnight without anything to eat., One of the defendants broke the lock and went into the house.—Jonathan Lydiatt said there were 16 squares of glass broken. ‘A sovereign would cover all the damage, —Each defendant Was ordered to pay 9s. damages, 55. penalty, and 12s. costs.

PRESENTATION.—Od Wednesday evening Mr Johri Nevrburn, who has left Lynlin for Widnes,was presented with an illuminated address and a purse of gold. Mr Newburn for many years had been connected with the Wesleyan body at Lvmm, and the presentation took place at a well-attended meeting held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. _ _

BAPTIF IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Wednesday even- 1 jug a tea and meeting was held in connection with this Society in honour of a visitor, the Rev. Mr. Jenkins, of Bucklow Hill. After the tea addresses were given by Mr. Brundritt, the president, the Rev. Mr. Jenkins, and Mr. Davies, and some impromptu speaking also took place. A paper was read by Mr. Hurstfield on the sub- ject—" Is a man's conscience guided by what he be- Reyes." LICMM MUTTAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. The chair was occupied by Mr. Richard Dutton. An interesting lecture on South Africa '; was given by the Rev. H. C. Wilkinson, a part of the globe of whirh he has a personal knowledge. To- wards the close of the lecture, a number of rings and various other specimens of native workmanship, snuff box, embroidered belts, &c. were handed round for in- spection. A cordial vote Of thanks was accorded the lecturer.

MASONIC FESTIVAL—The anniversary known as the Festival of St. John of the "Earl of Chester" Lodge, No. 1,565, was held in the Masonic Hall, Church-green, on Thursday. for the purpose of installing the W.M. for the ensuing year, and appointing and investing the officers. Brother Fairhurst was installed by Brother John Lewis, installing master. The W.M. afterwards proceeded to invest his officers for the ensuing year, assisted by Brother E. G. Parker, P.M., 1,565, The following officers were invested :--Bro. W. Hooper, J.W.M. ; Brother W. H. Pugh, S.W. ; Brother W. War- burton, J.W. ; Brother E. G. Parker, P.M., P.P.G.P. Treasurer; Brother J. H. Evans, P.M., P.P.G.S.B. Secre- tary; Brother John Marsh, S.D. ; Brother E. Morris, LB.; Brother W. Collins, J.(}.; Brother Edward Rouse, organist; Brothers John Taylor, J. W. Bruise, T. Swain, W. Millar, stewards. THE CHURCH TOWER RESTORATION.—A vestry meet- 1 ing was held on Saturday afternoon in the vestry of Lvrrim Church, the rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest, pre- siiling. Among those present were Mr. William Bailey. I Dr. Brabazon, Dr. Fox, the Rev. E. H. Lomax, and Messrs. T. P. Norris, T. Addenbrooke, J. Rhomer, Wil- liam Brazendale, A. Swanwick, T. Ardern, and Certain Jones. The object of the meeting was to take into con- sideration the question of rebuilding or restoring the Parish Church tower. A paper was read on the subject by Mr. William Bailey, one of the churchwardens. It was proposed to form a committee, consisting of the Rector, the churchwardens, and a few of the influential gentlemen in the district, to consider the question. Ow- ing to the architect, Mr. Crowther. of Manchester, not being able to attend through ill health, a resolution was proposed and carriedthat the meeting be adjourned for a fortnight, so as to enable the arehitect to be present. It was also decided at the meeting that the bells and the clock, together with the two belfry floors, be taken down forthwith.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT
COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held yesterday morning at the Workhouse. Mr. J. Rylands presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Greening, Ratcliffe, W. Darbyshire, BEd- harry, J. Pennington. J. Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (valuer). Vs-Luau's RittionT.—Mr. Owvs reported that he had made the following valuations,: The General Elliott Inn, Croft, gross £4B 10s, rateable DU 10s. Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton's premises in Buttermarket-street, War- rington: These premises were to a Urge extent closed for alterations from the beginning' of April to the begin- ning of October. For the half -ear he was of opinion that an assessment should be ma4e on Messrs. Skelton of ' gross £25, rateable £2l ss. and tTiat for the new occupa- tion the assessment should be divided thus: Mr. Charles , Roylanee, gross £5O, rateable £42 10s.; Messrs. Skelton, gross £25, rateable £2l ss. Messrs. Litton and Co., Bank Quay, gross £320, rateable £24.—The report was adopted. DEPRECIATION or PROPERTY.—Mr. Greening appealed against the assessment of the house in which he resides in Bewsey-road. The reason for the appal, he said, was that the property had very much depreciated in value of late years. He had offered the house for sale, with a view to going to reside elsewhere, and the only amount he could get bid for it, after he had gone to a great deal of expense, was £450. The reason alleged for this low bid was that the neighbourhood in which the house was was becoming so terribly smoky that nobody could live in it. WIS own experience on that point was a very vivid one, for when the wind was in the east all the property in that part of 13ewsey-road was enveloped in one mass of smoke.—A MEMBER: From the brick kilns P—Mr. Grisrisma : No; from Dallam Forge. It was getting so very bad that he wanted to clear out, but he felt that if hesold the property for £450, he would be giving some hundreds of pounds away. He also mentioned that the houses around about were assessed at a lower rate than his own.—The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to see that while Mr. Greening stiff lived in the house, his health had not deteriorated. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—ln the course of some conversation, Mr. GREENING remarked that if he had to sell his house for £450, he thought the Dallam Forge people should make up the difference, and there were other property owners in the locality thought the same. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN : I shall he glad if you can persuade them to do it. (Laughter.)—lt was tlien agreed that Mr. Owen be asked to re-value Mr. Greening's house. This was the principal business.
WARRINGTON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. There were present Messrs. W. Derbyshire, presiding; J. Green- ing. T. Jolley, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Grange, Pennington, Swinton, Kilshall, J. Rvlands; S. Sut- ton (clerk). Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector). TEE PENEETH DRAINAGE.—A later was read from the Local Government Board in which they stated that they had received a report from their inspector, Mr. Terry, after the inquiry recently heti:thy him, with reference to the application of the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Warrington Union for sanction to borrow £3BO for works of sewerage for the township of Penketh. The Local Government Board also inquired whether the consent of the Board of Trade had now been obtained to the execu- tion of such of the works as would be below high water mark.—The ASSISTANT CLERIC said he had written to Mr. I. C. Routledge, chairman of the Penketh Parochial 11 Committee, with regard to the above communication, and Mr. Routledge replied that he did not see for what object the committee had to go to the Board of Trade for sanction, as they did not propose to interfere with either the foreshore brook or any land below 21 feet tide line.—lt was decided that Mr. Routledge's reply should be forwarded to the Local Government Board. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Selahton reported that the births for the month ending October 31st were, males 19, females 13; deaths, males 1.3, females?. The

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

A monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day evening, Mr. H. Cameron presiding. There were also present Messrs. Dutton, Rogers, Harrison, Brazen- dale, Appleton, Forster, Thoma,son, and Ridgway (clerk). Mu. HENSITALL'S CLAM. On the reading of the minutes of previous Board meetings a discussion arose in regard to a resolution that Mr. Henshall should be paid the sum of £2O as compensation for damage done at his premises by reason of the bursting of a sewer, and the consequent collapse of a wall, for which he held the Board retponsible. A proposition was made by Mr. Brazendale to the effect thatthe minutes be passed, and an amend- ment was made by' Mr. Rogers to the effect that they be confirmed with the exception of the resolution referred to.—Mr. Roger's said that it waa no use to again raise a discussion on the matter. He objected to the resolu- den on principle, because the value of the wall that fell was only £B. He was Sure that it was not right to pay twenty pounds of the rate- payers' 'Money for something that had only cost £B'. The members were sent to that Board to look after the interests of the ratepayers, and he thought he was doing that by taking the course he had done.—Mr. Appleton. who seconded the amendment, said that if the Board paid the £2O it would be a scandal.—Mr. Rogers said that he was entering a personal protest against money being spent in the manner proposed; he had no other means of protesting than this.—The Chairman said that, to a certain extent, he sympathised with the proposi- tion of Mr. Rogers, and he agreed entirely with the argu- ment Mr. Rogers had used. But there were certain facts in connection with the question which he should like to mention. If the Board declined to confirm the resolution, and Consequently refused to pay the money, the only course open to Mr. Henshall would be to take the case into court, and sue the Board for the amount. If the Board refused to pay, it seemed very much like stultify- ing their action of a fortnight ago, and would tell against the Board, which would be very much like a house divided against itself. The members would not be unani- mous. There would be M:. Bratendale prepared to go into the witness box to make a statement, and Mr. Brpzendate was a member of the Board; and a builder and sewer constructor. He (Mr. Brazendale) might not know very much about the manner of conducting , public business, but the judge would . probably consider that he was entitled to some consideration, and would give him credit for knowing something about his own business. This, he was afraid, would tell very much against the Board. Mr. Brazendale told them that he had known for three years that this thing was going on.—Mr. Brazendale: I never said such a thing.—The Chairman said that it had been proved indisputably that the sewer, which was the main artery into which the

drain passed, was laid below the level, instead of having a proper flow, and Mr. Brazendale took the money of the Board for doing that work. There were a good many difficulties in the way, and he should be disposed to recommend Mr. Rogers to withdraw the resolution, rather than carry it forward.—Mr. Rogers: I am quite willing to adopt your advice.—Mr. Appleton :—By no means would I pay a penny. It is a scandal to the Board to pay double the amount that it cost.—Mr. Dutton: Will not you be content with the protest P—Mr. Appleton: I I would fight it out.—Mr. Rogers said it was perfecitiv clear that the main sewer was wrong, which influenced' him in withdrawing his resolution.—Mr. Appleton: If it is to be paid it should be by those who put the sewer down wrong.—Finally the minutes were passed, and the subject dropped. THE SEWAGE FARM.-It was reported that the willow crop was fairly good, and had now attained its growth for the season. It was resolved that the crop be sold. A QuEsnow OF RESPONSIBILITY.-Mr. Rogers said that there was one matter which he thought it was requisite should be made clear for the,information of the Board. Would the Law Clerk inform the Board as to the liabi- lity of the contractor for the sewers regarding his con- tracts, whether the contractor was liable for any errors or mistakes.—The Law Clerk said that it would take some time to go through the agreemept, and it was sug- gested that an answer to the question be given at the next meeting.—Mr. Rogers then said that if the con- tract showed that the contractor was liable he shou'd give notice of motion that the law clerk be instructed to sue the contractor for the nioney that had to be paid to Mr. Henshall.—The subject then dropped, it being un- derstood that Mr. Rogers would make the proposition he mentioned in the event of it being indicated that the contractor was liable. This concluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. Since this time last week the Stock Exchange has been, for the most part, in a state of suspended animation. With the close of the settlement on Friday many mem- bers left town in view of Tuesday being a holiday, con- sequently from Friday to Wednesday there was simply nothing to record in the way of transaction. American Tails have had a spurt, but it was not of long duration, and there is not much support from the outside public in these stocks. Mexican rails have ex- perienced some rapid variation during the week, and the mercurial nature of these stocks are such as to warn off Vie careful investor. • - On the other hand a company under the title of the Hydroleine Company, Limited, has been formed to ex- tend the manufacture and sale of hydroleine sanitary soap powder which has been carried on by F. J. Harrison and Co., at London and Leicester. The promoters in this case are content to guarantee a dividend of 7 per cent. Such a marked contrast between the dividends of two trading companies is worthy of notice, especially when the one which is content with a 7 per cent dividend appears to be a flourishing concern, while the one with the vague probabilities estimates of 20 to 35 is to acquire certain patents which may. not be worth the paper on which they are written. i• Latest advice s seem to encourage the belief of a fur- ther rise in South African Diamond Companies' shares, and also in some of the better class of gold mining shares. Since last week* rise of 3s. per share has taken place in Pinos Altos Bullion shares, and it is not too much to ex- pect a still further rise. In the company world there is still little or nothing to report. Condy's White Lead, with the bait of 20 to 35 per cent, dividend, is still being dangled before the public. From the Consolidated Esmeralda Mines information has been received of a field of 40oz. of gold to the ton.
I LATEST NEWS.

A serious outbreak of m‘easles has occurred at West Houghton and Deane, near Bolton. Lord Hartington will address a meeting of his consti- tuents on the afternoon of Saturday, December 3rd. A fire occurred during Thursday night in the stables of the Great Northern Railway station, Derby, by which five horses were suffocated.
At the end of the first week after the settlement of the Bolton strike there are still about a thousand men idle, the various firms being unable as yet to find them work.
Employers having conceded a substantial advance in wages, the strike in the South Staffordshire nail trade, which las, lasted two months, has practically termi- nated.

MA. COX, M.P., TO BE ARRESTED.-A special court, under the Crimes Act, assembled at Ennis, to hear the case against Mr. Cox, M.P., who is charged with speak- ing at a proclaimed National League meeting. Mr. Cox, however, did not put in an appearance, and after hear- ing formal evidence the court issued a warrant for the hon. gentleman's arrest. _ . .

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A BOTANIST.—At Leicester, on Friday morning, an elderly man named John Warren, described as a botanist, was charged with causing the death of Mary Wesley, wife of a local confectioner in a large way of business, by an unlawful operation at his house on October 13th. The prisoner was remanded pending an inquest and post-mortem examination. ANOTHER BATCH OF IRISH PROSECUTIONS. We learn that it has been decided by the Irish authorities to pro- secute all those who took part in the midnight meeting at Woodford, at which the Lord Lieutenant's proclama- tion was burned, excepting those who are already being prosecuted or imprisoned for other offences. These will, therefore, be Mr. James Rowlands, M.P. for East Fins- bury; Mr. T. P. Gill, M.P., Mr. David Sheehy, M.P., and Mr. Dennehy, secretary to the Lord Mayor of Dublin. DYNAMITE PLOT IN AMERICA. A New York telegram of Friday's date says :—Chief Justice Waite, of the Supreme Court, Washington, re- ceived on Thursday evening by the local mail a paper box resembling a valentine card-box, marked "Beauties of Tennyson. He unsuspectingly opened it and found an infernal machine, composed of a syphon tube, percus- sion caps, giant powder, an unknown liquid, and other , materials. The caps were connected with the cover by a wire. It is supposed the failure to explode was due to ' the wire being disorganised by the stamping process at ' the Post Office. This is supposed to be an Anarchist plot, and the police are striving to find the perpetrators.

MILL BROW MILITARY BAND, RUNCORN. The members of this band and a few friends had' a very pleasant re-union at Wilson's Hotel, on Thursday night. The band is composed principally of self-taught players who, during the past few years, have attained a position in the county that not only the members, but the town, has reason to be proud of. If, however, for.no other, reason they deserve the thanks and well wishes of the towns- people for the courage with which they instituted the open air concert in the summer months and the consistency with which the concerts were continued. The band are fortunate in having so excellent a conductor in Mr. Outhwaite, who has an admirable coadjutor in Mr. , R. Pierpoint. The proceedings commenced on Thursday with a dinner, capitally served by Mr. and Mrs Jackson. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. R. Frith, the president, and Mr. S. Pope was in the vice chair. Amongst those present were Captain Le Couteur, Messrs. Outhwaite, R. Pierpoint, J. J. Speakman, T. Riley, W. Lea, C. Cliffe, C. Beswick, George Thomas, W. Matthews, Moorfield, .icc‘. After the table was cleared, the Chairman proposed the toast of "The Queen and the Royal Family," which was duly honoured. The Chairman then gave a brief i address, n which he alluded in congratulatory terms to the uphill fight the band had gone through to attain their present position in the musical world. Wherever the Mill Brow Band went, it was now treated with the greatest respect and confidence. The progress made was extraordinary and was ant evidence of the great care with which they, had been trained by their leaders, Messrs. Outhwaite, Pierpoint, and Thomas. (Applause.)—Mr. Moorfield, in proposing the health of the president and vice-presidents, gave a very interesting I account of the origin of the band in connection with Mill Brow Sunday . School. The toast was drunk with enthusiasm' and Mr. Frith and Mr. Page responded. The Vice-chairman pro- posed success to the band in happy terms, alluding in complimentary language to Mr. Outhwaite and Mr. Thomas, whose names were associated with the toast. —ln responding, Mr. Thomas said the band had given 30 open-air concerts in Iluncorn, and in those concerts they had performed 183 pieces of music. (Applause.) They had also given open-air con- certs in St. Helens, Birkenhead Park.—Mr. Outh- waite, who had an enthusiastic reception, also responded in an appropriate manner.—Mr. R. Pierpoint gave the toast of the friends and supporters of the band in happy style.—Captain Le Couteur and Mr. T. Riley, whose names were connected with the toast, responded. "The Press," proposed by Mr. C, Cliff e, was responded to by Mr. Whalley on behalf of this journal. The proceedings were enlivened by vocal melody, songs being given by Messrs. Outhwaite, Pierpoint, Ince, and Chamberlain. Mr. James Cawley gave a recitation, and Mr. T. Riley a Lancashire reading. Mr. Wilson Blackledge, humourist, of St. Helens, contributed much to the amusement of the company by his clever and versatile character sketches and songs. ,0„

div.head: MAYORAL BANQUET AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: MAYORAL BANQUET AT ST. HELENS.
£lO
£lO
£lO

The Assembly-room of the Town ilail had a pic- turesque appearance on Wednesday evening, when his Worship the Mayor (Alderman David Gamble, C. 8.) commemo-ated the completion of the fifth year of his mayoralty by entertaining the princi- pal gentlemen of the neighbourhood. The guests included aldermen, Councillors, and borough officials, representatives of the clergy ,of different denomina- tions, &c. The Assembly-roma was prettily and taste- fully bedecked. On the platform was a charming arrangement of rare exotibs and plants from the conservatories at Windlehurst, Haresfinch, and Victoria Park; and these formed a pleasant contrast with the paintings and other decorations of the hall. As the guests arrived they were received by his Worship in the Coun- cil Chamber; after which they were, conducted to the Assembly-room, where the banquet was served. Mr. James Bennett, of the Royal Raven Hotel, had been en- trusted with the arrangements, and their carrying out gave every satisfaction. His Worship the Mayor pre- sided, and he was supported on the right hand by the Rev. Canon Eyre, M.A., vicar of St. Helens, and on the left by Mr. T. Brawls (town clerk). The toast list included "The Queen," "The Prince and Princess of Wales, and the rest of the Royal Family," "The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese, and other Ministers of I religion, "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," "The Magistrates," "The Chairmen of Committees," "The Town and Trade of St. Helens," and "The Vice. Presidents," The proceedings were tastefully interspersed with the efficient rendering of a musical programme by a glee party selected from the Liverpool Vocal Union by Mr. George Barton. The following gentlemen received invitations :—Alder- men D. M'Kechme (mayor-elect), James Harrison, J.P.„ T. Cook, J.P., James M'Bryde, J.P., J. C. Gambit, J.P.; Councillors R. Pilkington, J.P., C.
